(Mother Rosa)

The New Edition from the original of the Work of the Servant of God Anna Rosa Gattorno is now given for reprinting: TRIALS AND CONSOLATIONS OF THE SOUL ON THE PATH OF PERFECTION.

A FOUNDRESS RECOUNTS HER EXPERIENCE OF FAITH IN A BEAUTIFUL SYMBOLIC POEM, edited by the Most Reverend Father Làzaro Iriarte, Capuchin Franciscan, Professor of Spirituality at the Pontifical Athenaeum Antonianum in Rome.

Gattorno is one of the most beautiful and generous souls of the second half of the last century. Born in Genova on 14 October 1831 into a family of good social standing and deep religious sentiment, she grew up, educated especially by her mother, in a sound moral and Christian upbringing. At 21 she was given in marriage to Gerolamo Custo, by whom she had three children. Left a widow at 27, she devoted her whole self to works of charity toward the sick, the poor and the suffering, guided by the ecclesiastical authorities. In 1866, at 35, the Holy Father Pius the Ninth, in a private audience, traced out her life: she was to put into effect the inspiration received from the Lord to found a new Congregation. The Pope lays it upon her: it is the will of God. From then on the Servant of God takes flight, with absolute dedication to the will of the Lord and with a generous commitment of her whole person to accomplishing «the Work of God» entrusted to her by the explicit will of the Holy Father Pius the Ninth.

From Piacenza, cradle of the new Congregation, the «Work of God» spread rapidly, with a flowering of souls who, following the example of the Mother, dedicated their lives to their own sanctification and to helping their neighbor toward sanctification, in the service of the humblest and most generous charity. With the blessing of God, the Work stretched out its branches luxuriantly, guided with a sure hand by the Servant of God under the impulse of the Spirit, the «Governor»; and at the end of her life, at 69, on 6 May 1900, Rosa Gattorno could offer to the Lord, and to Holy Mother Church, her Work, the fruit of love and sacrifice, rich in well over 4,000 Sisters spread across 369 Communities.

This book, TRIALS AND CONSOLATIONS OF THE SOUL ON THE PATH OF PERFECTION, written by the Servant of God, is meant, more than as an intimate spiritual experience, precisely to describe the development of the WORK.

On this point Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, for many years Gattorno’s Spiritual Director, expresses himself thus in the Roman Process: «In my recent reading of the printed text, I ascertained that it was nothing other than the true history of the foundation and development of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which the Servant of God had artfully wished to conceal under figures, allegories and the like, so that the mission she had had in this matter of the foundation should not come to be known. I was able to perceive with certainty what I have said, because I was perfectly acquainted with the facts related in that book in allegorical form. These facts were moreover confirmed to me by the Religious, who either took part in them or in some other way had knowledge of them» (Roman Process, 1st Witness, session V, foll. 54/56).

Princess Emilia di Fitalia, friend and benefactress of Gattorno, who had the two previous editions printed at her own expense, for her part testifies: «The Servant of God published a book with the title given to it by Cardinal Guarino, which I believe is the following: “Consolations and trials etc.”. This book consisted of allegories and symbols referring to the History of the Institute and to her own, since it was connected with its foundation» (Ibidem). This book caused the Servant of God a great many troubles and sorrows. The Holy Office, which examined it, ordered in 1898 that it be withdrawn («reponatur»). In 1982, ten years ago, I had occasion to occupy myself with Rosa Gattorno through a Votum requested of me by the Congregation for the Saints on the «state of normality or otherwise of the Servant of God Anna Rosa Gattorno, with express indication of its nature and degree in relation to any impairment of the personality», precisely in connection with the book «Trials and consolations etc.».

From careful study of her writings and life, from the testimonies of those who were close to her, and from all the internal and external criteria, I had to conclude that the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno was a person rich in high qualities, with perfect self-mastery, remarkable psychological balance, great practical abilities and, as her vast correspondence especially shows, a constant exercise of charity in understanding, directing and comforting others.

Gattorno’s book is nothing other than the description of «her path»: not only of her path toward perfection and intimate union with God, but the «path» of the whole «Work of God» entrusted to her by the explicit will of the Representative of Jesus on earth, the Pope.

This «path» she travels not trusting in human and earthly helps, but trusting in God alone, closely united to her Crucified One. «My Crucified One», she exclaims fully thirty times at the beginning of her book, and from the Crucified One she draws the strength and energy for her hard journey. He sustains her in illness, guides her on the right path, enlightens her, warms her, teaches her to suffer, defends her from every danger, adorns her with his grace, fills her with sweetness. «My Crucified One», she exclaims, «subdues the humanity, gives vigor, energy and strength to the spirit which, victorious, rules over all the powers, and so well do they remain subject» (Trials and Consolations, p. 49 f.).

The road to be traveled is hard, wearisome and very long; often she is weighed down by sorrow, weariness and loneliness, by the snares of the evil one and of the false shepherds who, under various guises, seek to turn her aside from her way; but the Crucified One sustains her and gives her the strength to walk through so many dangers.

«My Crucified One filled me with joy and with heavenly discourses taught me to travel that way, assuring me that it was He who had traced it out for me alone, and that He had never found anyone [?] to lead along this path, so sorrowful, yet so pleasing to Him» (Trials and Consolations, p. 59).

The work the Lord has entrusted to her is immense, and she, guided always by her Crucified One, hastens generously from one field of the Lord to another. She goes in search of good «laborers», whom she places in the field, defends and protects from every snare and from the false shepherds, so that the field of God may be cleared of weeds, flourishing and luxuriant, rich in fruitful harvests of every good for the salvation of souls and the glory of God.

The Work of God is a ship sailing amid a thousand dangers, on which she raises the flag bearing the words «To Suffer–To Love», which she steers to the feet of the Vicar of Christ, the Pope, and which with the passing of the years makes great progress.

«After a great struggle, my little ship came out much more beautiful, and it was elegant: it had its gilded rudder, a most beautiful compass; no longer the beggarly sail, but an elegant flag that bore written: To Suffer and Love» (Ibidem, pp. 323-324).

«The ship was making great progress, the sea was favorable to it, it ran under full sail. Small as it had been, it had become a very large ship and well equipped, with strong armor to be able to defend itself from the enemy. It goes on gaining ground, it conquers many cities and towns. The enemy roars and every so often manages to butt at it: but nothing! it drives them back, for it is bound with iron. Ever victorious. It enters great ports and flies the flag: To Suffer and Love!» (Ibid., p. 326 f.).

Rosa Gattorno throws herself with all her enthusiasm into the path the Lord has traced for her, a path among thorns, sufferings and contradictions, among snares and dangers; but she goes securely because the Lord tells her: «It is I who guide your steps». Into the field of God she advances serene and victorious, upheld always by the Crucified One and by the certainty of doing the will of her Lord.

«In the Work of the Lord», she writes, «philosophy, theology and calculation have no place: all empty chairs!… A poor slave am I, I never studied and I understand nothing: one thing only have I sought to study and to perfect myself in this subject: the will of God! To seek to do it blindly, in perfect abandonment in him, like a slave faithful to her beloved Master» (Ibid., p. 324).

In this absolute fidelity to the Lord, even to immolation, lies the whole greatness and fruitfulness of Mother Gattorno.

Father Làzaro Iriarte, emeritus Professor of Spirituality at the Pontifical Athenaeum «Antonianum» in Rome, who has already given us a valuable book, «The Spiritual Physiognomy of Rosa Gattorno», presents to us today, with great love and great competence, the new edition of the book written by Mother Gattorno over four years (from 1890 to 1894), which she called «History», but which was later printed under the title given to it by Cardinal Guarino, Archbishop of Messina: «Trials and Consolations of the Soul on the Path of Perfection, described by a Servant of God».

The distinguished Professor Father Iriarte, with fine intuition, has given the Work an agile, slender form, so that it may be read with pleasure and without fatigue. He has grouped the narratives into fifteen chapters, bringing out the central element in each of them, and then highlighting in the subtitles the various aspects of the spiritual experience. In this Father Iriarte has followed the indications already expressed by Canon A. Pennino of Palermo to the Princess di Fitalia, in the letter he wrote to her in 1897, before the work was printed: «Another modification I judge indispensable is to divide in some fashion the various events, which are all described and narrated in the work in a single breath. The reading would certainly prove more pleasant and easy if it offered some pause from time to time».

May this book, written with such richness of images, with such spiritual unction, but above all with great love for God and for souls, and very often under the direct impulse of the Lord, as the Servant of God herself testified, bring light and comfort to all the Daughters of Saint Anne who model their lives on the teachings and examples of the Mother Foundress, and to all souls who wish to place themselves faithfully at the service of the Lord, following their own vocation.

FR. PAOLINO ZAVARELLA, OFM.

Biographical note.

Born in Genova on 14 October 1831, she married in 1852. Left a widow in 1858 with three small children, the last of whom died shortly after the death of her husband, she gave herself fully to the interior life and to works of charity, living in great austerity and penance, favored with extraordinary mystical graces.

In 1866 she began at Piacenza the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which spread rapidly in Italy, in South America and in Eritrea. Faithful to her mission of To Love and to Suffer, she was purified by atrocious interior and exterior sufferings, by temptations and unceasing struggles.

As foundress, she was an incomparable guide of her spiritual daughters, tireless in work, in visiting the houses, and in communicating with the communities by means of thousands of letters.

She died in Rome on 6 May 1900 with a great reputation for holiness.

Among the qualities that characterize the rich personality of Rosa Gattorno, her ease in expressing her ideas and feelings with the pen stands out. She did not possess a high level of culture, yet she succeeded in explaining herself with an abundance of concepts and affections, in an altogether peculiar way. She also had the ability to vary her language and style according to the nature and the recipients of the writing. All her pages, however, are a living testimony to her exceptional spiritual experience.

Among her other writings, special attention is due to her book published during her lifetime under the title Trials and Consolations, both for the originality of its content and literary form, and for the events, historically uncertain, which brought upon the Servant of God the bitterness, borne by her with fortitude of soul, of seeing it withdrawn from circulation; and which later obstructed the normal course of the process of canonization.

Since at the root of those events there lay an incorrect interpretation of the purpose and content of the book, one cannot, in presenting this new edition, refrain from offering a kind of key to its reading, so as to grasp, along the fascinating sequence of so many images and so many symbolically described episodes, the guiding thread and the message the author wished to transmit. In this way the Daughters of Saint Anne especially will be able to feel the vibrations of the volcanic heart of their Mother in these pages which, after a hundred years, still convey all the anxiety with which she lived the birth and development of the Work of God.

From whom did the initiative to write the book come?

On the origin of Trials and Consolations we have the exceptional testimony of Cardinal Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte in his deposition at the Informative Process of Rome: «I had urged the Servant of God to write the history of her foundation; but she, out of her constant fear of coming out of her shadow, seemed to me not very disposed to consent. Then pressure was added from other persons, among them the Princess di Fitalia, a great admirer of the Servant of God and benefactress of her Institute. The Servant of God thus found herself obliged to yield. She set to work…». 1.

The initiative, therefore, came from Don Gennaro di Belmonte himself, who since 1887 had taken on the spiritual direction of Mother Rosa. And it is possible that the idea arose in him on reading the Memoirs of the Servant of God, those intimate pages whose secret she guarded so jealously.

M. Rosa «was not very disposed to consent», not only because of her reluctance to reveal the secrets of God, but also, it seems, because she found it difficult to describe the history of the Work of God. Indeed, an impersonal account of the facts and events of the Institute risked being reduced to a chronicle without life and without message; she could not separate the reality, objectively lived, from her own involvement in the design of God; the history of the Institute could not but be that of her own spiritual itinerary, with its alternation of days of light and of darkness, of interior and exterior struggles. And how could it be a true history without bringing in the persons, concretely the representatives of the hierarchy, who had played a role, positive or negative, in the journey of the Work of God?

Among the «pressures» that were added there were certainly those of the Daughters of Saint Anne, with the support of the Princess di Fitalia, Emilia Labecka, who was bound to the Servant of God by a very close friendship, and indeed venerated her as a true spiritual mother. Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini testified in the Roman Process: «Here is the history of this book: we sisters and also the Princess di Fitalia often pressed the Servant of God to write something about the Institute, about its origins, etc., because we were persuaded that this would greatly benefit the history of the Institute for those who would come after.

She, however, always declined, saying she was averse to writing, and that it would be of no use».

The same witness also informs us that the Foundress, having found a writing by her first secretary, Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino, who died in 1875, containing much information on the origins of the Institute, gave it to the flames because it spoke much about her. 2.

The Princess’s version, in her deposition at the Process, concerning the initiative to write the book might seem to contradict the two preceding ones. In 1894, when she was already busy having the notebooks of the original text printed, the noblewoman wrote to Cardinal Guarino, Archbishop of Messina: «During my stay in northern Italy I had occasion to approach a soul dear to the Lord, who enjoys very great graces. For the good of my soul she gave me to read certain books which she was compelled to write, driven by a supernatural force which she could not resist». 3.

In that case, the initiative would be wholly that of the Servant of God, or rather of her beloved Good, who drove her irresistibly to write. I think the two versions can be reconciled if we bear in mind the way in which Mother Rosa experienced the action of God when she wrote, and also when she entrusted herself to God in her exhortations. 4.

In the month of May 1890 she wrote in the Memoirs: «I cannot understand why, with absolute command, (my Good) imposes on me to write certain things that I do not even understand: I only feel that I write as if under dictation. Why this? What are they to serve for? I cannot keep silent that I feel a certain consolation in writing, although while writing I taste nothing; only on rereading them they seem to me to comfort and lift up; above all they teach much and lead to conformity with the will of God, a perfect abandonment in Him. It seems the creature finds much difficulty in it. Oh my sweet Love! and what greater delight can there be than that of doing your will?» (Mem. 11.3, p. 22 f.).

She set to work and let the pen move under the guidance of her Crucified One. In the letter of 20 May 1893 to the Princess di Fitalia, written shortly after the meeting at which she gave her the manuscripts to read, she promised not to make mention of her in the new notebook of the History she had begun, and added: «It seems this is what Jesus will want; and certainly my pen would have written badly. But what am I saying! Is it perhaps I? Oh! a donkey of this sort, who knows nothing! Oh! forgive, and consider that only from this ass of mine can such things be heard».

Emilia took on the task of bringing those writings to light, perhaps at the request of Monsignor Granito di Belmonte who, precisely at that time, was being assigned to Paris as attaché to the nunciature there. Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini continues in her reliable deposition: «At last the Servant of God, after our repeated entreaties and those of the Princess di Fitalia, brought herself to write something in the night hours. Then, when the said Princess came to Rome, most eager to have her writing, the Servant of God handed her the part that was ready and, when the Princess returned to Rome, on giving back to the Servant of God the part she had already read, she received the following part. After reading various parts, the Princess showed herself enthusiastic and begged the Servant of God to let her have it printed, saying she would see to the expenses…»

Mother Rosa gave her consent «after a little hesitation», but on condition of first securing ecclesiastical approval. Emilia then went to Florence with the notebooks already written, to have them examined by Canon Gonfalonieri, theological reviser of the diocesan curia. On 13 October 1893 the Servant of God wrote to her from Naples: «I learn from your letter that yesterday you would have arrived in Rome… Oh! how good you are to take so much trouble for me, showing those messes of books! Tell me frankly what he found: that they are dreadful, eh? I am anxious to hear».

The Princess noted in the margin: «The Mother wishes to know the Theologian’s opinion of the book».

The Florentine theologian, far from finding them «dreadful», gave in writing his «complete approval», encouraging the Princess to print them; so she wrote in the aforesaid letter to Cardinal Guarino, and later confirmed in her deposition at the Process. 5.

Date of composition.

Mother Rosa herself recorded the date on which she began what she calls the History, on the first page of the autograph: Year 1890 December 28.

She set to work with passion, interweaving figures and allegories with incredible creativity. On 14 August 1891 she was able to inform Don Gennaro in a letter written from Sampierdarena: «The fourth book is finished, I have begun the fifth. Again another manner is coming, but I do not know where and how to steal the time».

At the beginning of the sixth notebook she wrote: 1 December 91; at the beginning of the seventh: 20 January 1892. In little more than a year she had filled 834 pages.

Then she had to slow the pace. On 2 April 1892 she noted in the Memoirs: «Today, Saint Francis of Paola…, I made many promises, above all that of taking up again the writing of those fancies (so I call them); but it seems my Master desires it, and from this very evening I am beginning to do so» (Mem. 12.1, p. 47 f.).

The eighth notebook was begun on 14 November 1892 and finished on 10 December 1893. Judging from a letter of hers of 20 May 1893, it was while she was writing this notebook that she received the visit of the Princess di Fitalia and gave her the manuscripts to read.

The ninth notebook, the last, bears at the beginning the date of 9 March 1894.

A total of 1,289 manuscript pages. One must take into account the time she had to devote to journeys, to dealing with correspondence, to her spiritual notes, to external relations, to the formation of the religious, as well as to her long vigils of prayer; and one must add the permanent swelling of her arm, which prevented her from writing for long.

The original manuscript.

Fortunately the autograph that served for the Palermo edition has been preserved. It consists of nine notebooks, in the last of which only 19 pages are written. The handwriting is quick, but firm and perfectly legible. Thanks to the very faithful typewritten copy made by the sisters assigned to the Historical Archive of the Congregation, it becomes easy to compare the original autograph with the 1897 edition, since the manuscript pages and the printed pages are indicated in the margins.

On reading, one has the impression of a draft made in haste, taking advantage of odd moments of time, giving form to the pleasant or unpleasant memories she was reliving in her mind; this is confirmed for us by a testimony gathered by the Princess di Fitalia: «Sr. Teresa Sorrentino told me she had watched the Servant of God secretly while she was writing her book Consolations of a Soul at night, and had noticed that she wrote currenti calamo, as if under dictation». 6.

This last observation corresponds to what Mother Rosa herself confided in the notebook of her Memoirs on 2 July 1891: «For a long time now, everything I do I must do with such repugnance as I have never felt, and when I understand that my God so wills, I set to work at once. But I labor greatly, as in writing certain things of which, in truth, I must say I do not understand what I am writing, and to know what I have written I must reread it, and then stop: is it I who wrote this? what can my God want from these writings of his, or rather, dictations?

I greatly fear it is a very great illusion, but I keep repeating to myself: the ugly monster can make no gain from it. My duty? in everything, by the mercy of God, I manage well and I neglect nothing: time is left over, and I feel a strong urging with an interior voice: Go, write! — Yes, I answer, my Good, I go!

It is curious: I take the pen in hand, and I know nothing of what I shall write, I have not a thought, but always swiftly I feel it suggested to me, so that I have no time to form the words properly, so swift is what I must write. I do not know how to explain what passes in me; it is truly strange: when I am to finish, the spring stops, and I halt. I draw much good from it for myself, and I feel that, in reading it, the good lies wholly in the most holy will of God» (Mem. 11.3, pp. 34-37).

On 20 September of the same year she again observed in what way Jesus made her write things she had never understood (Mem. 11.3, p. 62 f.).

Whoever takes on the task of transcribing the manuscript realizes how true is what the author affirms: that, under the swift prompting of what she must write, she has no time to form the words properly. Indeed, there is no lack of incomplete sentences, omissions of certain particles, tangled hyperbaton; it is not always possible to understand what she meant to say. She constantly uses che in place of in cui, dove, etc. Both the conjunction e and the pleonastic particle ne, with verbs, are inserted superfluously. The pronominal forms gli, le, li are used improperly. Words of altered phonetics are frequent, that is, written as she pronounced them, for example: abberinto for labirinto, baglia for balia, mustro for mostro, tuono for tono, streppare for estirpare, d’ogni tanto for ogni tanto. Nor are some regionalisms and a few Gallicisms lacking.

The style, free from all affectation, is lively and colorful, wholly personal; the vocabulary varied and, in general, appropriate.

The text, continuous in a single stretch from beginning to end, has no divisions or titles.

The Palermo edition.

It was the Princess di Fitalia, after the favorable judgment of Canon Gonfalonieri, who proposed to the Servant of God the publication of the manuscripts. In January 1894 Mother Rosa expressed her perplexity on the matter and the answer she received from her soul-friend, Sr. Anna del Salvatore: «The first time she was asked whether the books I had written should be submitted for approval in Rome, she said: No! Then, now that I wanted to burn them, she answered: The Mother will never act against the will of God. Therefore I shall not burn them» (Mem., 14).

The Princess, on returning to Sicily, busied herself with the publication of the history. Toward the end of March 1894 she wrote to Cardinal Giuseppe Guarino, Archbishop of Messina, under secrecy, begging him, as one «versed in mystical science», to give his judgment on the manuscripts of a person whose name she concealed from him, since she wished to have them printed, convinced as she was that reading them could do great good to souls, just as it had done to her. She informed him of the approval given in writing by the Florentine theologian; for the moment she sent him the first two notebooks, and concluded: «Your authoritative approval would be the only one that would make me decide to spread these books». 7.

The Cardinal replied on 22 April, after having read «with all deliberation» the manuscripts he had received. Not only did he find them «free from theological errors», but very useful: «They describe, under images and figures, very well the trials and consolations of chosen souls tending toward Christian perfection and the extraordinary life…»

Here is the origin of a hermeneutical perspective that would have further consequences for the vicissitudes of the book, and of the title he himself suggested: Trials and Consolations of the Soul on the Path of Perfection.

He judged it «a book which may prove most useful to privileged persons and to pious persons». And he added: «I do not deny, however, that some polishing of the wording would not be inappropriate; but I think it better that the simplicity of the author be left, save for a few words in the revision of the printing».

He allowed himself only to add, on folio 2 of notebook 1, a brief theological clarification to the very beautiful passage in which Mother Rosa expresses the mystical experience of God’s dominion over the will, to prevent anyone from thinking that freedom is lost under the action of divine grace.

The Princess replied full of gratitude. Shortly afterwards she had the other notebooks sent to him; the Cardinal took them with him to his summer villa to examine them, as appears from two letters of his, one of 3 and the other of 8 July 1894. Emilia then asked that he himself take charge of «retouching» the manuscripts in view of printing; but the prelate excused himself, alleging his many occupations and his infirm health. The noblewoman insisted again on 25 July, in her own name and in the name of the author, «our slave of God». 8.

Mother Rosa, whose identity her spiritual daughter sought to conceal under this name, once she had handed over her last notebook, took no further care of the rest, leaving everything in the hands of the Princess and of the superior of the house in Palermo, Sr. Anna Maria Teresa Patti (Sorrentino), to whom she wrote on 25 September 1894: «I see you have sent the books (to Cardinal Guarino). Thank you; and if it is the will of God, it will turn out as you say; if not, they will give them to the flames: is that not so? For this I pray: since it is his affair, he will see to it». 9.

But the Cardinal persisted in his refusal. At the end of September he returned the notebooks to the superior. On 4 October he wrote to her, presenting the difficulty of finding in Messina someone who could worthily carry out the work of revising the original, and proposed that she herself take on such a task together with Sr. Serafina; «a cleaning up, preserving the style of a woman such as the author is», would suffice. And he pointed her to Canon Pennino, ecclesiastical reviser of Palermo, a good theologian and a trustworthy man, should some less orthodox expression have slipped through. He also hinted at other reasons which made it absolutely inadvisable to print the book in Messina. 10.

On 13 March 1895 the Princess was able to inform Mother Rosa that the notebooks were already in press, with the title suggested by Cardinal Guarino, to which the author herself had given her assent, but in this form: Continual Trials and Passing Consolations of Souls who Walk the Way of Holiness, written by a Servant of God. 11. The more sober form proposed by the Cardinal was adopted.

Of this first edition, which appeared in 1895, the Princess di Fitalia says in her deposition at the Process: «I had it printed in Palermo, in two or three parts, with the permission of the local curia». 12. She herself personally followed the correction of the proofs, while the revision of the text was the responsibility of Canon Pennino. On 29 November 1895 the printing of the second volume was still in progress, but with the hope of finishing soon. 13.

The book was published in two volumes by the Printing and Binding House «Boccone del Povero»; on the reverse of the title page was written: «With the approval of Ecclesiastical Authority». It contained only the first seven notebooks of the manuscript, that is, those the Princess had taken with her from Rome; the last two are missing. The historical archive of the Daughters of Saint Anne possesses the only copy that could be found of the five hundred printed. Probably the edition was withdrawn by the Princess herself in favor of a new, complete and more careful edition in a single volume; in fact, not even the sisters were given copies. 14. The fact is that, already at the beginning of 1897, Emilia was working on the re-edition. The Servant of God, as appears from a letter of hers of 7 January of the same year, would have wished, at the request of her devoted spiritual daughter, to take up the continuation of the narrative, but could not find the time.

In November 1897 the Princess obtained from Canon Pennino a letter of approval which, on the advice of the Servant of God (letter of 22 November 1897), she wished to be printed at the beginning of the volume, after that of Cardinal Guarino, who had died on 22 September of the same year. The Canon gave a fully positive judgment, but specified: «Not everything in this work is suited to everyone. It is not a treatise on Christian perfection, but rather the particular history of a soul called with extraordinary graces to promote in the field of the Church great works for the glory of God and the good of the faithful».

A good judge of the content, he had perceived the true purpose of the book, namely to describe the history of the foundation. Very probably he knew who the author was; and he suggested that she herself «explain with small marginal notes the meaning of the various scenes and anecdotes of which the whole work is woven». He considered it indispensable, in order to avoid the monotony of a text without any division, that it be distributed into days grouping the successive vicissitudes. 15.

The text was in fact reproduced as in the [first?] edition, without notes or divisions. The addition of explanatory notes would have contradicted the choice of a deliberately allegorical literary genre, adopted precisely to avoid the identification of facts and persons. The second proposal was very sound, but where was one to find someone to take on such a far from easy task?

At the beginning of 1898 the book was in circulation.

From what has been said, the criterion followed in the edition can be understood. The work of Canon Pennino and of the collaborating sisters, carried out, it seems, as the printer set the proofs, consisted in improving the wording of the original, above all with regard to punctuation and spelling, and then attending to grammatical sense. The aim [was] to make the reading easier. In [substance] [?] it can be said that the original was respected to the utmost; the edition can be considered fundamentally faithful, despite the freedom with which the sentences [?] were handled, to the detriment of the spontaneity [?] and of certain linguistic peculiarities of M. Rosa. Out of a regard for prudence, well justified, some pages of the eighth notebook of the original were omitted, in which a high ecclesiastical personage could have been identified, involved in an internal affair of the Institute that was very painful for the Foundress.

The intervention of the Holy Office.

Where did the denunciation of the book to the Holy See come from? The Princess di Fitalia, in her deposition, said: «I believe the enemies of the Servant of God made use of the first edition to cause her trouble. This book was then forbidden by the Superiors…»

According to information supplied to us by Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini, it was Count Barbiellini, son-in-law of the Servant of God, who denounced the first edition to the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, in revenge for the revocation, well motivated, of the power of attorney over the property of the Institute, signed by the Foundress on 5 March 1896. But there is no doubt about the source of the initial denunciation: it was a religious of an important congregation who transmitted a copy of the first edition to the Commissary of the Holy Office, with a letter in which he begged him to examine the book, which he judged «tedious, nothing more», but which might prove harmful to the 3,000 sisters spread throughout the world.

The book was submitted to the examination of the consultors of the Holy Office; their judgment having been negative, in the session of 28 March 1898 it was decided that the book should be condemned, but without publication of the condemnation, that an apostolic visitation of the Institute should be made and, on that occasion, all copies should be withdrawn. This decision was confirmed by Leo the Thirteenth on 26 April 1898. On the following day, 27 April, the decree was formalized: «Opusculum damnandum et damnatio non publicanda prò externis, sed tantum prò Instituto. Et ad mentem.

The mind is that an Apostolic Visitation be deputed to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne and, on that occasion, the copies of the said book be withdrawn». 16.

It is evident that this is not a condemnation motivated by the doctrinal or moral content of the book, which would have led to its inclusion in the index of forbidden books, but rather a disciplinary or formative measure, concerning only the interior of the Institute, whose execution was linked to the apostolic visitation; this lay within the competence of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, and was entrusted to the Benedictine abbot Dom Domenico Serafini. It began on 28 July 1898.

When Mother Rosa was presented by the visitor with a copy of the book, she acknowledged that she was the author, but attributed to the Princess di Fitalia the initiative of the publication. And, seeing that the copy he had brought was of the first edition, she herself placed in the hands of Dom Serafini that of 1897. Then, «still alarmed and shaken», she said to him: «Do you assure me there is nothing against the faith?» And the visitor: «No, against the faith there is absolutely nothing, only some exaggeration. But withdraw all the copies given to the sisters, not those given to outsiders».

That same day Mother Rosa had letters written to all the communities with the order to withdraw the book and, to the provincial of Palermo, to make the undistributed copies disappear. 17.

The visitor informed the Holy Office of the existence of the new edition, of which it seems he sent a copy; he pointed out that Mother Gattorno was convinced it had appeared with the approval of Cardinal Guarino and of Canon Pennino (director of the Boccone del Povero).

In the session of 3 August 1898 this communication was reported, and it was decided: the unsold copies were to be destroyed, the sold ones withdrawn, the Cardinal of Palermo «moneatur opportune», as also the Princess and the director of the Boccone del Povero.

The reply of Cardinal Celesia, Archbishop of Palermo, was not long in coming. On 17 August he wrote to Cardinal Parocchi, Vicar of His Holiness: he gave the history of the publication of the book; he denied that any approval had been requested of the curia of Palermo; and he reported that the provincial superior had been «most obedient» in handing over the copies of the book. In the session of the Holy Office of 31 August 1898 the reply of the same Archbishop was reported, in which he specified that he had not approved the book because «the approval of Cardinal Guarino and Canon Pennino seemed to him sufficient».

In another letter of 28 November the Cardinal of Palermo informed Cardinal Parocchi that he had received 200 copies of the book from the provincial; the Princess di Fitalia, just back from a journey abroad, had let him know that she had distributed copies in Italy, France, Germany and Poland, and had sent them also to America; and she had added: «After a fresh examination the book will shine again like a ray of the sun, ever pure but not easy for the vulgar human eye to gaze upon».

The order of the Holy Office was carried out with such docility, despite the resistance of some communities to being deprived of the book, that it has been possible to trace only three copies: one was found in Bolivia, another in the archive of the Princes di Fitalia in Palermo, and the third at the General Curia of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Even today it is not easy to determine what were the causes of so drastic a measure, aimed at removing the book from the hands of the sisters. Some clue may be offered by the answer given by Father Alberto Lepidi, OP, Master of the Sacred Palaces, when the Princess di Fitalia asked him, a short time after the prohibition: «How is it that this book, which has done so much good to my soul, must be withdrawn from circulation?» He answered: «The sun too does much good, but not everyone can bear it. To certain sisters too, not sufficiently balanced, it could do harm, because they might not understand it». 18.

And here Sr. Anna Camilla Valentini comes to our aid once again with her recollections: «When the Servant of God told us that no one would ever understand anything, we told her that we understood — and I in fact understood everything — and she would then answer us:

— You, yes, will understand something, because you are close to me. For the rest, if it can do you good, thank God for it, and I am very glad. Certainly, for the sisters who have not been close to the Servant of God, that book is somewhat obscure, because she speaks under symbols». 19.

Mother Rosa never showed displeasure at what had happened, not even in her confidences with the Princess di Fitalia. She used to say: «That book is Jesus’s, and Jesus will see to it». She foretold, however, to the same confidante: «This book will one day be read with fruit, because it is not I who wrote it»20.

When, in 1912, it was thought to promote the cause of beatification of the Servant of God, Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, foreseeing, with others, that that condemnation could create difficulties for the conduct of the processes, gave the appropriate explanations to the competent authority, in the hope that the measure would be revoked; and he obtained from Pius the Tenth permission to have the book read by some religious, in order to find confirmation of his conviction that the decision of the Holy Office was due to an erroneous reading of the content, an error caused in part by the title itself. In the enigmatic narrative a heap of pseudo-mystical fancies had been seen, whereas in reality «it was nothing other than the true history of the foundation and development of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, which the Servant of God had artfully wished to conceal under figures, allegories and the like, so that the mission she had had in this matter of the foundation should not come to be known». The Cardinal made himself guarantor of such an interpretation, since «he was perfectly acquainted with the facts related in the book in allegorical form»; and he had been confirmed in it after a careful examination carried out, with the aforesaid pontifical authorization, in collaboration with two of the sisters best informed about the events of the Institute: Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega and Sr. Anna Celsa Speranza, both intimate collaborators of the Foundress and later, in succession, superiors general of the Institute21.

Unfortunately the appeals made by the eminent Cardinal and by others, that the judgment of the Holy Office be reviewed, produced no result; the cardinals, in the session of 28 May 1913, ratified the decision of 27 April 1898, as we have seen.

The Informative Processes were carried out with all regularity, and on 30 March 1927 their opening was celebrated at what was then the Congregation of Rites.

But when, in 1932, the nulla osta was requested of the Congregation of the Holy Office, the answer was a Dilata, which paralyzed the course of the Cause.

Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, then Dean of the College of Cardinals, on 10 July 1933 submitted a statement to the Promoter General of the Faith, Monsignor Salvatore Natucci, explaining the origin, the content and the circumstances that had led to the intervention of the Holy Office. In 1936 he turned to Pius the Eleventh to obtain the removal of the impediment to the continuation of the Cause. The Pope asked for the opinion of the Promoter of the Faith, who gave it entirely favorable on 27 January 1937, after having officially requested a study from Father Stefano Ignudi, Conventual Friar Minor, on the edition and on the original of the book. The Cardinal died, almost a centenarian, in 1948, without succeeding in his purpose. In 1960 the postulator of the Cause, Don Giulio Bianchini, Salesian, made a new attempt, but the Holy Office replied by maintaining the dilata.

This time the negative judgment of the consultors was motivated by the disparagement of the shepherds that could be discerned in the pages of the book.

Finally the new Postulator, Father Antonio Cairoli, OFM, made a long report on the volume in question, demonstrating the error of interpretation that had motivated the measure of the Holy Office, while at the same time highlighting the ascetical, theological and ecclesial values that constantly emerge among the allegorical images, the struggles and the victories described. 22. And on 20 January 1978 he turned to the Congregation for the Causes of Saints asking it to intervene with the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith to learn the reasons for the dilata. This time the success was complete.

On 3 April 1979 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (formerly the Holy Office) granted the nulla osta, but still leaving pending a doubt about the «state of normality or otherwise» of the author of the book.

The Congregation for the Causes of Saints consequently entrusted to Father Paolino Zavarella OFM a medical-psychological study of Rosa Gattorno. His votum definitively dispelled every reservation23.

Why the choice of the metaphorical genre?

Rosa Gattorno’s culture is typically a culture of the symbol, to which the language of mystics in general refers, by virtue of the need they have to overcome the limits of human expression by symbolizing concepts that are experienced rather than mentally elaborated. 24.

Her exceptional facility for allegorizing and expressing her thoughts and feelings in figurative terms is apparent on every page of her intimate Memoirs. This does not mean that she moves in an unreal world of comfortable fantasy; in her letters the Foundress shows herself concrete, realistic, objective, and still more so in her instructions to the sisters. She knew how to face reality with courage and good sense even in the most difficult situations.

But the literary genre in composing the history of the Institute was chosen by her deliberately. She did not feel able to draw up a purely chronological account in which she would confine herself to the role of chronicler, making facts and characters file past as on a stage. She had lived everything intensely, and it continued to live in the memory of her heart. How could she put herself offstage in describing her own vicissitudes and those of her fellow sisters? And how could she speak of herself, turning the history into an autobiography, she who was so convinced that she was a mere instrument of God, a «donkey» incapable of any good?

Worse still had she been obliged to mention concrete persons, many of them well known, in whom she had found valuable collaborators and benefactors, but also tenacious opponents. She was not born to adopt feigned positions, gilding facts and conduct.

Finally, it was a question of the Work of God, and this could not be reduced to a succession of earthly events, without taking into account that God, the supreme Good, is the one who directs history and takes care of his flock.

The metaphorical covering offers her the advantage of being able to be honest with herself in her assessments of persons and in her way of tracing the ways of God in events. And it allows her to relive, emotionally too, the hard moments and the happy ones, making them present, and to project herself also into the future.

She therefore relied on her fertile inventiveness, placed at the service of that higher impulse which dictated to her the singular «fancies», as she herself called them.

Everything unfolds under the general allegory of an anxious pilgrimage, beginning from her own conversion, ever in search of the supreme Good, along a road traced out for her, now clear, now uncertain and confused, through valleys and mountains, forests, precipices, amid frequent dangers and temptations, snares of false shepherds, threats of infernal monsters that try to turn her aside from the road… At other times it is a voyage on a stormy sea at the helm of the ship entrusted to her… an endless journey, which she is bound to travel without ever stopping, day and night, because her presence is required in so many fields to be cultivated with her «workers».

The peculiar metaphorical terminology that fills the pages of the book can be grouped around the following concepts:

— way, road, path;

— woods, forests, plains, valleys, mountains, rivers, springs, streams;

— sea, shore, ship, helmsman, commander, lighthouse, port;

— cliffs, rocks, walls, precipices, abysses, caverns;

— serpents, dragons, beasts, wild beasts, monsters, wolves, lions, north winds [?], giants;

— night, dark, darkness;

— the luminous cloud, the voice, a friendly dog, mystical dreams, protecting angels and saints, friendly souls;

— fields, farmhouses, farmsteads, sheep, flocks;

— cultivators, workers (the sisters), overseers (the superiors), shepherds (ecclesiastics), hermits;

— peasant men and peasant women, little old men, little old women;

— churches, castles.

The Palermitan Canon Pennino, as we have seen, would have liked the author herself, for the 1897 edition, to explain in brief notes the meaning of the metaphorical narratives. We can imagine what Mother Rosa’s answer would have been had such a task been asked of her.

Later, when Cardinal Granito di Belmonte tried to have the censure of the Holy Office lifted, he made, together with the two collaborators mentioned, a serious effort to identify the facts and persons alluded to under the various images. Although all three were well acquainted with the life of Mother Rosa, with the development of the Institute and with the problems that arose, truth to tell the result was very meagre. In almost all of the 75 metaphors examined, page by page, they had to content themselves with noting: «we do not know», «perhaps she alludes…», «she seems to wish to allude…», «it is probably a question of»… It is observed that from the sixth notebook of the manuscript onwards, that is, in the manuscripts of 1892 and 1893, the allusions become more verifiable, partly because they concern things the Servant of God is living at the present moment. 25.

In conclusion, it is risky to claim to make a historical reading of the book on the basis of an interpretation of its symbolic devices, all the more so since the author does not even follow a chronological sequence of episodes. These, like the metaphors, are grouped and interwoven, often by simple association, according to the creativity of the moment. They are not invented facts, as in a novel, but facts worked over and lived while she writes.

An attempt at an outline of the content.

The second, more acceptable, proposal of Canon Pennino was «to divide the narration into days, grouping some events in the first, then others in the second day, and so on». But not even this aid to readers was introduced in the Palermo edition. It would have been a relatively easy task had the Servant of God set herself an organic plan to follow in her notebooks; but this way of working did not enter into her habits.

Nevertheless such an effort was necessary if the book was to reach today’s readers. A careful examination of the whole book makes it possible to discover a certain succession of connected facts, which could offer a track for the distribution of the text into «days», or sections, or chapters, with suitable internal subdivisions. And this is the service we have wished to offer readers in preparing this edition.

We have grouped the narratives, as can be seen in the Index, into fifteen chapters, seeking to capture in their titles some central element that gives a certain unity to the individual sections; the internal subtitles then bring out concepts or expressions of a more evangelical content.

The spiritual constants of Rosa Gattorno.

In Mother Rosa we can distinguish three entirely different literary genres: that of the Letters, that of the Memoirs and that of Trials and Consolations; but all three have as their common denominator the unmistakable imprint of her spirituality. In our book we find it expressed not in figurative language, but in precise and natural terms.

1. Cause, center and goal of the whole pilgrimage: the dear Crucified One. That cry — my Crucified One! — underlined and followed by the exclamation mark in the autograph, makes the first pages vibrate; it is He who changes suffering into sweetness. When, overwhelmed by sorrow for the insults she has suffered, she laments, the Crucified One, as his only answer, shows her his breast. She finds it sweet to climb the road of Calvary laden with the cross, with Jesus, at his invitation: «Take up your cross and walk!». And one day, finding herself in an exhausting tribulation, she hears the voice well known to her: «Only from the Cross does one learn to love!».

2. The Eucharist, source of vigor and consolation.

In her continual journeying, she often regains strength and the will to fight from the Eucharistic food, for which she sighs lovingly.

3. The pairing Love–Suffering. These are the two inseparable poles in the mission of Mother Rosa. In the midst of the sufferings and harshness of the way, the «sweetnesses of the Beloved» are not lacking. But when, lost in the middle of a dreadful path, she asks: «Where am I, my Crucified One?», she receives the answer: «Whoever loves asks nothing». Her great torment is the thought of having lost her Good, of being unworthy of his love. And she needs to feel herself confirmed in divine Love: «Love, for you are loved!». In the midst of hard exile, she sometimes sees herself as if transported into a paradise where «everything speaks of love». Another day, kneeling on the ground, with her forehead upon a stone, she prays: «From your mercy, my God, I want love! I am exhausted, but I desire nothing but love!» And the Voice answers: «It is not the time for sweetness, but for sufferings. Carry yourself along this way!». The most inspired pages, however, are those in which she describes the voyage of the little ship with the flag: To Suffer–Love. It is with her suffering, with her blood, that she will have to level the great mountain and transform it into a fertile garden. To a «worker» who confesses to her that she has served God until then «without loving him», she teaches: «Oh no! he wants to be loved, and more than work he seeks love».

4. The guiding thread: the will of God. On this theme one could gather a fine anthology from the pages of the book, beginning with the description, of great mystical exactness, of the moment in which God nails the will, repaying it with his own, which Cardinal Guarino felt obliged to clarify. Every so often she feels tormented by the thought: «Will it be the will of God?». Beautiful is the dialogue with an old man on the necessity of denying one’s own will and always seeking the will of God. In another lively dialogue with a Shepherd, who wanted to make her reason in human terms, she gave this answer: «I have no other science than the will of my Lord».

5. Faith and total trust in God. She calls faith «my anchor». She is sure of God’s assistance, although she often feels abandoned. And she takes courage again when she hears the biblical expression said to her: «Fear not: I am with thee!». She experiences the support of the saints and angels, intermediaries of God’s providence, in a special way of the sovereign Virgin Mary, of Saint Joseph, of Saint Michael the Archangel, of Saint Francis of Assisi, of Saint Francis of Paola. In uncertainties, often caused by the insidious proposals of false guides, her spirit seeks the gift of discernment, entrusting itself to the light that comes from on high; she hears within herself the anonymous Voice, which she recognizes by the instinct of faith, regains her peace and walks securely.

6. The sense of the Church. It may be said that this is the other guiding thread of the whole book. Mother Rosa is conscious that the Work of God was born in the Church and for the Church, which is the vast field of God; it is the «great ship» buffeted by storms, while the Institute is the «little ship», which she must bring «to the feet of the Vicar». She suffers for the sufferings of the Church and wishes «to offer herself as a victim to obtain the triumph of the Bride of Christ».

7. The evangelical virtues. Three Christian virtues above all stand out: fortitude, humility, poverty.

8. Harmony with creation. Exceptionally endowed with poetic sensitivity, and pervaded by the spirit of the Poor Man of Assisi, she opens herself to the beauties and the message of creatures. The whole book is almost a poem unfolding in the midst of nature. She feels her own states of soul as if mirrored in the mountains, the meadows, the streams, the plants, the little birds…

9. The discernment of faith among so many deceptive roads.

Rosa Gattorno is convinced, from her own experience too, that «the life of man is hard toil» (Job 7:1), a constant struggle between good and evil; that in the kingdom of God, for whose growth one labors, it is difficult to distinguish the good wheat from the tares; that a true instinct of faith is needed to find, among so many confused roads, often so alluring and specious, the one that leads us to Him who is the true Way: the supreme Good. Here is what we may call the philosophy of the poem Trials and Consolations: a panoramic view of the history of salvation, into which are woven both the personal travail of her spirit, amid alternations of light and darkness, of consolation and aridity, and the arduous task of the foundress committed, day and night, to protecting the «workers» of the Work of God entrusted to her against so many false guides, and to making of them courageous cultivators of the fields of the Lord. It may be said that in every episode this philosophy, or rather theology of history, is symbolized.

The repellent shadow of the evil one.

Whoever reads the pages of Trials and Consolations has the impression of an epic struggle against adversaries of every kind, following one upon another in the form of serpents, monsters, lions, false shepherds… Certainly, they alternate with worthy protectors, benefactors, excellent shepherds and cultivators; but it must be acknowledged that there is a predominance of gloomy scenes, of frightening situations that follow one after another with so many snares and terrors, as though the forces of evil were always placing the interests of God in the world in the balance.

By temperament, Rosa Gattorno was already inclined to look at human reality from a rather negative perspective; she herself acknowledged having this tendency to «see black», a kind of «wicked instinct of always seeing evil». Add to this her strong apprehensiveness, a soul prone to fear and anxiety. But it must also be borne in mind that persons who give themselves fully to promoting the honor of God and spreading good, with the awareness of being instruments of divine action, easily discover the forces of resistance, indeed the wiles of the evil one, in every difficulty that arises and in every disagreement of other persons with their own way of seeing the interests of God. 26.

However that may be, the Servant of God was sincere with herself; as has been said, we have here precisely the principal reason why she opted for the metaphorical literary form. She told things as she remembered them in her heart, whether the memory was lovable or painful, leaving to the Master of the field to judge, on the day of truth, «the quality of each one’s work» (1 Cor 3:13).

Criteria adopted in this edition.

1st. The title of the old edition, TRIALS AND CONSOLATIONS OF THE SOUL ON THE PATH OF PERFECTION, has been kept; although it is not the most appropriate to the purpose and content of the book, it has become almost inseparable from it. The added subtitle serves to specify the true nature of the work.

2nd. The text, entirely uniform in the original and in the Palermo edition, has been divided into fifteen «days» or chapters, which group the various sequences of episodes, distinguished by means of subtitles taken from the content. All this to make reading easier and to bring out better the relevance of Mother Rosa’s message.

3rd. In the dialogues, so frequent and so lively, the system used in novel-type publications has been chosen, that is, a new line with a dash.

4th. The transcription has been made directly from the original, updating punctuation and spelling. As far as possible Mother Rosa’s personal wording has been respected, with her peculiar hyperbaton, her dialect expressions, etc. As has been said above, Mother Rosa writes as she speaks, with a free pen, often leaving the sentence broken off, changing the subject, and passing in the use of verbs from past to present, and vice versa. She often leaves out particles and adverbs, and at other times adds them where they are not needed. Nor are phonetic alterations of some words lacking.

It has therefore been necessary to complete the sentences with clearly missing elements, placing them in parentheses when they are of some importance, to modify the word somewhat when the sense is not clear, and to suppress pleonastic particles that would make the reading obscure.

5th. The footnotes aim to clarify certain expressions and spiritual concepts, as well as to illustrate the most salient themes with references to the spirituality of the Servant of God, as attested in the Memoirs and the letters. As a general rule it has been preferred not to put forward any interpretation of the metaphors, except in certain very evident cases.

6th. Certain omissions noted in the Palermo edition — probably made at the indication of the Servant of God herself — out of regard for some personage whose identification would have been easy for readers, have been respected. The suppressed passages are indicated in notes in chapters 13 and 14.

Letter of Cardinal Giuseppe Guarino, Archbishop of Messina, to the Princess di Fitalia.

My blessed daughter in J. C.

In the very grievous sorrow that has deeply oppressed my soul at the death of my angelic friend, more than a brother, Cardinal Dusmet, Archbishop of Catania, the goodness of God has let me find comfort in reading the manuscript notebooks you sent me, which I return to you this very day.

In these most bitter days I have not been able to attend to anything else. I have read them with care and they are free of theological errors; indeed, under images and figures they describe very well the trials and the consolations of chosen souls tending toward Christian perfection and the extraordinary life. With exact gradation one sees without difficulty the progress of the soul on the way of perfection by means of sufferings, penances and resignation, and of avoiding curiosity and the faults that in the first steps were a hindrance.

One sees the loving Providence with which God guides souls until they attain the maturity of divine Love, which proves very useful to readers, who will certainly gain confidence in God.

There is nothing exaggerated in it; indeed, whoever has experience of such souls sees very well that everything conforms to the facts.

It is a book that may prove most useful to privileged souls and to pious persons. How well one learns from it the manifold snares of the devil, and the interior pains of souls, the various infernal arts, even by means of some unfaithful minister!

I do not deny, however, that some polishing of the diction would not be inopportune, but I think it better that the simplicity of the authoress be left.

If it pleases you, should you decide to publish it, I would give the book this title: Trials and Consolations of the Soul on the Way of Perfection, described by a Servant of God.

Do not forget me in your prayers; I bless you in the Lord and, with my respects, I have the pleasure of signing myself once more

Yours, Messina, 22 April 1894.

Your most humble and most affectionate Father in J. C.

x G. CARDINAL GUARINO, Archbishop.

Letter of Canon A. Pennino, of Palermo, to the same Princess.

Most Illustrious Princess, the judgment of His Eminence Cardinal Guarino, of renowned and blessed memory, in praise of the dear little work Trials and Consolations of Souls, which you with such zeal have had published, is so authoritative as to render my poor opinion altogether superfluous. Nevertheless, since I cannot refuse your kind invitation to say what I think of it, I shall tell you frankly what seems to me most noteworthy in it.

And first of all, I am fully convinced not only that there is nothing in it that could in the least offend faith and morals, but rather that it contains many teachings which may serve for the edification and guidance of souls, especially of those which, in the exercise of Christian perfection, are more exposed to struggles and temptations. They will find in it most effective lessons to make them value and practice full submission to the divine will, perfect obedience, confidence in hard trials, humility in the enjoyment of heavenly charisms, contempt of earthly goods, heroic charity toward one’s neighbor, the most ardent love for Jesus Crucified, the desire for sufferings even to the complete sacrifice of oneself. It is impossible to go through certain golden pages of this book without feeling oneself encouraged to the practice of all these virtues, and without raising one’s spirit up to God.

Yet it must be borne in mind that not everything in this work is suited to everyone. It is not a general treatise on Christian perfection, but rather the particular story of a soul called with extraordinary graces to promote in the field of the Church great works for the glory of God and the good of the faithful; so that those who have no such mission, and they are certainly the greater number, will find on many pages prodigious and sublime events which they may well admire but never imitate. Yet from these very events come forth those lessons of virtue which I have mentioned above, and which derive from the admirable conduct of this privileged soul, who goes on narrating with edifying simplicity her story, so varied in its vicissitudes, so interwoven with struggles, with dangers, with triumphs.

But in order that such teachings might prove clearer and more effective, I would think it very useful, Princess, that the pious authoress should explain with small marginal notes the meaning of the various scenes and anecdotes of which the whole work is woven, and which foreshadow the various stages of the way of perfection; since some of them prove very difficult to understand even for the most intelligent persons. The lack of such explanations seems to me greatly to lessen the usefulness of this work, and often to make its sense too abstruse.

Another modification which I judge indispensable is to divide in some way the various events which are all described and narrated in one breath in the work. The reading would certainly prove more pleasant and easy if it offered a pause from time to time. I would advise dividing the narration into days, grouping some events in the first, and then others in the second day, and so on.

This, noble Princess, is what I have thought to submit to you candidly regarding the little work which deservedly lies so close to your heart.

You, with your upright judgment and your cultivated intelligence, will know how to give it its just estimation; but in any case accept my good will, and believe me, with sentiments of the most sincere esteem,

Palermo, November 1897. Of Your Excellency

To the Princess of Palermo. Your devoted CAN. A. PENNINO.

FIRST

The Crucified One victorious.

Year 1890, 28 December.

My Crucified One! He led me along a road and on it I fell ill. He was my physician; in weariness He gave me strength; many times I slipped on the narrow path, and He held me up so that I should not fall and plunge to the bottom of the cliffs.

My Crucified One! I fell asleep numb with cold, and He warmed me so that I should not remain buried in lukewarmness.

My Crucified One! I was very deformed, and with His grace He made me beautiful, adorning me with His graces; He stripped me of the old man and I remained clothed as a gentle creature.

My Crucified One! He taught me to suffer and, like the honey of bees enclosed in those precious nests of wax, He preserved suffering for me: this was changed into sweetness. Every so often He gave me a taste of this juice, and with sublime lessons He made me understand how such exquisiteness was drawn from suffering, while nature rebelled against it.

My Crucified One subdues humanity, 24, and gives vigor, energy and strength to the spirit which, victorious, rules over all the powers, and so they remain well subject; self-love scatters and vanishes, is lost, and even its very name remains forgotten. Pride remains conquered and is looked upon as an instrument of disdain, as an enemy. One feels great pleasure when one sees them crushed and oppressed. Great consolation is felt by the will, which is overbearing; and this my Crucified One has exchanged for His own! It is sweet, infinitely delightful, no longer to possess it. Oh! how it would have rebelled had He not nailed it! 25.

My Crucified One! He took away my sense of taste, and so, mortified in all foods and with gluttony chastised, I had to struggle, but the strength of the Crucified One conquered.

Alone, on the road of beloved suffering.

My Crucified One! Halfway along the road a serpent cut across my path: I stopped! Whispering to me insistently, with persuasive ways it invited me to turn back. I was covered in blood, my limbs were all wounded: and I had gone only half the way. Almost overcome by its words I was about to go back, but my Crucified One stopped me and gave me balm for my wounds. When the most bitter pain was soothed, He put the dragon to flight; but too much still remained to climb!

My Crucified One! He left me alone and, like the bride of the Canticles (cf. Song 3:1-3), I went wandering through that forest seeking Him, taking one step forward on the path and another back. All the little branches were dry and all interwoven in the sign of the cross.

— Do you too join in my sadness? — I went saying; and I would stop.

My Crucified One with a great cross on His shoulders! He laid it on mine and, having taken from me the terror of suffering, left me an ardent love for it. I have loved it much and I love it greatly! 26.

My Crucified One! I implored Him and He heard me by placing the cross upon my breast, because I was not worthy to carry it on my shoulders. My Crucified One laid it very well upon my breast!

My Crucified One! When, face down on the ground for having no more strength under the oppression of pain, I was suffocating, He lifted me up and nourished me with His love. If my bones bent, my Crucified One satisfied me with the nectar 27 of His love.

So, walking among cliffs and forests, always on the path marked by His footprints, I did not notice that, all pierced with thorns, I was in pain; I felt the strength of a giant whenever I found myself face to face with people who said every sort of insult to me.

My Crucified One! He showed Himself beautiful to me and rejoiced greatly in what I suffered; then my love for my persecutors grew and, had it not been that they offended God by it, I would have wished them to be doubled. I found that they were leading me before Pilate and the judges; I was ashamed, but in my mind I meditated on the steps of my Savior.

My Crucified One! After a long journey I thought I was at the end; but, alas! a great dragon pursued me and sought with great force to hurl me down.

My Crucified One! He put it to flight, leaving me in the dark and off the path, without understanding, without being able to reason. 28. Everything was shut, a horrid dark night, and I could not understand where I was. I would have liked to reason, but this too was taken from me; and not even the comfort of tears was given me.

My Crucified One had pity on me and, having enlightened me with His light, made me once more regain reason and understanding; full of knowledge, I saw the abyss in which I found myself.

Oh! divine Majesty, what a beautiful work! With strength and vigor I undertook the labor of my journey; in a flash I find the path.

My Crucified One gives me the most sweet bread of angels and gives me a cloud as my guide. 29. Oh sweet journey! delightful the colloquies with which, along it, I was detained! I ran so swiftly that no human creature could catch up with me; neither mountains nor rivers were able to halt my journey. The sweetnesses of the Beloved were continual and all the suffering was such that many times I fell fainting.

My Crucified One showed me His wounds and I, full of shame, covered my face. I learned much, and I took refuge in those wounds; and my Crucified One was pleased.

Under the weight of her own sins Raised up by Mary.

Having reached the summit of the mountain, all joyful I said:

— So, is my journey ended? My guide replies:

— Far from it!

And He left me Full of dread, I did not know what to do. Go down? how? I looked for the way I had left, and could no longer find it. I could barely stand upright; all around there was nothing but precipices. How to go down? I seek my Crucified One. I had nothing but the deepest cliffs. I wept, I begged for mercy: nothing! I would have liked to rest, but the very stones were sharp. Horrendous spectacle! At the bottom of that abyss there was every sort of wickedness, and these produced in me the sight of all my sins! I became convinced of it. The terror, the torment I inflicted on myself, nothing availed to take away that sight and quiet my sorrow.

My Crucified One raised me up and, for an instant, persuaded me, saying to me:

— Woe to you, had I not led you to so terrible a sight! It is all My mercy.

I came back to myself and, while I seemed to be set free and persuaded, there is no escape! On the mountain I was alone, with so terrible a sight before my eyes. Every sort of sin was there, as though there were a light in them which let me see how ugly I was, deformed; and all because of such horrible sins! Cold, arid, weeping alone was my comfort. I sought with all my strength to find a means of escaping from so terrible a state! How to find comfort, if I could not find a living soul?

I huddled up, reasoning within myself: it is not I who wished to come up here, but my Crucified One who has led me here, a sign that everything was done by His will. Therefore I shall remain in so terrible a state as long as it pleases Him. These were moments of resignation which lasted but little.

— I have lost my God! I am made the target of His wrath! — I repeated anew.

Horrible sorrow, far stronger than death! I grew angry with my humanity and subjected it to every sort of suffering, thinking that because of it I had lost my God.

Without realizing it, I was taking its life, when my Crucified One, by means of a light, showed me that I should lessen the scourgings, since it was in no way an accomplice. Oh what a work! I stopped, and this deplorable state lasted in me like that of one revived from a swoon, who is not capable of having knowledge so as to desire.

After all this I found myself all at once in a forest. The variety of the trees refreshed me and I asked myself how God is infinite in His creation, since everything is of varied beauty. I ran here and there to see whether there might be a creature to bring me comfort. When it was given me to see someone, I would at once have liked to speak to him of the great work and of the sufferings of the divine fountain; but they did not understand me!

After a long journey in these woods, I saw from afar a lovely brook, in which a light was reflected that silvered it. I quickened my pace, but never arrived. Only the light shone in varied colors in those crystalline waters. “Oh!” — I said — “if only I could reach it!” Here I am, close by: it was the radiant Most Holy Virgin Mary! Face down on the ground, I loudly exclaimed:

— Most powerful Sovereign, loose my sorrowful chains! bring me to my Crucified One!

She told me that on that way God too was present, who was pleased with my yearning. And she vanished. I sat down and gazed at that spring, bereft of the beauty that had been reflected in it before, as if it joined me in the sorrow of being alone; it ran sadly, and I gazed at it, still absorbed by so great a vision and colloquy; I meditated syllable by syllable on what I had heard. I felt a great peace and joy. The murmur of the water and the solitude left me room to savor so great a favor 30.

Alas, I am lost! — «Whoever loves reclaims nothing»

While, sweetened again by my Sovereign, I was in so delightful a rest, behold, a great serpent comes toward me. I took to flight; but with its lunges it overtakes me. The fright was horrible; the more I ran, the closer it came to me!

My Crucified One stops me, saying to me:

— Why such fright?

— Oh! I am alone, and do You always leave me so? And nothing more! Like one who has been put to shame, I ran on silent and very careful not to leave the path. I met every sort of people and nemo 31 took any notice of my suffering. I found certain creatures of whom one could not tell whether they were human or savage. Everything was nothing and of nothing was I deserving.

My Crucified One made me hear, very inwardly, words of comfort and instruction. All closed up within myself, I walked; at every instant I stopped and tried to reason why I had been reduced to this. I raised my eyes, straining as much as I could to see whether I might glimpse the end. The more I walked, the longer the road seemed to grow. Where am I, so alone? and I would sit upon a stone weeping bitterly. Immersed in a sorrowful melancholy, I lamented.

So nights and months passed, always running without ever being able to find a little path, a comfort, a creature that would keep me company.

Weary and immersed in the deepest sorrow, the thought assails me that that road was the wrong one, that those footprints, which I had always believed to be my Master’s, were the enemy’s; and with force and violence I felt myself dragged to turn aside. Oh! That sorrow! Oh cruel state! I turn my gaze this way and that, alas! I am lost!

Swiftly a voice tries to persuade me that I had been mistaken, that I should abandon that way, that there was quite another for me which would have led me to the desired goal. Frightened, afraid, I listened to the voice, which seemed to me very different from that of my beloved. All confused, but very attentive to where this voice came from: — No! — I said —; it is troubled!

Having had this thought, behold, the dragon breaks loose and with other seductions importunes me to leave the way, exhorts me to take another less toilsome one, and assures me that he would have satisfied me and granted me an equal lot. Indignant, I turned round and in a severe tone ordered him to depart from me. Turning to the Lord with joined hands, prostrate on the ground I cried out: My Good! 32. My sorrow, the weariness, the solitude, the sight of this endless road in the midst of so vast a field!… Alone!…

— I ask help of you, heavenly angels! Tell my God that I am dying of sorrow. I am lost for so many days and nights that I have been walking without ever being able to meet a human creature! Every sort of serpent crawling over this arid earth, every sort of fright from continual encounters with ferocious animals and wild beasts that make me scream with terror!… Mercy! ask mercy for me of the Sovereign Mary.

Sorrow rendered me motionless and, in that attitude, rapt in sweet ecstasy, my Crucified One filled me with joy and with heavenly discourses taught me to travel that way, assuring me that it was He who had traced it for me alone and that He had never found anyone to lead along this way, so sorrowful, but so greatly pleasing to Him.

My soul was in bliss. He showed me that Saint Francis of Assisi traveled an altogether different way, very full of suffering with great thickets of thorns, but these were sprinkled with divine nectar 33. Of Saint Gertrude, oh! on her way she was much comforted, quenching her thirst continually at that divine brook which flowed along the way, and her guide always led her through most beautiful meadows. Of Saint Teresa, oh! how beautiful it was and, ever close to her guide, how she ran along that path without noticing it! it was rather a garden than a road.
