Of countless other ways (He spoke to me), but all more or less had their guide and, if weary, they rested tranquilly, and always found where to lay their head, and placidly they fed on the sweet sleep of love. Beautiful sight! sweet, great spectacle of the infinite wisdom! most sublime work! After such visions He said to me:

— This one is without earthly comfort, nor will you find savory plants. I desired a victim of love to place on so horrid a way; I am well pleased with it.

And without more I came back to myself.

— Where am I, my Crucified One?

— Whoever loves reclaims nothing!

All intent on walking and on remembering all that I had heard and experienced, for a long time I felt neither weariness nor sufferings, I reflected on nothing, as if I had with me another object that occupied me, to such a degree that nothing could distract me.

Weary, I sat down upon a stone and felt such a sadness that it dispelled that sweet thought and reasoning of mine. It was the repetition of what I had seen and heard, but this sadness was so strong that it took every thought from my mind. I heard turmoil approaching, a sound of war, a drawing near of people who were to molest me. In such a tumult, fiercely agitated: and what people are these — I said — who like ferocious beasts seem to want to devour me? In this field I am alone, and how am I to defend myself? I threw myself to the ground and prayed the eternal Father to save me. But, alas! they had formed a carré 34 and I could no longer free myself. When I turned to Heaven, it was bronze to me! Seized by heavy pain, I fell dumb, like one awaiting the decision, without understanding that this decision could not come. Horrible spectacle! these people, more enraged than ever, struck me, leaving me senseless; and, my fright being taken away, I stood observing the persons, without giving it serious thought.

My Crucified One with a most vivid light dispersed the tangle, and the persecutors fell silent and went away.

— Oh! my dear Crucified One! — I said — look at my breast, how they have beaten it! see how it remained aching and how crushed I am! My head was left as if it had been in a thicket of thorns! How did You permit such barbarous people to come forth? You knew that I was alone in that vast field where You had placed me, and why did You let them give me so many blows?

My Crucified One answered by showing me His breast and, without saying anything to me, vanished. Behold, the thought assails me that I had complained too much and that for this, without saying anything to me, He had gone away. I wept and the pain in my breast grew ever greater, 35, but I took no heed of anything and went on weeping, asking His pardon, with fervent promises that I would never complain again. I felt a sweet hand upon my head and, leaning upon it, a sweet refreshment calmed me, dispelling every fear, and I remained in sweet tranquillity.

But, since the intellect always wants to reason and to have knowledge of things that are mysterious, so, reasoning, I went on inquiring how it was, and whose was that sweet hand which had left my soul so well. Convinced that I lacked nothing, I had the most beautiful and great knowledge of everything. Oh! goodness of my dear Crucified One, who always in His infinite charity and mercy deigns to instruct this His servant who never succeeds in understanding; but I realize I am beyond reason.

SECOND

Insinuations of a false «cultivator»

With so strong a support I went through that vast field, of which I never managed to see the end. A murmur as of people toiling at work, and many tools could be heard being used. Eagerly I made my way toward the noise, which was always on my path. And behold a cultivator who was laboring to cultivate plants and seemed all intent that each should bend to the divine good pleasure. He had magnificent treasures which, as soon as I asked him whose they were, having welcomed me with exquisite kindness, he told me were God’s and that he felt he lived for Him alone. Oh! how blissful I felt at that instant!

Almost beside myself with consolation, heeding nothing, I stopped and begged him to speak to me of my Good, and whether it was long since he had seen Him. He told me great things and assured me that I would soon see Him. My Love! I took heart and told him that I had been walking this long road for a long time, and all that had happened to me on it; he went on assuring me that it was almost at its end, that I should not fear, since he would be my guide. With countless promises he showed me the beautiful work of divine Wisdom, which was enchanting. Forgetful of myself, I remembered nothing more and only, only burned and was consumed with desire that my Love might soon arrive.

He invited me also to sit down, and I agreed. He spoke to me of my future, namely that after that road I would have to travel another, stony one. But my Good never arrived. The sun sets, the sky grows dark: where is my God? Oh! what horror! Could this be a demon? — No! — I said inwardly. When lo, from his words I realized that he was the deceiver who in that solitude lay in wait for innocent souls, whose hearts, under the cloak of supernatural cares, he bewitched and wickedly brought to ruin.

In a flash I sprang up from my seat and swiftly took to flight; and I was so headlong that, on turning round, I never saw him again. I thanked His infinite Majesty with all the strength of my soul for having made known to me with such clarity what I would never in the least have understood. But the time lost? Reasoning within myself, at a slow pace, it seemed to me that the darkness of the night also worked to frighten me ever more; and a trembling…: I felt almost on the point of fainting. I leaned upon a stone and, weeping, asked pardon for that halt of mine. On the other hand (I asked myself): But could I have been mistaken?

Another man, with whom she will have to endure a slow martyrdom.

At daybreak I see in the distance most beautiful trees, and oh! with what pleasure I walked to reach them! When I was near these trees, another man, of a harsh and strange manner, asked me where I was going, and I, still walking, answered him that my dear Crucified One had placed me on that way, that I could not stop, but must needs travel it all. And I let him understand that at the end I hoped to find Him.

That man leaves me and I enter a magnificent wood; but to travel the way I saw traced there were many thorn thickets. I gazed at the beautiful plants with magnificent fruits, and oh! how gladly I would have tasted one! My Crucified One plucked a lovely fruit and gave it to me to eat; greater than the exquisiteness of the fruit’s flavor was that of having found my Good. I told Him everything, as also about the second encounter I had had; and He told me that for a long time I shall have to fight with this man. I shall have to suffer terrible pains.

— My Love! — I said to Him — I am ready for everything, provided that Your divine will be satisfied.

The Crucified One resumed:

— It will be for you a slow martyrdom. And He vanished. I remained as if enraptured.

— And where shall I find this man? How shall I be able to run without You, my Good, in the midst of this thicket of thorns?

A fright invaded me; but because of what my Good had left within me I was all fervor and vigor. I said nothing, and began to set foot on such sharp thorns; and running I quickened my step, not caring about what was to befall me. Alas, days and nights passed, running thus, when I came upon a brawl among people of every sort. I saw that man and, before I came near, he insulted me with coarse words. I lowered my head and held fast to the words of my Crucified One. When the brawl was over, he too went away, and I said within myself: what a horrible position! I turned all around, without understanding how and where all that tumult had vanished.

Two good creatures appear before me and exhort me not to look at that man. Nature would quickly have consented and with pleasure would have gone away from that path. But, alas, I was not slow in meeting him: what ill-treatment, how many insults suffered, how many fears and frights did I not have to endure! Every time I met him, the treatment was new. I always reflected on the exhortations of those two creatures, but the will of God always presented itself: if He has so ordained, what is to be done? For a very long time I found him on every road. Then my Crucified One delivered me from him.

A new field inhabited by demons.

I entered a new field of bitter torments, because demons of every sort dwelt there.

Each had his mission to torment me. What horrible fright! The field arid, I parched with thirst, nowhere could a little brook be seen. These infernal dragons offered me some of their water: according to what they said it would have relieved me and brought back peace, and I would have become free; and they would have left me in peace, in possession of great treasures.

Thrown to the ground among those sharp stones, which, being in the possession of those ugly ones, were fiery, I cried:

— My God, have mercy on me! Where are You, my Love? Here alone in so terrible a struggle!

The war grew worse; they whispered to me every sort of word.

— Most holy Mary, sorrowful Virgin, have mercy on me! Nothing! One of them, with a squadrone in his hand, 36, rushes headlong before me to wound me. An invisible hand stops him and puts him to flight. Another ferocious one, with a very sharp iron, tries again to seize me, but does not succeed. They grapple together and try to assail me. I, thrown down thus, was numb with fright and hardly dared to move; I tried with my gaze to utter words, but could not.

In a second a thousand scenes changed, each more frightful than the other. Horribly enraged because I would not consent to give myself to them, they sought the means to kill me, but never succeeded. They would come within a few spans of me and, like a flash, (I saw them) plunge down and take to flight.

Days and nights passed, always under so horrible a game; I rose to look at that horrid field, and nothing could be seen. A distant lament, coming from a deep prison, could be heard, and oh! I am lost! Of whom am I to ask an account of my God? These ferocious lions, when I uttered so sweet a name, mocked me. I would have liked to flee; but how, if there was no trace of a road and not even the path existed which until that hour my Good had marked? Even this no longer existed!

I began to run across that field with great speed; but what amazement! after walking so much, I realize that I am always at the same point: horror! Cruel labyrinth! How to get out? My God has abandoned me and given me over to these infernal dragons! With force I turned round and ordered these terrible serpents to leave me free, to depart, leaving my path free so that I might go to my Good.

They vanished, and in an instant the field changed, the way became free for me, and with quick and sure step I sought to run. Only every so often I turned round to see whether any of those dragons were there. An interior voice said to me:

— How can you fear, when they obeyed your command and returned to their prison? How can you doubt it?

It is true! and I thought that, if at such a command they took to flight, it is a sign that the one who gives force to my word is my God! Therefore my fears are ill-founded!

«Do not fear: the field is mine, and these assaults enrich it»

While I was reasoning thus, I did not notice that I had entered another field, where many people were at work. As soon as I noticed it, I stopped. Approaching a kindly peasant woman, I asked her what she was sowing and whose that field was.

— Oh! — she answered me — it is God’s! These creatures are all intent on cultivating these plants well, (so that) they may grow beautiful and be pleasing to my master.

Oh! enchantment! I stopped and with hurried questions desired a prompt answer; when she tells me softly that I should not stop any longer, but should go running to a field where need required it; there they were awaiting me. How will it be? What can it be? My Good! it is His will. I noticed that I was trembling and, almost weeping, I said to myself:

— Alas! at least I would have liked to stop. But in a threatening tone (she said to me):

— Woe if you desist! Yes! you will find a heap of torments, but so God has ordained!

I fell silent, and set out where I had been commanded. Horrible fright! As soon as I entered that labyrinth, there were torments of every sort. And that man! Oh! how many souls he had fewer [?], and where are they? Nothing!

Dismayed with fear I did not dare utter a word. A thousand insults were spoken to me, every sort of obscenity invented! Silence: a barrier stretched in such a way that it was forbidden me, so that if my Good came I would not have possessed Him. 37. I felt I was dying; I would have broken every iron to pieces; but, bound by sorrow, I fell fainting to the ground.

My Crucified One! When I rose, I saw nothing around me. Oh! Love, where were You? Is this field the one in which I was before? Weary and almost motionless, I shed great tears.

— Do not fear! the field is mine and these assaults enrich it.

Other intellectual knowledge (He communicated to me). I resumed my journey and, going through all those uncultivated fields and others with wicked people, who sought to put poison into the heart of the beautiful and gentle plants, I courageously succeeded in snatching many of them from their hands and carrying them with me, and, finding good ground, I planted them, begging whoever had charge of them to water them well, for they were for my God. But I shed many tears whenever I found myself among certain cliffs where there were beautiful ewe-lambs: and who was to be the shepherd to defend them from ravenous lions?

At that ferocious sight I was anxious and, without fear or human respect, but as a faithful slave, I hurled myself upon the shepherd, and such was my fury that I frightened him. Disheartened, he threw himself to the ground and I ordered him to give me the beautiful sheep. They ran happily and, skipping around, those dear little lambs came to me and, on hearing me sing praises to the most holy Virgin, they rejoiced. I do not know how I would have wished to make known this sovereign Virgin, Immaculate Queen! I realized that my language was new to them. Having put them in safety, I set out, ever on the tracks marked out for me.

A great ship about to be wrecked.

After a few hours’ walk I arrived at a beach and could no longer see any sign, but only sea. I turned my gaze to both sides to see whether there were tracks, but nothing: only an immense beach of soft sand. The murmur of the sea, the scorching sun, caused me a great fright. Prostrate, I began to weep, like one waiting for what she was to do. After a long prayer:

— My Good! — I exclaimed — my Savior! Oh! how happy I would be if I too, as You made Peter walk upon the sea (cf. Mt 14:29-31), had such a lot! Oh! trace the way on the sea too, that I may run!

But nothing! A great wind rises and the sea is more agitated than ever, and all of a sudden it becomes frightful. From afar something could be glimpsed. Meanwhile, lifted by a wave and swiftly brought near, a great ship that was about to be wrecked. On its sides could be seen certain monsters in the form of fish, which were trying to sink it and plunge it into that abyss. At such a spectacle I threw myself to the ground and, with all the voice I had, I asked for help. The work of the monsters grew stronger and at every instant the ship seemed to me submerged. Weeping, I called upon my God, almost fainting from sorrow and fright; my Savior draws near to me:

— Why doubt! — He said to me — the ship is Mine and cannot sink.

I remained in ecstasy, and the sea became all calm. The sky was serene and the ship, under full sail, was approaching the harbor. Turning to my Good,

— I am exhausted of strength! — I exclaimed.

The fright, the sorrow lest it be destroyed, were making me die!

How? have you forgotten My promises? — He said to me.

Taking me by the hand, He made me go up on to the ship; and my Good vanished. All strengthened and full of courage, I ran everywhere to see what was needed and asked everyone what they required. I noticed that something was missing, namely the helmsman. The captain was troubled; the greatest anguish reigned among all the passengers. At my first meeting with the commander I received an insult:

— How are we to go forward, if we have no one to put at the helm? Why did you not let me go ashore, as we were, and provide myself?

As though I had been the cause, he grew ever more furious, and the others took part in it.

She takes the helm and guides the ship into harbor.

What was to be done? To reveal that it was my God who had led me and given direction to the ships was not fitting for me. All submissive, I offered to stand at the helm, assuring them that we would soon arrive at the harbor of a great city and that I myself would supply them with everything. They fell silent, but with a look of little belief. They sat down and I at the helm.

I perceived that an invisible hand was sensibly turning the helm and gave the ship a great speed. Alas! I never saw the harbor drawing near; the night was dark and a murmuring could be heard. I cast a glance around: here and there small groups of people who were murmuring. The captain, first of all, called me ignorant:

— Surely this creature will bring us to ruin!

They were almost about to come and take the helm out of my hands when, clothed with a superhuman power, I sprang forward and in a severe tone ordered them to stop whispering, or else, once we reached harbor, I would send them all away. The captain looked at me with a sneer and was studying the way to throw me into the sea; but a most vivid light made me penetrate into his soul, and bolder than ever I turned to him, saying:

— You, first of all, shall get off this ship! I need no one to keep the compass; I shall find others, better ones.

Then, in a most severe tone of voice, I said:

— My God needs no one!

Behold, there came into our sight a great and shining lighthouse, which assured me of the desired harbor; and our beautiful, graceful and immense ship goes straight to the mouth of the harbor, where there were lovely little boats and other ships which courteously greeted us, waving their flags. And with great festivity we cast anchor. All these people were dismayed; the captain hardly dared to speak to me and came around me with the others, because they were afraid that I would put them ashore. And then I began to say:

— Creatures without faith! that God of infinite mercy who has saved you from so cruel a shipwreck, how could you fear that He would fail you in your needs? Creatures of clay! seek to lay aside your own judgment, lift your gaze on high and seek to fill your minds with noble sentiments, reasoning not as human creatures; but, voyaging from harbor to harbor on so beautiful and well-built a ship, you must never fear meeting with disasters.

She defends the ship against two monsters of hell.

When everything was in order and I would gladly have taken rest and, before anything else, thanked my God, behold, a dragon passes before me in fury. Where can that monster be going? I said within myself. It left me in such strong agitation that all my nerves felt it, and, seized by great fear, I struggled. I was alone! In the harbor, what person was there who knew me? Awaken those people to whom, shortly before, I had reasoned that they were people without faith? 38.

So, while I was reasoning thus, another, more loathsome than these monsters, passes right beside me.

— Oh! my Love! — I exclaimed — come to my help, or else I die of fright.

A terrible voice whispered to me, saying:

— You are in my power and have arrived where I was awaiting you. You have no escape! only in me! Horrible fright!

— No! — I cried — I have my God!

Sneering, he said to me:

— You are abandoned!

How many horrid things he made me hear, overturning all that my God had done in me! And he said that he was absolutely the worker and that there was no longer any remission, and that with an army of other fierce dragons he would break the ship to pieces; and I heard the creaking of its ruin.

— No! — I exclaimed — You shall be put in the irons of your exile! Oh! what terrible fright! I would have liked to be mistress enough to order him to leave me, but I could not and it was not given me. My mouth shut tight, my mind nailed down, how to free myself? After so fierce a combat I fainted and, more enraged than ever, that chief dragon gave me a heavy blow on the forehead. Starting up, I cried:

— No!

I could utter nothing else. He was preparing to give me further blows, when my Crucified One, standing upright, beautiful with an exquisiteness of love, raises me, revives me.

— Why did You leave me so cruelly — I said to Him — at the mercy of such ferocious dragons? Had You been slow to come, they would have killed me without my being able to utter a word and call You!

He interrupts me with a smile and leaves me alone again, but tranquil.

FOURTH

A field besieged by a wolf dressed as a shepherd.

I look around: nothing could be heard. Weary, I fell asleep. When a voice wakes me, saying to me:

— Go down and go into that portion of the field; there a little flock is besieged by a wolf dressed as a shepherd.

Without heeding anything else I ran and, having gone a long way, I arrived in time to seize that shepherd; and, victorious, I brought the little flock to safety. I made sure of it well; and then I set out in search of my way. Find it? Not at all! A spectacle presents itself before me, namely the destruction of an entire field. There were pleasant shepherds, who seemed all intent on cultivating it and restoring it. One of them stopped me, addressing sweet words to me, telling me not to enter, because I would meet many serpents.

— Tell me, I pray you — I answered him —, how did such a sad destruction ever come about? The trees burned, the plants dry, heaps of earth all stony…

But he pointed out to me the workers he had under him to cultivate it. While he was telling me many things, I stood looking at his workers, and all that they were doing was not cultivation, but they were putting worse things upon that field. But he went on telling me that certain evildoers had reduced it to that state who, having entered by force, (had) stolen and laid waste whatever they possessed. And he wanted to tell me many other things, but I courteously took my leave. But he, insistent, held me back, begging me to listen to him. I had no interest in it and, without caring further, I began to run to make up the time I had lost. Yet all those tales had troubled me and brought (everything) to my mind so confusedly that I ran without heeding where I was. After a long walk I realized that once again I was approaching the devastated field.

— How is this, my God? The path is traced by You, for it bears the same shadows; and why do I see myself near that ugly field?

The laborers had increased: some were eating, some were sitting, others were trading and had set up a market. What fright! Night was drawing nearer; I looked to see whether another way could be glimpsed, but in vain.

— And yet it is this one, and it is traced by my God!

I stopped, not daring to approach. A murmuring could be heard. And how, here alone? I sat down and, weeping, called upon my God. I would have liked to find a cave in which to hide, but all in vain. The fear that they might see me was terrible, I trembled from head to foot. Two pretty little birds came around me; they too seemed to me frightened.

Turn back? What ever am I to do? Nothing! And resolutely I turn back. Spectacle! Worse still: a few steps, and I find myself right in the same field. How can it be? For long hours I have walked, and now I am in the same field! Where shall I take refuge? These are not cultivators, but lost people. They were gambling away all that they had taken in that devastated field.

Frightened, I wept, having covered myself with certain great thorn bushes so as to pass the night without being seen. A strong agitation invaded me; I begged God to come to my help. The night was dark; between sobs and fright I stayed attentive (to what) that band of evildoers were doing. They get up and take to flight: some ran this way, some that; in a flash the field was left free.

Comforted by a son of Saint Francis.

Alone again!

I did not know whether I should get up and once again set out on my way or wait for the morning. I hear a person approaching with slow steps: Alas! my God, I am lost! Wrapping myself more than ever in that thicket of thorns, I waited for him to pass. I hear that he stops and, with a long sigh, offers a prayer of thanksgiving to the most holy Virgin. Poor me! He goes on praying and addressed most beautiful prayers to the Virgin. My God! thorns had entered every part of my body and I felt I was fainting with pain.

Meanwhile day broke. And oh! what a surprise! It was a son of Saint Francis of Assisi who, as soon as he saw me, said:

— Are you here?

All trembling, I answered him:

— For pity’s sake, tell me where I am! I am alone, abandoned by my God. I no longer find where. I walked a long time and found myself in the same field. Tell me something of what my God has said to you. Is it He who has sent you here?

— Oh! is it not He — the friar resumed — who saved you from the destruction that those evildoers wrought in the field?

And he related the event to me. I was frantic to know whether my God was the One who was pleased with so much suffering of mine.

— Tell me — I said to him — what He said to you.

I saw him rapt in ecstasy and, at that sight, I fell face down on the ground, weeping, immersed in my nothingness and annihilated, torn with sorrow, because I was unworthy to be able, I too, to see and converse with my Good. I conceived such aversion for myself that I would have dissolved from the sorrow I felt, and I was about to faint when the servant of my God told me that I was greatly loved by God and that He was much pleased with my suffering; and he told me many things, exhorting me to walk on that long path. With his reasoning he was a great comfort to me, but he made me anxious because I did not decide 39 his ideas on many things. Beautiful!

Having reached the top of a little rise, behold, the road ends! How? Looking at each other, we stopped. A warrior comes at full gallop with drawn sword, and what happened? That son of Saint Francis draws back and leaves me alone. What was I to resolve? As soon as he was near me, all trembling with fright, he asked me where I was going. I answered him:

— I am here by the order of God. Having said this, he passes before me and resumes his gallop.

— Oh — I said within myself — had I gone together with that servant of my God, I would not find myself here alone, without a path to run on this cliff. Where and how shall I be able to free myself from here? Where was that messenger going? What will become of me, poor creature, without a guide, without a road? Oh! I am truly lost! O most holy Virgin, pray my God for me and tell Him that I am dying of sorrow. Hard to me is the thought that, through my fault, I lost the Being of my life! 40.

Hours and days and months I had to remain thus in so hard a position. My pasture was roots of grass; my rest in the midst of thorns and stones. Every so often I fainted, but nothing troubled me, because a greater sorrow invaded me; all was sadness, no song of birds could be heard, a silence all around and, on the other side, there were nothing but cliffs.

— I was wrong! I should have gone with that servant of God.

A most sweet voice tells me no, and that this friar was to travel another road, and one, for him, too disastrous. Thinking over what I had heard, I said within myself: — Whose can this voice have been?

I raised myself a little, but I hear a whispering in those bushes. Alas! what can it be? Surely a serpent! I got up and, looking all around, saw nothing new. The whispering grows louder and (I hear) that bramble of gloomy silence change in an instant into shrieks of every kind. A thousand dragons, all enraged! some were cutting those bushes, some overturning great stones and, as they looked at me, they roared.

What my fright was is better imagined than described. With labored steps they gained ground; the work was thunderous. Flee? and where, if I saw them all around me? They began to move certain stones so terrible and of an immense size, and they set them on their shoulders like feathers. When, all exultant and as if each were armed with whatever was on that height, what do they do? They rush upon me, they load me with blows. With all the voice I had, weeping, I called upon my God; they were almost about to finish me when an angel, with drawn sword, scattered them.

The uncultivated path becomes a beautiful garden without cultivation — The Rose!

And there remained so beautiful a plain, with a pleasant path without stones; but I could not persuade myself that, without strength and so ill-treated, I would be able to run. In fact, at a slow pace I went along that way, but, lamenting thus, I said:

— If only that angel had said a word to me!

Every so often I sat down; I would have liked to pray, but exhaustion did not allow me; I reasoned with my intellect and felt a deathly sadness. A skeleton comes near me, tells me that I should think of him, that he was a priest. 41.

I felt all aching from the blows received, but I felt no inclination to give any thought to anything. Oh! hard prison of this life, which divides me from my Beloved! But another thousand years, if I must do His most holy will, I am ready for them!

While faith alone at that moment was my anchor, so, holding fast to it, I stopped to contemplate creation: the little plants of daisies, lilies springing up among the bushes of rushes, so luxuriant, could be seen here and there. Oh! how beautiful they are, though uncultivated, these little plants! I turned my gaze to other lilies of the field, beautiful in their whiteness and their simplicity: they too are without cultivation! This voice I heard inwardly and I delighted in it. At last that uncultivated path became a lovely interweaving of magnificent flowers. Oh! I see the Rose too! Oh! most holy Virgin! As though not content with gazing at so beautiful a flower, I drew near and kissed it.

— Mary, Mary! most holy Virgin, Mother of my Love — weeping, I said to her — Tell me: does my God no longer love me?

I heard a voice that said to me:

— Yes, you are beloved!

— Is it possible? — I repeated to myself.

Oh! I kept gazing at the rose. How could it blossom so magnificently in the midst of other ill-grown bushes? how could so magnificent a plant spring up? My voice:

— And yet there is no cultivator!

I went over one by one such lovely little flowers, but the rose held my gaze upon it, melancholy though it was. Therefore so lovely and magnificent a work can only be my God’s! With a deep breath I sought one among these, which I did not yet see. Oh! my God! where are the philosophers, the moralists, the ascetics, the theologians who, with their science, could manage, all at once, to change an uncultivated bush into a lovely and magnificent garden?

— But, Love! — I repeated within myself — Those bushes that have remained there, and these so battered, scattered, without the least flower, indeed with dry branches? Oh! I understand well: they are my imperfections! I saw one that was all thorns. Alas, I feel Your reproach for them, and it is for this that my God formed them all and made them come forth in a moment. But that, that which I long for, I do not see!

And so, frantic with the sorrow that those ugly bushes (caused me), and keenly feeling the torment of the reproach, I flung myself into that thicket of thorns and strove that this loathsome humanity should pay the penalty for them. I would have been exhausted had not, all of a sudden — oh! what a spectacle! — they been changed into a field of magnificent carnations, each more beautiful than the other. I leaped among them and held them pressed to my breast and kissed them. I could not shed a single tear. My Love! My Love! Rapt in ecstasy and pressed to my Good, the blood of the pricks was flowing; I saw them as if changed into lovely pearls and rubies. A lovely angel was weaving a magnificent crown of them: what a size! I could not understand how it could ever rest upon that field, and I asked my God whose it was.

— Of My Work — He answered.

Indeed, it was only a small portion that had been worked, but it was of a circumference that I did not succeed in comprehending: only with blood must it be finished. 42.

She teaches the little workers to cultivate the field.

I remained alone; everything vanished. An immense field with little creatures who were working. How is it they are so little? A strong voice said to me:

— Teach them to cultivate this field well, because a good harvest must soon spring up.

The field (was) most vast and, leaving the way, I placed myself among these creatures and chose the heaviest spade, so as to lighten the load of the workers; and with all my strength I taught them, taking for myself the ugliest work, and from them I asked only that they might sow here and there where I was taking care to put the manure; and I asked my God that He would make me alone feel the pains of the work, because they were very little and I feared they would faint. What a marvel! My God heard me, and so, happy, I toiled as much as I could.

Oh! sublime work of a God! There were certain of them who from one hour to the next grew strong, and could be seen working with extraordinary strength and growing well. This work of the divine mercy was magnificent!

While we were working with eagerness, I saw a monster in the distance running toward the field. I left the spade to the biggest one and, heeding nothing, I climbed over walls and hedges, and managed to overtake it. I seized it and

— Stop — I said to it — in the name of God! Go back to where you came from!

And it went away. So worn out from walking, I would gladly have sat down to tell (this) to my God and to pray Him never to permit these monsters to come out and go into such lovely fields, where the wheat is already about to grow.

No one shall rob the field of God!

I heard a shriek and turned round. I saw unknown women who, like furious lions, were coming toward me. A voice says to me:

— Leap over this cliff and pay no heed to them! Go to the bottom of those cliffs, where you will find a seducer who is maliciously stealing from Me a soul dear to Me.

Without heeding anything else, I climbed over those cliffs; at the place pointed out to me I saw a shepherd who was speaking breathlessly; I set myself to listen, and he was teaching many things against the Work of God and overturning history with ill-restrained sarcasm. I stepped forward and the commotion became general. My God! where ever are those women? what can have become of them?

My voice said to me:

— Here am I!

The shepherd tried to load me with courtesies and insistently wanted me to take (rest).

— I take no rest — I said — I shall rest only in Paradise! 43.

But (he remained) firm. How was I to send him away? Seeing that there was no end to it, in an imperious tone I ordered him to depart and never again to have the audacity to return. Oh! how enraged, from the lamb he seemed, he would have torn me to pieces had it been permitted him. But, sure that no one could touch a hair of my head, motionless and firm I sent him away. I cleared new ground and went back. Along the road I said within myself:

— Soon I shall have to find those women.

My Good had announced to me that they were waiting for me. And here they are, with hands on hips: they insult me and, thus furious, they spew forth horrid ignorances [?].

— What am I to answer them? — Inwardly I questioned my God. He said to me:

— What did I answer in the house of Annas?

That is: I kept silent. But they grew angrier still, and hardly knew any longer (what insult to hurl at me), and they would have liked to be able to beat me.

— My God! — I said — let them give me at least the slap that You received, and not just one, but rather a great quantity: they will serve me for all the failings I may have committed with this portion of my body.

— In due time! — my voice. When they had finished shouting, they wanted to take from me certain things I had in the field.

— Oh! no! — I answered.

Enraged, they protested that they would (have) them. But not at all! Firm, no one frightened me:

— No one shall rob the field of God!

Seeing that they could in no way attain their purpose, they threatened me strongly that from afar they would make me feel their vengeance; and they went away.

One of those little workers held me tight, urging me to give way to all that those women wanted.

— I understand — I began to say to her — why you have remained so little; you have not taken care to nourish yourselves well with the exquisite bread of the Work of the Lord. God gave you His exquisite liquor to drink and you, if you do not wish to become worms, learn to live and grow in God.

Poor little one! she did not understand the language; and she becomes proud of her own knowledge.

It is the time of the rod.

As we went along, I prayed much that my God might grant me the good fortune of finding a little hut in which to leave the little worker, fearing that, if I took her with me, she would have to meet with other hardships and that this unhappy one would faint on me and I would have to lose her in the middle of the road, in a grave where there would have been nothing but great north winds.

We found a pleasant person who invited me to her house. I thought that I could not turn aside from my path, for I felt myself (driven) by an invisible hand to run.

— Leave this one alone? — (I said) within myself.

— No! — answered my voice.

Then an old man comes near us. All out of breath, he tells me to hasten my step, for in a field there were a few creatures in extreme need. I begged a woman to accompany us. When we arrived, the need was grave; I took one from the field and, with the one I had with me, I entrusted her to the old man. All joyful, he led them away with him.

Having set myself to work, I did not well understand the intrigue whereby the whole harvest of that disordered field was put into a great ditch which gave off a horrible stench. My God! the old man who came to warn me I no longer see; and I saw in the distance groups of people, in whose souls one could observe that they were waiting for what was to happen. I had the head of that field called, but he did not come. The women workers come forward and insult me; this was their greeting.

— Tell me — I said to them —, where is your guide?

In a more than insolent tone they answered me that he will come no more. And (down came) abuse. My voice:

— I am with you! it is the time of the rod! Turning to them:

— Well then, go out, all of you! even [?] she who refuses to listen to the voice of God. If you have made a hotchpotch of the field, I with the strength of my God shall draw from it fine linen to weave gilded cloths. Away, creatures of mud! your nature shall crawl upon the earth like the serpent. Be converted and return, creatures hardened in the mud!

All in disorder, one began to run this way, another that, and nothing came of it. At last I enter the farmhouse, I find the guide there with a fierce shepherd, who were awaiting the result of the struggle, sure that I, having drawn back, had abandoned the field. Never! On seeing me they were troubled, they remained dumb; and I looking at them! Meanwhile I hear within me a voice that says to me:

— Use My rod of the temple! (cf. Jn 2:14 f.).

— Let them go out of here! — I began to say. But that shepherd with a long beard, which would have frightened a lion:

— I, go out? No! no!

I took out a thick cord and, without heeding anything else, began to strike right and left. What can I say! At that instant I seemed to have become so great and strong that, when they had fled, I looked around and found myself alone.

A dull lament could be heard: with a faint voice it was asking for help. Approaching where I heard the lament, I found a dying old man. I felt myself shudder: it was the one who had come to call me! I gave him much help. (Seeing him) numb with cold, I took off as many garments as I could and put them all on him; but the poor man asked me for the Bread of eternal life. I was not slow in having everything brought to him and, in the kiss of the Lord, with words of gratitude, he expired blessing God. Oh! what an impression I felt!

The lot of a creature who fails in the promises she has made.

Meanwhile my thought (was): what will become of those creatures who went away? Spectacle! A picture is presented to me of the future of a creature who does not correspond to the graces of the Lord and with disdain turns her back on Him, casting the precious gift to the ground. That soul was so strange, so penanced, that it tore my heart to see her. An iron bit crossed her forehead as though it were crushing a rebellious part. I well understood its whole meaning, for it was her own will: the proudest power, which rules over all the others, because pride (is) self-love that will not stay subject to any obedience and judges in whatever way pleases it most.

Horrible suffering! An iron bit gripped her brow tightly, and she was bound to a stock (in such a way) that she could not move in the least! Finally, she was languishing with thirst; crystal-clear water stood before her, but she was forbidden to drink of it, because she had made herself unworthy of it. Every part of her body was tormented by certain ugly beings who stood around her and gave her immense vexation. Oh! what a sight! I looked at her a little and then, unable to bear it, I tried to turn my gaze elsewhere.

— Oh! my Good! If they could perceive these pains before leaving this earth, they would be converted.

My voice:

— They feel them, they feel them even in this life, but they do not see them!

— Certainly, if such a picture were seen, no creature would dare to fail in the promises made.

My voice:

— If this were painted at every step, their obstinacy would overcome every terror. What did Judas not do?

Oh! what did I not experience! Thus torn and at the same time frightened, I saw before me a young seducer. He asked me why I do not think of him, and how I could trust myself to be alone on that road. Resolutely I answered:

— I am not alone!

With a sardonic smile he says to me:

— Oh! you believe yourself safe and strong enough?

— Certainly: I tell you that what I lack is supplied by my guide, my Master.

— I shall do so much — that young man went on — that I shall win!

I, indignant at such an answer,

— I fear nothing! — I said to him, and I passed on swiftly.

And he overtook me with other manners, and I saw that he was a seducer of souls. But I had to deal with him on account of certain tools which were to serve me for that field. But what a terrible thought and what loathing was caused in me by a shepherd who (was) a few steps away and who, instead of busying himself in defending me, let so terrible an evildoer torment me with words.

— My Crucified One! drive this man away, teach me how I must defend myself in such cases. My Love, how sweet are your words!

Along the way I was thinking that so many souls will remain a prey, because they lack light. A voice lets me hear that God does not fail to communicate it to them; but it is they who do not want to listen; and in the depth of their heart there reigns a germ of carnal affection, and this rules in them with chief dominion.

Hard struggle with the great eagles in defense of a field.

So intent on listening to this reasoning, I did not notice that my path was surrounded by great eagles. Why this? It was beautiful and at the same time spectacular, because each one had its own portion to defend, and from the beating of their wings one could tell that what the other eagle wanted troubled it greatly.

Each of them had a badge, but an infinity of subalterns, I mean inferiors; in appearance it seemed that they were submissive, and yet it was they who had their factions, and what they wanted to defend. Truly fine! for they plotted together and had so much cunning that they managed to seduce the leaders and make them do what pleased them.

Oh! how fear invaded me! One of them held tight under its wings an affair concerning a field that was beautiful, well cultivated. A malign spirit invades it; it wanted to make havoc of certain portions of it. Whom does it make use of? Of a great eagle: it shelters it under its wings, takes up this affair, and how it worked! I took great pains to see whether I might be granted to undo that tangle, but it was not possible.

Weary, I sat down upon a stone and fell asleep. The din of their wings woke me every now and then, but I would glance with indifference and then pay no heed. One, bolder, came to wave its great wing almost in my face, but still I was not disturbed.

Turning to heaven, I said to my Good:

— Have these great eagles much longer to work?

Having said this, there arrives one of an extraordinary size, and they all gather around it; a murmuring, something clamorous, could be heard. It was something curious and interesting to see that eagerness; they were telling their affairs; that terrible and frightful eagle cast certain glances at me.

— What will happen? Yet I felt nothing of fear. After a long time they went away. And the big one? It came round me and, wishing to frighten me, made me see that the whole of that field was in its power, that I should withdraw, that I had nothing more to do there.

Oh! here indeed the struggle became horrible. Firm at my post, I continued the work, being very careful that the eagle should not steal from me the work already done. It begins to screech and to make its clamorous voice heard everywhere; but nothing! It devised one thing uglier than the other. At last it gave a loud screech:

— Ah! turn off this path, or I shall hurl you down! I remained silent and inwardly asked God what I ought to do. My voice:

— Be calm! fear nothing.

Having heard this, I let it do as much as it wanted; but everything it did was a continual redoing, and it never came to complete a piece of work; its bustling about was something to behold. Every now and then certain shepherds would pass by and take fright; they asked me how I could stay with this ferocious animal without fear; others pitied me, saying:

— Poor thing, what a bad field she has taken up to work!

And they left me, going away with quick steps. Others scolded me, telling me that that work was not for me and that I should go away. All who passed by, even great personages, they too had their say, mocking me! I was made a laughing-stock by all; I did a piece of work, and the eagle undid it for me.

A royal personage came, and even he told me to stop, so that this eagle might withdraw.

My Love! how am I to defend myself? how can I tell them to withdraw, although I understand it to be a diabolical art? But I cannot manage to make that personage understand that the eagle is moved by fierce instigations to turn the field upside down. Thus distraught, with slow steps, I no longer reasoned. With all the strength of my soul I asked my Master what I ought to do; but I understood nothing; only this tangle grew murky; I was intent on the field and on the workers.

At last this great eagle, having been given full power, was about to set foot within the hedge, and a great multitude of others draw near to it. My Crucified One stops them and puts them to flight. Turning to me (he said):

— Into my work no one shall be able to enter nor do it the slightest harm; these are false laborers, who laid waste that field, because it was not mine!

And he left me. With what eagerness I worked I cannot describe; but always fearful of not knowing how to cultivate plants and fields well. Whenever one of these plants happened to wither, oh! what sorrow!

A fine future for the cultivation: there will be countless flourishing fields.

I was hesitating over what I ought to sow, when there comes before me a person (who had) the semblance more of a heavenly creature than of an earthly one, and in great haste she tells me to go with her, that they were about to lay waste a field: much hoarfrost had fallen and very thick fogs did not let the workers see where they were, and what had remained (was) blighted by the fog.

— How can I leave this ground to succor another?

— If you delay, all is lost! — a voice, insisting — No more reflections!

Together with that creature I set out toward the place where one, panting, was running. We passed through the midst of unknown people, but very barbarous, who had plotted to kill me; but I passed without being recognized. Having arrived at the place, a tumult of people: they wanted to seize the land. With a loud voice I ordered them to go out. But the plots, the vengeances they were devising, were something horrendous.

There approaches me a soul so beautiful and gentle; she assures me that those people roar, but will be able to do nothing to me.

— Tell me, I pray you, blessed soul, who was it that sent you? Perhaps you are a heavenly messenger, and my God has sent you here to defend his field? Tell me what you have kept in your heart.

At these words, spoken with great speed so as to have the answers, (she added):

— I have nothing else to tell you. And she remained sad.

— Why this sadness of yours? You have quite other things to tell me!

She comes close to me and, with an air of compassion, speaks of the future of my cultivation: that there would be countless flourishing fields; and something beautiful, that my God took delight in them and by his visits made them fruitful, leaving them great treasures.

— Oh! how happy I would be to be able to meet him! For pity’s sake, tell me in which field he is accustomed to go, for I want to be found there.

With an angelic smile she answered me that it is in the very field where I am, that it is not the workers who do much of that work, but the Lord himself who brings the work to completion, giving it an exquisite adornment.

But still I did not feel satisfied with her words, and I would have wished her to tell me other sublime things about my Good. But she fell asleep and, however much I asked her to wake up, I could never obtain it. The thought came to me that it was not sleep, but rapture; I fell silent and placed myself near her as if I might hear something. Prostrate on the ground, I prayed my God to let me (listen) for a single instant. O goodness! having drawn near, I heard her discourse; it was so beautiful! she was describing the future of two souls, and of one who was at the point of death: how beautiful she was! I did not notice that little by little I was becoming absorbed. A weaving of sufferings of a new kind: the end was an Eden of delights! When it was over, we spoke together, and I would never have wished it to end.

FIFTH

Victorious with the power of God

A loud rumble as of war, and the earth shook beneath my feet. She (the angelic soul) vanished from me; (I remained) alone. Every sort of noise could be heard all around; but something worse: a ball passes before me, and others fire, like so many pistols vomiting balls, each of which, I would have said, was bound to hit me. I shrieked and, with all the strength I had, I begged for help from that blessed soul who had gone away. Nothing! Louder: the air was covered with smoke; I seemed to have a wound in every part of my body; so I felt it, sensibly. That firing went on and on.

With a strength not my own, I hurled myself toward the fire and ordered it to cease. It stops: I look all around, I see nothing but smoke; and I, without wounds, am strong. I go near a door, but as soon as I would have opened it, behold, more fire! All trembling, but full of strength, I step back, halt, and command those dragons to have done. Swiftly I opened the door, woke the workers and led them to the field; but what had happened to me always remained in my mind. How gladly I longed to have a creature who would have understood me, so as to tell her what had happened and receive enlightenment! I always remained alone, studying what its meaning might be!

Meanwhile a war breaks out among those workers; so I ran to make peace among them; one of them was so angry that she came up to my face with insults, threatening to beat me. My voice:

— The rod!

In a severe tone I ordered her to withdraw and, stepping forward, (I said):

— Unworthy slave of this field, leave me the tools, and away! if you do not want anything else to befall you.

Turning round with the rage of a lion, she gave me a look, launching herself to fall upon me. But with force I struck my heel upon the head of that serpent which had so possessed her, and she stood still. I went on telling her:

— Turn your face elsewhere and never dare to turn your gaze upon this delightful field, which for you shall be nothing but privation for all your life!

With quick steps she went away. Exhausted, I sat down on a dry bush, rested my head on the palm of my hand, and considered the infinite power of my God: how in a flash he communicates his strength, his power, to the weakest and most inert creature! hell submits to the voice of a wretched being, loses its ferocity; the rebellious and enraged creature remains crushed, submits and, humbled, can no longer speak, and goes where its intention and will are contrary to going.

And yet, my God! to so great a commotion man is subject every day, and hell burns with fury whenever it can find room to win a barbarous victory, because it is never persuaded that it is crushed. Rebellious is its blood, and so the furious hatred and the vengeance that devours it keep alive its conviction of its own victory!

In that rest I felt myself being strengthened, when two ferocious lions come before me, roaring with rage. A voice that seemed to come from them, as loud as could be:

— Over us you hold no power, and all our power shall be victorious over you.

With a tone of voice so sonorous and impetuous, certainly not mine, I ordered them to shut their ferocious mouths and to remain still. Turning to my God (I exclaimed):

— Mercy, O Lord!

They do not move, but they frighten me. I gathered my strength and ordered them to leave me. And they stood motionless, with a ferocious look: the pupil of the eye was a black ember and all around it red like fire; the eyelids, so many long hairs, and the eyebrows likewise. They moved only their paws, which had long claws, these too fiery. How great was my fright! from head to foot I was a single trembling and, ever more frightened because I never saw them move at my commands, (I prayed):

— Oh! most holy Virgin, Mother of my God, come to my aid, crush these two lions as you crushed the head of the serpent!

Nothing! A voice came out of the depths of the earth that said to me:

— You are in our power!

— No!

And yet they stood still and motionless. Another voice:

— If you are hardened and wrought by the chisel of God, by us you shall be reduced to fragments!

I climbed upon a large stone so as to have the means to flee. A more terrible sight I never had to see: from where the voice came there issue monstrous giants:

— Prostrate yourself and weep! beg us for mercy!

— That shall never be!

— And it shall be now!

— Never!

— Do you resist?

— I shall always resist!

A deep cavern opens, and an infinity of souls, who had been vanquished, assure me that I too shall have to be like them. With all the voice I had I called upon my God: nothing! More than ever they advanced and appeared sure of seizing their prey; the two lions laid their paws upon the great stone on which I was standing. When I perceived this, I drew the crucifix from my breast:

— Stop!

They do not move; they remain thus motionless, and a deep silence falls over the whole valley. My soul was upheld by an extraordinary strength, but my humanity was more than ever cast down, while one of these, the most enraged, mocks me, saying:

— Your power is not enough to drive us out, whereas we here in a single instant can possess you.

The desolation is indescribable, the stopping of the breath, the nerves were writhing… My voice:

— You possess all power!

With a piercing voice (I ordered them):

— In the name of God, return to your chains!

Oh! what was the horrible upheaval of that land! It seemed that the sky had lowered itself and joined the earth; everything had been turned upside down; where had my stone been flung? I saw nothing more.

Roses gathered among the thorns to offer them to Our Lady.

I found myself in the middle of a rose garden all in bloom, only (that) the long thorns pierced my whole body. I stood motionless looking at the beautiful roses, but I was so disconcerted that I did not dare to pluck one and make the offering to the beautiful sovereign Mary; I felt the pricks so strongly that I was afraid to make the slightest movement. I looked at the sky and remained silent. I hear a step approaching: who can it be? I would have liked to cover myself with those leaves, but I did not find enough of them. He comes near me, asking me why I was crouching so among those thorns, and whether I did not notice that there were many roses to gather which were too full-blown:

— What do you fear?

I remained silent; I did not know what to answer him. Who can it be that invites me to come out? how shall I get out, since I am in the middle of the rose garden? That gracious young man goes on:

— Eh! where is your faith?

I felt myself shaken by those words; I sprang up, I ran with quick steps among the thorns and felt nothing of pricks, only the pain of the first ones I had received: they gave me most acute pain. I gathered the most full-blown and kept them all in my lap to offer them to the most holy Virgin. And that young man was watching me. When I found myself almost at the end of that rose garden, he addressed other words to me, saying:

— And the thorns?

Full of shame, kneeling with my face to the ground, I asked God’s pardon; and that gracious young man made me rise and with a sweet smile (said to me):

— Peace be with you!

And he left me. Having finished gathering those roses, having come out of the rose garden, I set out to reach a temple and lay the roses at the feet of the Virgin; but, however far I walked, I never arrived. I found many shepherds and always asked them where the house of the Lord was and how far it was to reach it, and whether there was an image of the most holy Virgin: they all answered me that it was very far off, that I had too far to walk.

Weary, a sharp pain seized me from the wounds, which were still bleeding. I sat down:

— Oh! my Love, sweet comfort of those who suffer, my strength! invigorate my nerves so that I may reach your feet!

But, overcome by weariness, I fell asleep.

When I woke, I had the beautiful rays of the moon upon my brow, a brightness by which everything in those fields could be very well distinguished, as by day. At first, the thought of the night…, alone!…, I felt something of fear; but at once there came to me the thought of the words of that young man: Little faith! and of having passed through that rose garden without a single prick. At this reflection I grew calm.

I awaited the morning to set out on my journey again. Meanwhile I open my lap where the roses were: oh! no longer roses, but a great providence! My voice:

— Walk along this path: you will find those who groan, and you will provide for them; moreover, a great number of these little ones: you will take care of them, bringing them into my field; there is a good shepherdess there: entrust them to her watchfulness. Hard struggle to save the workers in danger — Helped by a mysterious old woman.

After a short way, as many of these creatures joined the others, before arriving I had a great number of them. Having reached the hut, the shepherdess came forward, all joyful: what a gracious welcome she gave us! All animated, I presented to her these poor creatures who no longer had the appearance of human beings, so badly reduced were they. What was my amazement! She went close to the most deformed and caressed them and, eagerly, would have wished all at once to give them the greatest care. I stood in admiration and rejoiced at how God had deigned to put so much charity into that heart, and how he will take delight in it!

At this reflection, I begged her to let me too render my service; but no sooner was I tasting immense pleasure in tidying those little bodies than, behold, my voice:

— Go, run with all the strength you have! Great lions have set out from a forest to go and strike terror into one of my farmsteads, where there are dear country girls.

I ran swiftly; I arrived near the cottage, and they were coming in fury. I stepped before them armed with my Crucifix:

— Stop! — I cried.

They halt; but, roaring, they make me understand that they do not want to turn back.

— In the name of God, go back! You have nothing to do here.

They go back, tumbling one over the other. I believed I had fulfilled my mission and calmly made my way to the farmstead. I went in and found the country girls, some of them sleeping and others standing idle; others, on seeing me, would have liked to run away. I asked for their guide and they answered that she was sleeping. I asked them many questions, but I was little or not at all satisfied with their answers; meanwhile I heard a loud din: what can it be? Not even at this were they roused, but those who were busy kept casting glances at me!

The din draws nearer and I go out quickly. Horrible sight! Giants of men order me to leave that labyrinth — so they called it — which was their property. I went up to them and (said to them):

— Why do you want me to leave this farmstead, when my Lord sent me here to defend it and to save those poor shepherdesses who are in it?

Two of the most bearded mock me, ordering me to withdraw.

— Never! — I answered them — I must fulfill the will of my God!

The struggle grows strong; with force I called for help: no one moved! At last another, more terrible, comes up to me:

— Withdraw! They do not come because they are already mine, and the guide sleeps, because she lies drowsy in her lethargy of all her evil ideas; she is a mire of pride! She awaits her wages from us.

I felt myself freeze.

— No! go away! Cast your wages into the abyss!

What a combat! My legs were giving way. They were gaining ground more than ever, because whenever they were close to me I would step back so as not to be touched by such fierce men.

— Stop! do not come any further! Enough! you are too bold.

They mutter together, and I hear them say:

— Let us arm ourselves! so we shall cut her to pieces.

— Cut me to pieces? Nothing else will happen in me but (to have) accomplished the will of my Lord, who sent me here to defend this farmstead.

— The inhabitants are ours!

— Not all of them!

Barbarous people, they move in fury. But a great and immense work! A large body of cavalry comes in fury toward me; and it was a charge. At this sight, those assassins fled, and I found myself surrounded by such gracious light horsemen.

— Oh! good people, who has sent you here? Their caparisons dazzled me; they gave me no other answer.

— Clear the farmstead as quickly as possible! Out with all those who are in it: leave the two who are about to arrive from work.

So it was done. Having come out of the farmstead, everything had vanished. Alone in the midst of those unfortunate girls, who made me toil to urge them to walk! Meanwhile I was thinking of the words: «Run there where there are dear country girls!»

— My God! these certainly are not according to your heart, they cannot be «dear» to you — so I kept repeating to myself.

My voice:

— The two whom you left are most dear to me. Did I not go in search of one little sheep when I had 99 (cf. Mt 18:12)? So, will there be no more hope of setting these back on the right path?

I wearied myself exhorting them, but they were words that fell among the stones: one could see that they drew no profit from them. What to do? Having arrived near a river, they sat down; I invited them to follow me, as the hour was late. Unwillingly they followed me, and having arrived at a field where there were good people, I left a portion of them there.

At last I found a good old woman and begged her to help me set on the right path these creatures who for a long time had been living within a farmstead whose master was the Lord. She listened to me attentively, but did not stir at all to help me; I begged her so much that she consented and, going up to them, with eloquent words she exhorted them to return to the way of the Lord. So great was the pleasure I felt in hearing her speak that I stood as in ecstasy.

After a long discourse they began to throw on the ground certain things that gave off a stench, and they trampled on them. What are they doing? The good old woman laid her hand upon their heads and then said to me:

— Not far from here there are certain good cultivators: you will hand them over to them, so that they may teach them to cultivate the fair ground of their souls.

And having said this, she vanished. As we went along they talked among themselves; I understood them little. A few steps before reaching the cultivators they stop and, with big tears, thank me. Confused at having done nothing, I was almost moved: all that I did — I told them — was all the work of God, I had done nothing.

— That old woman, from the wild beasts we were, destroyed us and remade us perfectly.

Where — they said to me — did you come to know that old woman?

— Just as you came to know her.

— Let us go back and look for her!

I perceived that this thought of theirs was from the enemy, so that they would turn back and not reach the cultivators.

No! — I added — let us go on, for with those good cultivators too we shall find pasture for your souls.

They were persuaded and, having arrived, I handed them over to those good shepherds and withdrew. What was my surprise at seeing beside me the gracious old woman, who in a loving but severe tone enjoins me not to turn back, because I would have found barbarous people.

— Must I, then, stay here without moving?

— No!

I look and see no trace that might set me on that path. (Seeing me) so troubled, the old woman began to comfort me:

— Come with me, for I will lead you to a safe place; and remember not to make such mistakes another time: before leaving those shepherds with those shepherdesses you ought to have made quite sure whether God had traced the path for you.

And meanwhile I set out together (with her), but what terror I felt within me! Who can this be? Meanwhile voices of vagabond men could be heard, and I hastened 44 my step as much as I could. I heard the sound of a little bell: so we are near a temple — I said to myself; — but she spoke no more. Having arrived at a small square,

— Here we are! — she said to me, pointing out the church.

Oh! how relieved I felt! I tried to thank her in whatever way I knew, but she, smiling at me, made me enter that beautiful little church all lit up. I turned round, and she was no longer there! Casting myself on the ground I thanked the Most High and then asked him who that lady was; a voice:

— One day you will know!

But her words remained well engraved in my soul. 45.

A hermit, worker of prodigies. «God works great things in Himself and through Himself alone».

Having come out of the temple, I at once looked to see whether my path was traced, and with joy I set my foot upon it, running without deviating. But a poor hermit — so he appeared to be — stops me, asking me where I was going. In passing I answered that that way had been traced for me and I could not stop. But he at once added that the same Lord had given him many faculties and that he possessed great treasures. He showed me a beautiful garden, and that he used its fruits for the sick, and whoever ate them was healed, and moreover shared in the graces he had. But how can that ever be? I thought to myself. No sooner had I had this thought than he added that it was not a single tree that produced these fruits, but rather each one had its own virtue. What can it be?

With great respect he invited me to enter it. Out of eagerness to see what my God was working most wisely, I entered. Where am I? On every side there were trees with lovely fruits, and he told me how they had been tasted by an infinity of souls, and that they felt great things and prophesied. Many things I heard with pleasure, others frightened me. He spoke of God with eloquence, and one could see that he had much fine knowledge; but I always kept my foot ready to move on, however much I was begged to stay. No! I wanted to take my leave.

And so, going on my way, I found a good soul who, on seeing me, at once asked me whether I had seen the hermit. Without stopping I answered that I had seen him. She accompanies me and tells me of great wonders. Every now and then she asked me whether I believed it:

— Why not?

But seeing that I never answered her, she begged me to tell her why I listened thus in silence.

— Good woman, as to what you tell me of all that the hermit works, my mind and all my intellectual powers are wholly occupied with the great and majestic divine ordering, and how God works great things in Himself and through Himself alone, and the creature lends itself for the use of the divine ordinances, as when he gives to one of those apples the virtue of healing 46 that sick person, always by means of faith. She interrupts me and, with insolent words, scolds me, wanting to persuade me that it was the hermit who worked great things by his life of mortification, and that, having earned such power from God, he worked at his own good pleasure. I shuddered:

— Either you are a seducing soul or one in need of instruction! Have you ever heard tell of my God, absolute in all things?

But interrupting me, she invites me to turn back and go together to the hermit. My voice:

— Onward! it is not the time; another time you will see him! Running, I went away and saw her no more; I reasoned by myself:

— How fallacious are the opinions of men! how they deceive themselves (in believing that) at the mere sight of so little suffering one must by right have his treasures from God! Oh! truly many crooked ideas and narrow beliefs soon fall into heresy!

I met another shepherd of souls, and this one too stopped me and asked me whether that path led to the hermit. Curtly I answered him:

— Yes.

But he, coming close to me (said to me):

— Perhaps you are coming back from there?

I made no answer. He turns back and accompanies me, seeing me alone. He kept following me. In a severe tone I asked him what he wanted.

— One word only: whether you have spoken with the hermit.

— I have spoken with him.

— Have you brought back fruits and gifts from him?

— Oh! poor slave! I do not possess even a corner where I might lay up treasures.

— So you do not desire any? And yet, if you come back with me, I assure you that he will have more than one given to you.

Politely I thanked him.

So, you make nothing of the graces and treasures of the hermit, which are given him by God to dispense?

— One grace only I desire — (I answered) with a deep sigh that came from the depths of my soul — and it is to be able to fulfill perfectly the will of God! I desire nothing else!

But he became ever more pressing and kept on speaking to me of graces, and asked me a thousand questions. Tired of listening to him, I begged him to withdraw, as I had nothing more to answer to his questions. Embittered, he leaves me. 47.

Two false guides try to turn her from the path.

Weary, I sat down, thinking that it would have been better if I had gone with that shepherd to see the graces that God worked through that hermit. All of a sudden I heard a horrible noise and perceived that I was in the dark. Oh! how that path was changed into a cavern! a thousand voices could be heard shrieking and begging for mercy. I am lost! Most holy Virgin, heavenly hosts, come and illumine this cavern: I am dying of fright! The roaring of lions, the shrieking of wild beasts, the rumble of continual thunder, the cries of lost people dragging chains: among the irons bolts could be heard snapping. Mercy, help, take me out of so terrible a hell! And such becomes my terror that I was about to faint. A gloomy voice:

— From me alone can you have help.

And he showed himself all charity, but I did not see him. I trembled like a leaf in the wind; I felt my strength failing me. What then? The bold monster stretched out his hand to me and said to me:

— Come with me, and I will show you the way out.

— Oh! no! — I cried — if it so pleases my God that I remain, even torn to pieces by your ferocious beasts, I shall remain here to fulfill his divine will.

Seductively he provoked me; but, just as my humanity, in decline, was about to give way, a gracious hand seized me and, in a bound, I found myself in a most beautiful and gracious cloud: wherever I turned my gaze, I saw azure. How I breathed an air of whose fragrance I could form no idea!

— How beautiful you are, and gentle! Sweet is your breeze! I looked around:

— Where can the one have gone who brought me to so gracious a place?

I felt myself reviving and my strength returning; I tried to settle myself well in it, without thinking of anything, forgetful of the past. My voice:

— You have still too much to fight!

The cloud vanished, and where am I? I look attentively to see whether the path is traced and, quite sure of setting my foot rightly upon it, I set out on the way. A few steps on, a shepherd stops me, all wrapped in a heavy cloak.

— Eh! stop! — he says to me — Where are you heading?

where are you going?

— The will of God will lead me.

With strong threats he orders me to stop.

— Never!

He accuses me of having done great damage in a field of the Lord, and that the cultivators who are there are about to be lost because of me, and that I should quickly think of going to help them. I looked around and saw that there was no other path except the one I was following. With submission I answered him that it was not granted to me to do this, it not being the will of my God.

How he flew into a rage! he hurled words of fire at me; but he was never able to make me deviate. He joined me, and yet he was running. Oh! how that company of his pained me! He tried to delude me with heavenly tales, but they produced something painful in me. Having arrived in a forest, he took fright and would not enter.

Accompanied by two little birds.

Most happy, I entered it alone, without caring about anything else. I kept running where my path led me. Every kind of birdsong could be heard. Two very beautiful ones come near me and, singing, keep me company. Every now and then they would make a lament; and I asked them what was the matter, I asked them whether they were hungry. How charming it was! with a sweet song they made me understand no, and they hopped all around me; and then once more they fell into sadness and made their lament. I tried to persuade them and invited them to let themselves be carried, for I would have kept them in my lap; but no!

— You are right not to come with me, because certainly I could give you nothing good, laden as I am with infamy: for this I am reduced to this state, being unable to have my God. Only fields and crags, thorns, mountains! I possess no woodlands for myself. You are right to make me hear a mournful song, for I well understand the approach of a terrible misdeed. God bless you for the charity you have in following me; but I pray you, end your lament, for I feel it is too painful to me.

Who would believe it? They stopped and, silent, followed me. Having arrived near a brook, they began to sing with many others who joined them, and they were so many that they dazzled me and, like a dense swarm, prevented me from continuing my way.

I halted:

— What do you want, dear little creatures? A voice says to me:

— Stop!

As soon as I sat down near the brook, they all vanished; only the two companions remained with me. Now they would go close to drink and then, so charmingly, they would look at me as though they wanted to invite me to drink. Beautiful and crystal-clear was that water; but I do not thirst for this water, but rather I feel a great burning thirst for that of the Samaritan woman. She too had offended your heart, and yet (you) quenched her thirst (cf. Jn 4:7-26).

More than ever those two little birds sang and hopped near me. For a long while I stayed up on this stone: a rustling began to be heard. A big serpent was coming toward me. Without heeding anything else I threw myself into that stream and cried out; but that ferocious animal could do nothing to me. The two little birds always around me. What to do? Get out of the water? I shall certainly find that ugly animal. So I remained perplexed.

— Oh! my God! command these two little creatures, made by you with a heavenly charm: tell them to show me the way I must take. Oh! how I feel all the oppression of this journey: alone! the path broken off! what to do? Night is drawing on, and here, in the water, will you leave me to remain? I shall die of fright! No! A voice:

— Look!

— Where? — I said to myself; and they kept on drinking and then looking at me. In the very stream lay the path. Running, I said to myself:

— Dear little creatures, I understand well. 48.

They were not inviting me to drink, but pointing out my path to me. How many sharp stones! how many frights from the howls of wild beasts! And I never saw the end. At last, having reached the end, whom do I see? That shepherd who would not come with me comes up to me grumbling and tells me an infinity of stories. I stayed and listened, but unwillingly.

The night was far advanced; my two companions had stopped on a tree a few steps away. He invites me to stop, assuring me that it was the will of God and that the two little creatures too had stopped; and that I would see by the fact itself that it is God who so wills, and that my path would never vanish, but I would find it the next day, since that night I would do him a great charity, for by my stopping he would be helped and so, confessing his illness to me, he would be healed of it.

I stopped, and what the shepherd said came to pass. The next day, with a thousand thanks, he accompanied me onto the path, which I found beautiful and better laid out, for I walked without feeling any discomfort in my poor feet, which were still wounded from the way made in the water. New adversaries and new dangers.

I have lost my God!

I walked for long hours without discomfort, and so beautiful and gracious a creation was pleasing to my sight and also to my affection. There was a moment when I took delight in it and, without noticing, let natural feeling feed upon that delightful view. Walking thus, I found a shepherd and he asked me where I was going.

— I do not know!

— Are you sure you are walking the right way?

— Most sure!

— Are you not afraid of meeting people who may molest you?

— No!

And he went along with me.
