He told me many things about the duties of submission that we have, and that souls make much gain when they are guided in everything by their suffering: they have a hundred per cent gain. Meanwhile I kept gazing at such dear and beautiful delights of the plain, without paying heed to being accompanied. I gave a deep sigh:

— How beautiful you are, O valleys and delightful hills, bushes gilded by the reflection of the sun, clusters of lilies!

And I stopped.

— A gloom takes hold of me: I can no longer reason. Only my God, who created you, and certainly you serve him better than I do and graciously adorn his earth… I, alas!

And I made a loud lament, without noticing that there was a shepherd with me; and I ran in haste like one who seeks to rid herself of an unbearable weight. The poor shepherd stops me, begging me to go more slowly, and to make use of him if I had something that gave me pain, for he would have relieved me in everything. With a gesture of surprise (I said to him):

— What? you still here? I need nothing: One alone I seek, but I do not find him; He alone is all my happiness.

He wanted to persuade me, but to no avail. Meanwhile he drew close to me and, with persuasions, wanted me to heed him in every matter. I continued on my way. I saw a wall before me; there was no longer any trace of road: only a very high wall. Oh! how I felt my breast bursting with fright! The shepherd seemed triumphant at my halting and so he said to me:

— With me you will have to stay!

I shrieked aloud, in case I could be heard by someone, but nothing! A big dog came running.

— My God, I am lost!

But no: the dog puts the shepherd to flight and I remain near the wall, alone. After a few moments that poor beast comes back and, all panting, comes up to me.

— Poor beast! I do not know how to show you my gratitude, having nothing to give you: I handed everything over to my God.

And he, as if he understood the word, thanked me with charming movements.

— Who sent you? Have you no master?

He took the hem of my dress in his mouth and, turning round, I see in the distance, which I could barely make out, people sitting. Who can they be?

— Are those your masters?

Wagging his tail, he lies down on the ground near me. What can it be? He was very beautiful, but I did not dare to touch him. I knelt down and prayed, beseeching God to show me where and how I may cross this wall: there is no way out! After much supplication, I fell asleep.

This poor beast came to wake me, placing a paw on my arm.

— What is it? — I said, crying out.

I see near the wall something like a rise, (by which) it would have taken little to climb up. At once I perceived that it was the path prepared for me, and I quickly climbed. Only, having reached the top, how was I to get down? Such a height!… Throw myself down? The dog was barking, but did not climb. I turned round: a band of evildoers were running to reach me. I threw myself down and landed upright on the path. Running, I reached a farmstead.

— Oh! good people! defend me, for evildoers are running to outrage me!

A gracious country girl comes before me:

— Do not be afraid, for no one will dare to enter this farmstead.

She asked me who I was.

— A poor slave, who for a long time has been sent by my Master here and there. To my misfortune I am not capable of doing anything good, being a compound of wickedness and imperfect in all my actions. Oh! how I would deserve to have been driven out already, were it not that he is infinitely merciful.

She comes close to me and, in all confidence, tells me that the shepherd whom I had left is hatching great plots to oppress me and is working together with others, who want to do so much as to reduce the work of the Lord to a sorry state. Oh! how troubled I was! At once I asked her what I ought to do, and how she knew it. (She said to me):

— Many things I heard with my own ear, and you will have much to suffer. All his threats terrified me. Do not be troubled: they will lose.

But this assurance of hers gave me no peace at all and, in a kind and gracious manner, she dismissed me, telling me to hasten my step so that night would not overtake us on those roads. Where shall I go? what will become of me? what will they do to me?

Still running, I reached the end of the road and there was a bridge to cross. Whether it was that (I was) wholly absorbed in what I had heard, or permitted by my God, I found myself on the top of a crag. Seeing that precipice, I at once launched myself onto the bridge. But, what terror! I perceive that it is in mid-air, without any rail on either side, and down below a river where the water rushed in great billows: a terrible sight! I would have liked to turn back, but there was no longer any kind of path. I look and look again, I find absolutely nothing to hold on to. Go forward? and how? Those planks were swaying. With all the voice I had I called for help to my Lord: no one! I gathered all my strength and on all fours tried to reach the end. Never! I pressed the Crucifix to my breast: and nothing! From afar a loud lament could be heard, and I looked: it was a dear creature who was weeping bitterly because she saw me about to be swallowed up from one moment to the next. I made signs to her not to grieve, but she went on.

I seemed to be at the end, when one of those who were to maltreat me comes forward and gives the bridge a violent shake. Oh! then indeed all the planks swayed, and there was barely a small crosspiece for me! I remained clinging to it. That poor creature who was weeping came close to me and called out loudly that I should get off quickly. But how? She, more frightened than ever, kept calling me, but did not dare to come near. The bridge breaks loose and I plunge headlong into that great torrent, caught up between the current and those stones. I felt myself dragged along without a shadow of being able to save myself. I struggled with all the strength I had: I remained bound (amid) the ebb and flow of this immense river. I was about to faint; I had nothing left in me but the thought of my God alone! The river rises, and a great roar of the water! Here I am, thrown onto the bank into a bush of big thorns! My God, have you abandoned me? And so, torn with sorrow, I wept bitterly.

One refreshment only I would wish: my God, whom I have lost!

Alone! I heard nothing but the noise of the water, and the fear kept growing in me that this river might come and seize me again. I got up from that bush: and where am I, and to what state am I reduced! I was streaming with blood from every part of my body. I look at my wounded hands and feet: oh! how to remedy this? And I wept with loud sobs and called upon my God. There was no trace of road; the sky grows black, and the thunder and lightning terrify me. I almost fainted; when loud cries drew near, and they were the voices of men.

— Angel Saint Raphael, have you no pity?

But I (could) pronounce these words only very badly. A rumbling of hell joins those voices, which I heard coming toward me at a great gallop; a great light comes down, and how? Two gracious angels intertwine their wings; they wrap me in them and carry me away, leaving me in a cottage where there was no one but an old man and an old woman, saying to me:

— Here you are safe; the battle of those who wanted to kill you (is over); do not fear, they are defeated and have gone away.

These good people showed me a thousand kindnesses; but such was my pain, and also the hurt that the wounds caused me, above all one so deep, that I had no voice to answer what they asked me. They began to say:

— Do you know those two who brought you here?

Coldly I answered them:

— Yes.

— They left us some refreshment to give you.

— I need nothing.

— You see that you do not know at all who those two were.

Coming to myself (I said):

— Oh! good woman, be patient: I am in the utmost sorrow; I feel myself torn apart! Ah! have pity if I do not answer you!

— But I tell you that they left me something to refresh you.

— Oh! one refreshment only — I answered — I would wish: my God, whom I have lost!

— No! — they both answered.

— And if that were not so, he would have come to my aid.

— What are you saying? — (replied) these two old people in a loud tone.

— Do you know where he is? Oh! why can I not see him?

— The two angels who carried you here on their wings were sent by Him.

And resting my head on the palm of my hand (I said):

— I ask your pardon, O good people! My wounds, the so tearing pain I feel, the fright that still makes me seem to be in that torrent…!

And I fell silent. The woman comes up to me and hands me the balm that the two angels had left her, saying to me:

— The two angel messengers have left you this to soothe your wounds.

I looked at it; but, weeping copiously (I said):

— Never shall I use it for myself! My Crucified One had nothing for his wounds. I kiss it, and with care I shall keep it for the sick.

And I went on weeping. Behold, once again the two messengers!

— Oh! my deliverers, I give you thanks! I pray you to tell me where is my Good? my Lord, when did you speak to him? what did he tell you to tell me?

— Nothing! Only that that field, which those evildoers wanted to destroy, will yield beautiful and gracious plants; your blood has watered it very well. The enemies have all been put to flight and, on your return, you will rejoice to see how flourishing and tall the wheat is. 49.

They vanished.

She receives from a kind lady the plan of the road to be traveled; it is snatched from her by a shepherd.

Which way shall I have to go to reach this field? There is no road. These two old people tried to console me and told me many things, all about the life of my Lord; but while they would have liked me to share in them, they did not notice that I felt keen sorrow at them deep within: the sufferings of my God caused me such sorrow that I burst into floods of tears. And they were convinced that I loved my Lord very much. The old woman took me by the hand and, raising me up graciously, showed me the field. And I added:

— And the way to go there, where is it?

All of a sudden I perceive that there is near me a servant of God, who died in the odor of sanctity (who says to me):

— Here is the road!

— I, set foot on so disastrous a way? And how shall I have the courage to ask the one you tell me I shall find, who will give me the exact plan of the way I shall have to go?

Having said this, he answered me no longer to hold back, but to obey, for it is the will of God. I fell silent and set out at the beginning of a long road. Behold a shepherd, and at once I asked him to give me the plan of the ground I had to travel, that this was the will of my God and that I was doing this part out of obedience, and I was doing it all mortified. He looked at me, and then answered me that he would give it to me as soon as possible. And so I waited for it calmly. Then a kind lady hands me, by order of that shepherd, the plan of the road I was to travel.

Without further answer I set out and, along the way, I was very mortified because I had not at all begged that dear lady to come with me; I grieved not a little. Reasoning thus, I see that on this way there were only bushes and uncultivated plants. But where, my God, is the beautiful field that you have promised me? Nothing! I began to weep and make a loud lament, because I was tired and night was drawing near; nothing could be heard but the howls of wild beasts. What torment is this? I went on reasoning and running. When the night is far advanced, there comes before me a shepherd, all in disarray, who stops me, snatching from my hand the plan that that lady had given me, and rudely abuses me and, mocking me, leaves me. 50. What to do? where to take shelter? Almost bewildered, I threw myself face down on the ground and besought the Most High to come to my aid. A voice:

— What? for so little do you lose heart?

With a rush I rose and, running, reached a very large estate, where a man of God lived, and having run to his feet I begged for pity and mercy. Such was the welcome of that angel, more than man! Having heard my reasons, and seeing me in such a sorry state, he did nothing but pity and encourage me, telling me that I would soon have my new plan, and that he blessed my journey, which was very pleasing to God. I took heart and asked him whether it was really true that my Lord, in these terrible combats of mine, remains satisfied and accepts the continual torment of this journey of mine.

— Very much! — he answered me, and that I should not doubt that he would keep his gaze continually upon me.

I began to tell him that I am always alone, because he left me so, and that he should tell him that I always desire him near. He assured me that he would do everything. And he dismissed me. Oh! what was my joy!

I was not slow to be troubled and become sad, because I had indeed found a harsh shepherd who ordered me to stop running, that by now there is no longer any road for me to reach that field which I had set myself to run to. What to do? My voice:

— Run! and do not be distressed, because I am always near you. Awaited by many workers in the field sanctified by the presence of the Lord.

A gentleman comes up to me and assures me that my desire will soon be satisfied. And I waited always in peace. Another comes and begs me to make my way to a certain cottage, all in ruins, for there the gentleman who had things to hand over to me was waiting for me. I ran without delay and truly found someone who handed over to me a small cottage, so that I might work that little garden, which was all in poor condition. I worked at it unceasingly; but there was a big serpent hidden there which, whenever I withdrew for a single instant, undid the work. And for a long time those walls had to remain so. When I least expected it, behold the kind lady who comes to meet me and puts a check on the workers; and in a moment the work is completed. But it still had to be inspected so as to obtain permission to occupy the fine building. I received many kindnesses from this lady, and moreover she wanted to help me in my needs; but nothing availed me, because she left me little leave to make any journey, and there was always joined in me the ardent desire to walk a great deal so as to reach that field which they had promised me. Without heeding anything, I made a dash and went away running, full of a strong desire to arrive.

Already I was beginning to see very great trees; the way was beautiful. Every now and then I would meet a little country girl, always very gracious, and they assured me that it would not take long to arrive; another assured me of its beauty, another told me that much produce is to be drawn from that field. When I was almost near, there comes before me one more gracious than all the other country girls and, as soon as she saw me, she embraced me, saying:

— Oh! it is you whom we have been awaiting for so long! May you be blessed by God!

— Tell me, who are you?

— A worker who is waiting for you to give me work. But how many like me there are over there!

— Have they all already begun to work?

None of them. I tell you that they are all waiting for you. How did you know that I was to come?

For many years we have desired to be able to serve the Lord by working in his vineyard, but it was never granted to us. We shed many prayers and tears, but nothing! We saw the field beautiful and always flourishing, but greatly in need of being cultivated. Beautiful plants! and many are spoiled at the root. At last, after so much sighing, there came a fair and gracious shepherd, at the mere sight of whom we remained in ecstasy and, with supernatural ways, he announced your coming to us and promised great things to whoever shall be faithful to you in the work. And he vanished.

— Ah! — I gave a cry — It was my Lord! Tell me where he stopped to speak to you and the ground on which he set his most holy foot.

Oh! how breathlessly I ran to see where my God had been!

— A few steps more — the country girl began to say — and we are there.

What was the palpitation, the indescribable joy! This poor girl tried to calm me and strove to stop me so that I might catch my breath. Here it is! I threw myself on the ground and with all my soul kissed and kissed again that ground. And then I would have wished to enclose it in my breast, which was throbbing strongly. The poor girl, who did not yet understand, and whose heart had not yet tasted and experienced the effects of the love of God, looked at me, and then (remained) unmoved, bored, and what is more, held a low opinion of it. I gave no thought to anything, but that ground… Here, my Love, you have been! Oh! how strong is this thought! I gathered up that ground carefully. But no! I must carry this earth with me, and I pressed it tightly to my breast. My voice:

— No! no one shall be able to trample on this; my angels stand guard over it.

Oh! how painful the parting was to me! I did not insist. As soon as I arrived I truly found a beautiful, immense and gracious field. The workers all around gave me a great welcome.

— Tell me, have all of you seen my Lord? and heard him speak? Oh! how beautiful he is!

— Not all of us (they answered). They invited me to sit down and were eager to make me observe the beauty of the field. There were fruit trees of every kind, and of many of these they made me observe that a small woodworm had crept in around them, which was gnawing at their pith, and they were dying. Other weeds, which spread long around the vine, took away its sap, and it could not (bear fruit). Among almost all the wheat cockle had sprung up. From the sight, together with the account, a serious thought took hold of me: so vast a field, with such a variety of cultivations, and so few workers! I leaned back pensively; but my voice:

— Who will do this? you and the workers, or the Master?

I was ashamed and, smiling, I told those dear creatures to set to work. Several of them tell me that they lack the tools and that, if I do not provide them, they cannot obey me.

— Without faith! Come with me!

But these sat down. Others, who were the greater number, followed me. Having arrived, and each having been given her work, behold, they all had most beautiful tools. I see one who had them more beautiful than the others, and I was eager to know the reason, and who had given them to her. Without the others noticing, I go up to her and ask her from whom she had received such beautiful tools. With the greatest respect she says to me:

— From you!

— What? — to myself — I did not notice that I had given them to her.

— With your own hands — she answers.

And I looked at her without saying anything more. I well understood the mystery. Oh! my God! Such great goodness!

And so, working, in a short time the field was made clean and all the plants luxuriant.

Beautiful is your work, my God!

Those who had remained seated we found rotted, dead from idleness!

What a surprise for all! I entrusted all the others to the one who had the most beautiful tools and, with the blessing of my God, I would have wished to remain with them.

My voice: it is time to reap! Go where there is great need: you will find something to do. 51.

Struggle against importunate thoughts, and against the temptation to give up suffering.

I took leave of those creatures and set out on my usual path. Ah! how wearisome it was! In that solitude certain insipid creatures, buzzing like flies, whispered certain silly nonsense into my mind; they amused themselves by taking away my good thoughts; and in my conversing with my God, giving him an account of what I had done and asking him for what I needed, these became so importunate; strongly interweaving their disjointed words, they formed a very strong, insistent confusion, and as though they had taken possession of my mind, they did not allow me to dwell rightly and calmly on any reasonings other than their insipid suggestions.

It was a struggle! My intellect rejected them strongly, and so the combat grew fierce.

Who would ever have thought that as many more would come upon these big flies and take possession of my mind, or darken my intellect! I thrust them aside with all my strength, and behold, at once they were masters on the other side. In short, it was a curious business: they would have liked to take from me the power of thinking of my God, filling my mind with silly thoughts and, had they succeeded, putting me in a state of anxiety. What did I do? I ordered them to leave me, for they bored me enough, and took refuge at the feet of my Crucified; but nothing! With force they tried to drive me even from that dear place. They made immense efforts; though such small creatures, they were far more trying than the big ones, because in the inanity of their buzzing there was an unbearable tedium. It was curious when these paved the way for the big ones, for these took their theme from the small ones and passed on to the coarsest things, whispering them into my mind; and they insistently wanted me to consent. But I stood firm! The struggle was ridiculous in itself, because with open eyes I discerned their maneuvers well. On the other hand, it weighed upon me to have to drive them off all the time; meanwhile they took from me the taste for the prayer I wished to make, so that my God might deliver me from so painful a state. And when I ran, they pinched me and stopped me.

After a long and painful encounter with these tiresome creatures, I seized in fury a good dose of sharp thorns and, mastering their entrance well, I remained free, breathing the gentle air of those delightful fields.

I remained silent, with my mind resting on the side of my Crucified One; I felt that I was gathering strength and fine insights for the way that still remained for me to travel. Then I perceive myself near a cavern, and the road traced to go inside. The fear: where shall I go in that darkness? who will be there? Oh! all trembling, I no longer find the support of my God, because as I approached that cavern He withdrew.

Having walked for an hour groping and weeping, I asked my God to have pity on me and to open a light so that I might see where I was: nothing! I hear a terrible rumble and shrieking voices. Alas, I am lost! I turn to go back: behold a thick wall that does not allow me to return, and I shrieked all the louder, calling upon my God.

I hear armed people approaching me, and they say:

— Let us kill her!

Ah! how I felt myself fainting! I fell dumb and tried as best I could to hide; but nothing! At last I hear roaring: these are lions! Oh! most holy Virgin, help, have pity on me! Nothing! One of these takes me by the hem of my dress and says to me:

— Do you see? He who led you here is the very one you love so much! Have done, once and for all, with suffering so much for Him; come with me and I will lead you to a charming palace: there you will find every sort of delight and you will be happy; you will have nothing left to desire.

— Oh, no! — (I said) while this monster was reasoning thus — I want to suffer with my God! And he, worse still:

— And where is He? Here you are in my power: come willingly; if not, I will take you and carry you wherever I please.

What terror! Every nerve in me was trembling. Like a flash of lightning an infinity of things passed through my mind. I commanded him to leave me and to go back whence he had come, loathsome dragon! But nothing! Others joined him with torches of fire. I was lost! Already my mind could no longer form any thought. Shrieking aloud, I called upon my God; but they raged all the worse. I summoned all the strength I could, but I fell back again. One of the most terrible seducers, a still more loathsome spirit, comes up to me and tried to pity me; had it been granted him, he would even have caressed me with his loathsome hands, or rather paws; but he did as much with words. Oh! how terribly he spoke to me:

— Will you love Him who makes you suffer so much, while from me you will have nothing but joys?

Saint Michael, defender and guide.

— Away! I want to suffer for my God!

At last he says to me:

— Come, for I will lead you out of this cavern and be a faithful guide to you, so that none of all the lions that dwell in it will be able to harm you.

— No! I want only the guidance of my God, not yours. Go away, infernal monster!

— Then, if you do not consent, I will give orders to these who stand there to devour you, and you will be led to a horrible place. You will die torn to pieces by the beasts.

— Away! — I shrieked, calling my God to my aid.

This ugly one, seeing that I was abandoned — so he believed — hurls himself upon me to seize me. A strong voice, with a most vivid light:

— Stop! What belongs to God you are not permitted to touch.

Every noise dies away. The cavern is lit with a beautiful light. I raised my eyes to where the voice had come from. Oh! who could it be! Michael the Archangel! (who said to me):

— From now on, by order of my God, I shall be your guide, your companion on your long journeys.

How I tried, with all the power of my words, to thank my God for having sent him and given him to me as my guide and defense! But I was utterly exhausted. I wanted to thank Saint Michael and made signs to him that he had brought me such great consolation, and I wanted to find fitting words to thank him: the more I strained, the more my strength failed. Having come out of that cavern in a flash, he made me sit down beside him. How beautiful he was! He sheathed his sword 52 and looked at me with compassion. I said to him:

— I feel so exhausted that I cannot bear up for breathlessness.

— Well then, I will give you a little of my food and it will certainly restore you, giving you strength enough to undertake your journey.

He began to speak of my God and I was in ecstasy over it. Every now and then I interrupted him:

— Shall I have His love? Shall I see Him again? Is He not angry with me? Has He forgotten my common miseries? Is my journey very long? In this valley where I now find myself, will He come here?

And then he told me great things; and again I remained in ecstasy. In the end it was one continual ecstasy. Meanwhile, each time I remained thus, I felt that I was gaining great strength.

— For pity’s sake, do not leave me, stay with me always!

He answered me:

— Always! — and vanished.

What? “Always”, and then he leaves me! I felt full of strength: and how? and from whom did I receive so much nourishment? How sure are the words of my Lord: Man does not live by bread alone (Mt 4:4)!

And so, pondering this, I walked along that delightful path. One thing alone grieved me: that he would always be with me, and yet he has gone away! 53.

VI

A gentleman who willingly hears talk of God, but consults witches.

Many hours of walking had passed and I already felt the weariness of it. I see in the distance a long train of carts approaching, almost all of them empty. What pleasure I felt in the hope I had of being able to climb onto them! And so it was: with their speed they reached me in a moment; I begged those good people to have pity on my weariness.

— Come! get up on one, the emptiest!

And I found no difficulty at all. As it set off at a run, behold, a battalion of devils, all armed, tried to overturn the cart. Oh! what terrible fright! Oh my Saint Michael! where are you? Here he is with his sword drawn, putting these dragons to flight, and he stays with me. Having reached a certain point (he said to me):

— Here you must get down, for there are people waiting for you. And I saw him no more. As soon as I entered so delightful a garden, I see a man of enormous height; he comes before me and asks me what I want and who I am.

— I want nothing, only to do the will of God, who has sent me here. I am a poor slave of my God!

— What and who is this Lord of yours?

— What? you, in the midst of so many delights, do not know the Creator of all these precious plants and flowers of yours?

He begs me to sit down and give him a proper account of what I was telling him. He listened to me with patience and an eagerness to know. After a long discussion, he shows me that he had lived for many years on that estate of his and had never heard anyone speak of God.

— But how can that be? There is even a church close by and, surely, there will be a religious there. In that very place my Lord is to be found.

He answered me that this was meant for his peasants, but not for him. So he had always believed.

— Are you a Jew, then?

— No: I remember that they always told me I had been baptized.

I look around me and see no one. Night was drawing on and I could no longer even think straight. An inner trembling took hold of me, a terrible distress, because I feared that he might notice it. He began to say:

— Your agitation is understandable; although (I take) great pleasure in hearing you, yet you make me sorry for you. Go and rest in that cottage (which he pointed out to me): there you will find good people and you will spend the whole night. Tomorrow I shall expect you.

I thanked him for his courtesy. Taking out of my pocket a lovely little picture of the most holy Virgin, and holding it out to him, I said to him:

— This is our great Mother and Queen of heaven and earth, the Mother of God.

He took it with pleasure and I begged him to kiss it. He did so. And I went away. On the way I found my angel Saint Michael, who accompanied me as far as the cottage. As soon as they saw me, these good people kissed my garment and overwhelmed me with kindnesses; they wanted to give me something to refresh me, but I had no need of their refreshment, only of that of my God. With all of them gathered round, I began to speak of my God, that for Him alone and through Him we must live. A comely peasant girl rises and, coming close, told me that she was warning me against speaking so much of God, because certain persons were in that house who would do me harm. And she told me about that gentleman who, with his feigned manners, had led many persons to perdition. How can this be? — I thought to myself — and yet my angel led me here, and it was certainly he.

When she had finished her account, behold, that very gentleman wished to speak to me and, drawing me aside into a corner, told me that he knew I was in great need for the cultivation of a field and that he had brought me large sums of money, so that I might go on taking on workers to make the field flourish more and more. With what distress I took that money! I looked at him and trembled, always standing firm in my place. I said to him:

— May my God repay you this charity of yours a hundredfold. But more than this, I would feel happy if it were granted me to hear that you are among the number of those who love God so much. He remained thoughtful, and then said to me:

— What advantage shall I have in loving that God who is so much on your mind?

— Oh! — I exclaimed forcefully — the advantage of eternal life, filled with every good and, for ever, an eternity of joys!

— Explain it to me — he said, moved.

I began to speak of the holy Gospel and told him that these were the words of that God who is to judge us; and what a terrible sentence awaits the rich: He says that it is easier for a ship’s cable to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter paradise. 54.

What do you think of that?

And he, once more:

— Who brought you here?

— It was He who spoke to your heart to give me alms.

— I keep some witches and consult them now and then. Before coming here I consulted them and they told me that they can know nothing. They begged me not to let you go where they are.

— Oh! I will tell you who they are! They have dealings with the devil; they are possessed and they fear that my God will unmask them, and that is why they tremble.

After a long discussion he begs me to come back to his castle. My voice:

— No!

I thanked him and answered that I could not. He made me a thousand promises, and told me to ask him: whatever I wanted he would give me.

— No!

He flies into a rage and tells me that he would have me carried there by force by his workers. I felt an icy chill through my whole body.

— My angel! My God!

He mocked me and said to me:

— My witches told me so.

— Call them, and we shall see if they come!

— I shall win!

And already he was beginning to call his men. Just when he thought himself victorious, my angel took me by the arm and, in flight, carried me into the middle of a field where, for want of means of subsistence, all the workers were perishing, and the field was already largely untilled. 55.

A worker under the baneful influence of a shepherd.

While distributing the work I noticed that one of those workers was not healthy and had to be removed quickly, so that she would not pass her sickness on to the others; and so I left her without work. But I had much to struggle with, because she was very proud; motionless, she would not on any account leave that field; neither entreaties nor threats availed, but she wanted to remain fixed in that place. I could not understand what support she had to be so resolute, when I turned and saw a shepherd coming who strongly protected her, assuring her that I had no power over her, but that he alone could place her and keep her wherever she pleased. Seeing this, I was saddened, because that resistance of hers brought much disorder.

I commended to God this matter of such importance and then thought to myself that my angel would see to it. I cannot describe the mockery the devil made of me, deriding me wherever I went. He jeered at me:

— Go on, call your angel; but I alone carry off the victory!

Meanwhile he blinded those two unfortunate ones by hardening their ideas. They swelled with pride and grew ever more sure of their victory. The seducers fiercely played their part and they were convinced, but instead of working the field they stood feeding on their victory.

A dragon comes, very fierce, and announces to me that I shall soon suffer a heavy defeat and that, once they had the victory, I would have to feel horrible pains. I thought that this last part he says will unfortunately be true, because the struggle was becoming fierce. But the certainty that my God would win gave me courage. While I was reasoning thus, I see beside me a most dear creature, who said to me:

— Be at peace, for in a little while you will be victorious; but much else remains for you to suffer.

And she vanished. Who could it be? My angel? No. My voice:

— Leave this ground and run until you find the track marked out by me.

I do not hesitate a moment, and setting foot on the path marked out for me, thinking of what I had left behind, a deep melancholy was my companion. I was not aware that I was climbing, when I find myself on a great height, and I notice that I had beside me a devil who had the form of a simpleton and was making an infinity of foolish antics around me, hopping and laughing; and then he vanished. What can this be, my God? Where and how will this road of yours end? I felt my strength failing and there was still a way to go, when I look all around me and see nothing inhabited. A murmur could be heard in the leaves of the trees; and another night was drawing on and the path was growing dark. What was I to do?

Having sat down beside a tree, weeping and praying, I sent forth a lament. Could it be that ugly simpleton who has imitated the way of marking the road, and that it is not from you, my God? I called my Angel to my aid, but nothing! Trembling with cold and fear, I clutched my breast, sobbing. I fell asleep. A loud rumble awakens me and I find myself covered with a thick woolen blanket. Who could it have been? A voice from the midst of a bush says:

— It was I.

Alas! Then a woman rises and graciously tells me that a gentleman came to her house (and she points out her hut to me) and asked her to bring a blanket to the wayfarer who had fallen asleep, so that she would not die of cold, and to watch over her.

— His words were so gracious that I could not say no; I only did what was asked of me.

— I do not know how to thank you, good woman. God will reward you.

She begged me to come and take some refreshment at her home.

— No, good woman — (I said) weeping — no.

And this poor woman consoled me. She would have liked to know the reason for my tears; but, sobbing, I set out along the path that never ended.

Numerous young workers for a new field of the Lord.

At last, voices could be heard in the distance. Who could it be? A great number of young girls, running toward me with all their might! and I hastened my step more than ever. As soon as they saw me they exclaimed loudly:

— Blessed be you in the Lord! A terrible hurricane carried away everything we had and, however much we prayed the Lord to come to our help, seeing ourselves lost, we could obtain nothing. Only a young gentleman told us to take this road, for we would find a cultivator who would accept us to work in the vineyard of the Lord. And, from the description he gave us, it is you!

And all of them, vying with one another, pressed close to me.

— Well then, tell me, what was this gentleman like?

— Very handsome!

— And where did he stay behind?

— We do not know!

I gathered them together and invited them to follow me, because there was still a road marked out. And so they did. But after long walking, one of them began to tell me that she did not feel up to making so long and so wretched a journey, and preferred to go back. There were no arguments to convince her. How much distress I suffered! But others too, until in the end half of them remained halfway along the road. What my anxiety was I cannot describe.

At last we find a good shepherd and, greeting us, he invites us to his house. And what mercy! he makes us a gift of his estate, and begged me to have it worked for the greater glory of God. I lost no time in setting all these workers in their places, and I left one of them as guide. A strong voice, which commanded me to make all possible haste and to go back to help those who had not wanted to come with me.

Weary, without delay I turn back; but I had taken only a few steps when a rough man comes up to me and says:

— Run, for those creatures you left on the road are dying. I stop, seized by the thought that the voice I had heard so strongly had been His, and that I must go to sufferings. They are the cause of their own trouble and, surely, now they would like help. I stood perplexed, when my angel comes up to me:

— Jesus forgave the lost sheep and went seeking it to bring it back to the flock (cf. Lk 15:4-7). Charity must have neither reasons nor limits.

So the voice was my angel’s and, greatly mortified, I ran to find them again. When I reached the first ones, they were in a sorry state from the many ill-treatments they had received from the infernal dragon. Reaching the others at last, who had very nearly fallen into the infernal precipice, I gathered them all together, and we prostrated ourselves on the ground to thank the Most High and to beg Him for His grace and mercy.

In this land of labor, where nothing but tribulations and crosses is found, the grace of God alone is the comfort of immortal souls, which remains to us for the sole passage from this life to blessed eternity.

Continuing to talk, we came to a cottage. My voice:

— Stop! for here there are good people and you will find work for these poor peasant girls. I was surprised to see again those two good old people who had once before given me shelter, though far from these parts: the fields were different, the cottage different, but the two old people were the same, who welcomed me with great gladness and handed over their estate to me, begging me to put my workers on it.

When the estate had been set in order, I lacked only the one to leave in charge of these inexperienced peasant girls. The good old woman, seeing me so thoughtful, begged me to tell her why I was so preoccupied, and I disclosed it to her:

— Because I have no one to whom I can entrust these workers. She offered herself and assured me that she would take great care of them, that I need not fear in continuing my journey, and that, when I find her, I should send her to her. I thought this to be an ordinance of my God.

A false saint tries to persuade her to place herself under his guidance.

This road I was running along was very wretched and, when I had covered a good stretch of it, I hear a man’s step approaching; and the more I ran, the more he did too. I turned round and:

— Who are you, in the name of the Lord?

He answered nothing. He kept at a certain distance from me, but always followed me. Fear was overtaking me, when all at once he stops me and says:

— That holy shepherd is waiting for you; he has things of great importance to tell you.

— No! I see no track other than the one I am walking. Leave me, I cannot!

He flies into a rage and threatens to beat me.

Do not come near!

Shrieking, I called upon my angel. A very charming little boy comes up; he had his locks tied back, covering his neck and spreading over his shoulders. At this sight I was electrified.

— Oh! tell me, who are you?

The man stood as if paralyzed. I threw myself on the ground and tried to draw near.

Do not fear! run with me without straying from the path. Unfortunately you will meet the saint who says: do not believe; listen, but be careful!

— Do not leave me!

Still the man came on, but always at a distance. He made a sign on my forehead. I had knelt down to kiss his feet, and he told me that the fruits of that saint’s garden were not good and that whoever ate of them would be badly infected, because a plague had been grafted into them.

— But your tales frighten me! it is better that I do not go there. And as I said this, he vanished. What was I to do? and where and how was I to save myself?

— Here is your dwelling!

I trembled with fright. The one who had been coming after me I saw no more and, as soon as I arrived, he came to meet me and with compassionate words invited me to sit down. I held my Crucifix tight. Pointing out his garden to me, he made me observe a quantity of flowers: the violets, of a (rare)

beauty, gave off a sweet fragrance. How beautiful they will be in the heavenly homeland!

— Oh! certainly — I said to him with a long sigh.

He began to tell me that my guide was too austere and that he had to speak to me, on behalf of the Lord, about leaving so rigid a way of life, for he must teach me another way. He made me believe many things. Night was falling, and I well understood that my poor mind did not know where it was; he pressed his reasoning so closely that I was left completely upset; with images he tried to persuade me of the truth of what he said. Finally he concluded that I was entirely deceived; that until that moment God had so willed it, but that through him He was giving me a new direction; that it was an eccentricity of mine not to want to submit.

Always silent, I never dared to disclose what I had gone through in so many long years and what had taken place between me and my God. I was on the point of wanting to leave, when a comely young woman comes in, and (he) told me that she was a great soul and that he was her guide, (and she was so) obedient that for this she was endowed with heavenly graces. While he was telling me this, the young woman went into ecstasy. When questioned, she said a word here and there about my future and nothing more. But it was useless: the words of that charming little boy were always before me. But why, my God, have you made me come here?

At last I wanted (to leave), but it was not possible: what distress! I turn my gaze this way and that, and see nowhere to flee.

— Here! — that false good man said to me.

But I was not slow to break free: with the strength of my God, in a flash I found myself outside, struggling with many other sanctimonious women who surrounded that place. Oh! how I lamented and wept bitterly, because he had made me so many threats if I did not do what he told me! What gave me least peace was that I did not know the reason why I had had to go there.

So, leaning against one stone and seated on another, because no trace of a path could be seen…: oh! can it be true that perhaps my God will want to give me a guide, as He does to the others?

Oh! why do I flee from it, when I have always desired it? And I wept. Behold, the same man comes up to me and, with pressing words, tries to persuade me. My soul was caught between two millstones. And that is not enough! he told me fiercely that I was lost if I did not heed him, and that I would have many graces if I submitted to him. His words revealed his snares, and I felt relief; but his seductions were so fierce and so well ordered that it was difficult for me to be sure of the good. Meanwhile, with his insistent manner, he gave me cause for suspicion.

— No! — I answered in a resolute tone — By far other words and works have I lived and walked until now.

Having said this, he flew into a rage and poured out his venom; but just as I was about to be overcome, behold, a most vivid light seized me, and (I found myself) in a delightful wood.

“Alone, without a cultivator, I have grown up, and beautiful.”

Here and there lovely lilies of a most sweet fragrance. Here, in the midst of so vast a wood, nothing is found but very great trees. I go up to the lily, and dare not touch it: beautiful and white (as it is), it reproaches me with my blackness; the plain daisy, it too seems to me to refuse to be touched. Finally I see, between three trees in the middle of this angular plot, a magnificent rose; I stop and throw myself face down on the ground. How beautiful you are! And my breathlessness and oppression did not allow me to utter a word, when, kneeling with difficulty, I prayed to the great Mother of God, most holy Mary.

The three trees, equal in height and in girth, and this rose, are nothing other than the symbol of your Mother, my God! I told her many things, above all what had happened to me with that false shepherd.

A voice said to me:

— Later on you will see the good you have done. And it seemed that from that lovely plant there came forth a voice that said:

— So beautiful did I come forth without a human cultivator.

Oh! how I rose up and, full of joy, felt myself in bliss!

I sat down nearby to enjoy so beautiful a sight, when I see a beating of wings and a large animal, of what kind I could not make out, was whirring about me; it gave certain roars and every now and then came close to bite me; but I was frightened of nothing, I almost paid it no heed; when it seized me by the arm:

— You must come with me!

Oh! then I struggled and held on tightly to one of the three trees; but already I felt that it was about to overcome me. My angel, with drawn sword, strikes it, threatening it. I was left utterly exhausted.

— Do you see what you let me be reduced to?

(And he), coming close to me:

— How have you understood this truth that you heard from the hidden voice: “Alone, without a cultivator, I have grown up, and beautiful”?

— That it is the will of God that this poor slave (should find herself) alone on the thorny path of the journey, so that His most holy will may be perfectly accomplished.

— Is that not enough? You must teach no one to walk thus, because no one has entered upon this. It is the will of God that each one should have his own guide.

Having said this, he vanished. How was I to understand this mystery? For me alone! Unhappy one! to what have my wicked deeds reduced me! And I began to weep. An old shepherd came up to me and asked me the cause of my weeping. Nothing! And I ran, and he, old though he was, followed me. I turned and begged him to go away, for I needed nothing, only what he could not give me.

— You are mistaken — he said to me.

I halted:

— Do you know whom I am seeking?

— Certainly: it is God, then!

— How do you know?

— Because I come on His behalf.

— Oh! tell me!

— He has placed a new delight in you; everything is greatly well ordered. Your anguish is moved by love and, so as not to let you die of languor, burned by the flames of His fiery love, He holds this communication in suspense.

I was beside myself!

— For a long time yet?

— That is reserved to Him alone.

— Tell me: who are you?

— My spouse will tell you — and he vanished.

Saint Joseph! he was very handsome! And I sat down (thinking): “The Mother of God will tell me!” Then I shall see her, I shall speak to her! Oh! when? And I sighed:

— How painful is the journey of this life! A voice answers me:

— And just as meritorious! Get up, and do not lose time! Go to the top of that mountain, for there are some shepherd girls there who do not take care of their sheep, and so several have been lost, and others are about to fall over the edge. 56.

She frees some sheep at the mercy of a hireling shepherd.

I climbed up as best I could. Having reached the top, I find nothing. Where are they? I set off in search and found them selling all of them for a few coins, and the one buying them was a shepherd whom it was frightening merely to see. There must have been a great many.

Stop! — I said to him — The master of this flock sends me here, and He demands an account and the preservation of His sheep.

Meanwhile I look around me and see several of them falling over the edge. Running, I caught them and, putting them together, I sought an exact count of the lost ones. The shepherd, enraged, begins to insult me, threatening to strike me. The others took his side. He no longer reasoned; fiercer than ever, (he snatched) from my hand a little stick which had served me for climbing: with this he wanted to strike me.

— Stop! I do not know why so much indignation against one who has never done you any harm.

— I want the sheep, they are mine!

You are mistaken. Let us sit down in the name of God and reason, and then you will see whether things are as you say. Who is the master of these?

— I do not know! — he answered me.

— And how can one buy, if the master does not consent?

But the cunning sellers, with agreed signs, told him that they were the owners and that he should hold firmly to that bargain. He grew fiercer than ever. Turning to them (I said to them):

— For what reason do you labor so hard to obtain from this man the audacity to want what is not yours, but God’s?

They fell silent. But the foolish shepherd was quivering with rage. I gathered the sheep and was already setting out on my way, when those keepers seize me and want to be paid. I stopped and with a smile (said to them):

— Go to my Master and He will give you the wages you deserve.

They hurled a thousand insults at me. At last they withdrew; and I walked on with my sheep so as to reach, before evening, the dwelling I hoped to find for these poor little things. But night is coming on and nothing is to be found. My God! have pity on these poor little things: I fear that they will take fright and run away again, and that I shall lose them.

Nothing! I stroked them, but already they were dropping with sleep. Oh! how great a distress I felt! I thought of inviting them to rest and tried to make them a little place as best I could near the trees. But my distress grew ever greater. No! Silently they accepted my invitation and, having lain down, while they rested I kept watch so that they would not be troubled by the wolves.

Meanwhile I prayed my Lord to deign to give me a poor but decent farmhouse in which to place these poor little sheep.

Weary, overcome by sleep, without realizing it I fell asleep. But I (was) woken by one of them, who was troubling the others and, whispering in the ear of one and then of the others, had unsettled them. In a loud tone of voice I ordered her to stop, for it was time to offend God no more. And we resumed our way, all in silence. I broke that monotony by telling them of the beauties of creation, that my Savior had made all this, that everything is made and created in excellence, that man is ungrateful for so much love. They looked at me, they seemed glad to hear such talk. Oh! how precious is the fulfillment of His will!

They looked at one another, but it hardly pleased them [?]. At last a lady comes up to us who said nothing but:

— For a long time I have been looking for you!

And, accompanying us, she begs me to enter her beautiful castle.

— Here — she said to me — you must leave these little sheep with me.

And she assures me that she would raise them well for me. My voice:

— Leave them!

And so I did.

Fear of running off the road: a false shepherd offers to guide her.

Having left them and returned to my path, I began to run without ever seeing the end; I felt so weakened that I sat down, praying earnestly to my Jesus to deign to put an end to my anguish: for I greatly feared that I was running along this path outside His will and that it was nothing but a diabolical illusion, and that so, in the end, I would find myself in a sorry state and far from my God! A thousand turmoils assailed me; I tried to fight, but did not succeed. I stopped, sitting in a grassy field and, weeping, I spoke with those little flowers of the meadow:

— How happy you are to grow according to the will of God!

And I?…

Oh! unbearable sorrow! Nothing could be seen but sky and fields! And in the midst of them, my path! Horrible fright! There comes before me, without my noticing from which side he came, a giant dressed as a shepherd; he stops and asks me what was the matter and how I came to be alone in that field. And then he began to tell me that it was imprudent to remain alone like this; that he would keep me company and would serve me in all that I might command him. I interrupted him:

— I need nothing. Go on your way. At these words he scolds me harshly, and (says to me):

— I know that not even that holy shepherd could get a hearing from you. Consider that you are in need and, if you do not take just and right measures for your journey, you will find yourself in a precipice. The voices that you think you hear and that you take as your assurance are not according to the will of God.

I began to tremble from head to foot; a cold sweat covered me. Is he telling the truth? is he reasoning rightly? Oh! he kept repeating to me that this is how it will turn out for me! But I answered nothing. And he noticed my agitation and pressed me ever harder. He cited a whole heap of women saints to me. At last he told me to answer him:

— I repeat: go away!

He flew into a rage:

— Your obstinacy will be your ruin!

What am I to do? — I reasoned within myself — I felt that I would gladly have wished to speak, but how? Will it be the will of my God? On the other hand, in the abandonment in which I found myself, I would have said that it was the will of the Lord. What am I to do? I tried more and more to persuade myself. My voice:

— Tell him that you will seek one.

I repeated this.

— But no! — he said to me — I am the one you must have.

Then, feeling great strength within me, I answered him:

— What are the proofs?

— I come on behalf of the Lord.

— That cannot be!

— Your speech is not that of a submissive creature. What signs do you want in order to believe me?

— The first, as I was taught, must be full trust; and then, to know who you are. For my part, I have neither of the two.

He was silent for an instant and then told me that he was a conqueror of souls; and that for this reason he was grieved for mine and wanted to help me save it.

With fine manners I tried to dismiss him, but I did not succeed. I began to run, and he kept on talking and coming along to accompany me. Already my agitation was such… I prayed, I wept, I called upon my angel, my Savior; but nothing! So I am truly lost, there is no more pity for me; I cannot approach this shepherd, my soul feels a terrible aversion to him. What distress! But if it is your will, I am ready and at once I submit with all pleasure. I desire only that your Majesty be fully satisfied. My God, have pity on your slave!

He told me that he would be my defender and whatever dragon might come, he would put it to flight; he would assist me in the work… The promises were endless; beautiful the way he described to me: when, all of a sudden, a band of devils invade those fields and come to attack me. Oh! how my defender takes to flight and, running, leaves me alone with that band! What are the promises of men worth! how quickly they forget what they say!

Alone to struggle with these demons! What am I saying? My God will come to save me. Meanwhile, how much they did! they were terrible things. After they had well vented their rage — but they never touched me — they began to fight among themselves. Meanwhile I ran on in the hope that they could not catch up with me; the noise they made was frightful; but the sorrow, the confusion that shepherd had put into my head, did not let me think of the fright I should have felt if they had pursued me. When they had finished fighting, a portion of them breaks away and comes running to seize me. Oh! what cries! how I ordered them to turn back!

— Stop — I cried at last — in the name of God! Do not move.

And they stood motionless as statues. The others, further off, roared; and these, standing still but with fiery eyes, looked at their companions, saying to them:

— Come and set us free!

How bound up in himself the devil is, so that he does not understand and therefore does not reason. Proud, because he asks to be freed only by his own: he wants no subjection whatever.

Horrible spectacle! the others did come to free them, but what happened to them? they too remained motionless. What a scene! They could be seen beside themselves, but unable to move; only their eyes could move. Meanwhile I continued on my way. Every now and then I turned round and always saw them in the same position. My voice:

— Command them to go back whence they came.

And turning to them, I so ordered them. I saw no one any more.

Among serpents and other creatures of God, who protect her against false shepherds.

I went along thinking to myself: where and how will this long path end? Meanwhile night was drawing on, but I gave myself no concern about anything. The moon silvered the plants, lit up the path clearly and, running on thus, oh! how beautiful you are, Mary! You held Jesus pressed close to your bosom; your heart ever enjoyed the highest union, and in the hidden secrets you shared in the great ordering of the whole world, all of it subjected as a footstool beneath your feet. You tasted inexpressible delights.

I, a slave and a wanderer from valley to valley, like a weeping willow beaten by the winds with its branches broken, feel all the fierce oppression of a melancholy spirit, which keeps running, hoping to arrive at clasping the feet of its Master and telling Him that only the pity and mercy of God can save it and give to those drooping branches, which are almost withering, life, vigor and beauty, paying no heed to the ill-grown trunk, all knots because of the continual actions badly performed. 57.

Reasoning thus, in the morning (I) arrived near a large rock and, weeping copiously, I lamented. Here and there I saw vipers and every sort of beast coming out; but my sorrow was so great that I paid no heed to anything. A serpent rears up and climbs onto the stone:

— You too, O fierce animal, have been created by my God. Surely in your nest you will have given glory to your Creator. Only I!..

And at this reasoning it stops and looks at me, as if it wanted to comfort me.

— From your make it is easy enough to see how wicked you must be: striped skin like a tiger’s, ears erect…

What! it began to hiss and, in an instant, a swarm of them came.

— You are very happy, for you have so many companions and all live subject to you, and care for nothing but to obey.

And all of these, gathered round the first that had come, looked at me. I kept weeping and they, spellbound, stayed near me. So am I to make my journey only with serpents and vipers? They are created by you and I cannot do them the least discourtesy. I had nothing to give them; I am poor, but far poorer is my soul: it has lost its God! He gave me over to the serpents. My voice:

— What are they doing to you?

Oh! how I came back to myself!

— Nothing! but I cannot help (saying) that their company is hardly pleasing to me. I feel, however, that I am not afraid. The only thing that makes me converse with them is the thought that they too are created by you, my God.

Another hiss, and they appear by the hundreds. A fear begins to come over me, and woe if one or another moved any closer to me! I would have liked them to withdraw; I did not dare to move, because I feared being attacked by these beasts. Oh! what distress I felt! But at last I asked them what they wanted and why they had come. Oh! what a shock I received! All together they began to make certain ugly faces, so that out of fear I too began to shout, and they still louder. I tried to move, and still they came closer. I invoked all my advocates in heaven, and my angel, my God, the most holy Virgin: but nothing!

I turned round to see whether there were any human beings. Oh! what fright! That tall man who was approaching at a run! But instead of feeling relieved, my fright grew. Oh! how to flee? He was together with the saint of whom I have already spoken above. A violent trembling seized me, I shrieked at the top of my voice, and I begged help of the inhabitants of heaven: You, you who are near my God: ask Him to forgive me and free me from so terrible a situation.

Behold, the two come near and ask me if I want help.

— No!

What was I to think? The beasts, at the sight of these two, stood still and silent. Nothing! Again I said to them:

— Go away, for I am better off alone.

But they insisted and in the end wanted to force me to consent to go along with them; that I should not fear, for the beasts would not trouble me in the least.

— No!

Again other strong insistences, and they would have liked those serpents to trouble me, so as to have more scope for making me go with them.

— No!

They sat down beside me, telling me the greatest things they had seen of my God [?], that He Himself had sent them to me to help me in that terrible moment in which I found myself alone, and that it was entirely the will of God that I should obey them.

— No!

Seeing that the serpents remained ever silent, I turned to them:

— Are you too in league with these? You may withdraw, for I feel no fear either of you or of them.

What did one of these two do? He provoked the biggest of these beasts to frighten me. No! the poor thing stayed still and looked at me.

— You understand well that they are not on the right path.

Oh! would that I had never said such a thing! Worse than the vipers, they hurled themselves upon me with very threatening words. They wanted to frighten me.

— I fear neither men, nor seas, nor mountains, nor forests, nor wild beasts! My heel stops every movement.

— It will certainly not stop us!

— And yet here you will stay and I shall go away.

What can I say? The vipers had become my defenders; they stood listening and, when they saw these two coming close to me, behold, all of them reared up and hurled themselves forward; and those two, so as not to be bitten, took to flight. Left alone, I thanked these animals for the defense they had given me. And they again shrieked loudly.

— What have you seen? Must I stay and live among you? If it is the will of God, I will gladly stay even among you.

A voice, very far off, sobbing, was asking me for help; and these shrieked loudly at it.

Dialogue with a little old man on the will of God, and on the evil of one’s own will.

I began to run to go and help the one I heard moaning, but the little beasts placed themselves in front of me and, having barred the road, I was not able to pass. I ordered them to leave me and to withdraw into their dens; but quite the contrary, they looked at me with compassionate eyes and would not let me pass. And this voice made itself heard more and more.

While I was struggling thus, a good little old man passes by and I ask him, as a favor, who was weeping, whether he had seen anyone who needed help. Laughing, he told me that he had seen two shepherds on the top of a hill, who were badly guiding some women laborers in a field, and this was so badly ordered that he, when he was near it, turned off the road so as not to see so much disorder.

— But, good man, do you hear the weeping?

— Oh! do not believe it; it is all hypocrisy. If you saw how many they have deluded! They all do their own will, because they do not know the will of God.

They have an infinity of tools for working, but they bend their backs little or not at all to work. They feed much on great illusions and, when a good worker came among them, who was a zealous shepherd, because he wanted to take away tools, he was driven out. They live without fruits, they feed on flesh…

How the old man’s talk consoled me. The beasts too stood listening to him, without moving. The voice is heard no more.

— Before long a great number of those women will arrive here. Fear nothing; they will go back put to shame. The victor will be you.

I begged him to stay with me and said to him:

— I would like to go away from here, but these beasts hold me back. Moreover I can no longer see any path on which to walk, and this points out to me the will of God! Your spirit is well governed: the will of God is its possessor. Oh! For pity’s sake, stay with me, tell me something more of my God, for I feel such ardor to see Him. My thirsting soul seeks Him everywhere and burns with a strong desire to speak to Him and to be united with Him as its one center.

— In His will your soul finds Him again.

— Oh! too sweet it is to do it and in everything to find a reversal of one’s own will, for one who does not yet possess it! I feel a strong revulsion at the mere thought that man holds so much to this will of his, while it is so contrary to that of God. How to make him understand, and still more taste, this sweetness of the will of God? Man seems a slave, because he does not know how to renounce what enchains him in order to have Another who guides him in everything and with great sweetness leads him to the blessed life. He answered me:

— Man is blind through his own will and because of it he suffers without any merit.».58.

Snares of two false shepherds.

And he vanished. The beasts shrieked. Those people arrive and begin to blame me, criticizing me in a thousand ways, saying that only beasts could live with me; they said every sort of insulting word to me; but I was happy, because I tried to keep close to my Savior, and what they said to me always seemed little in comparison with what they had said of Him. They called me stupid; and they marveled at other things too, because I had not wanted to listen to their shepherds, and said that pride was my mistress. Silence! So I felt I should do in the depth of my soul, and I rejoiced in it greatly. At last they accused me of insolence because I did not answer. I broke the silence:

— What ever should I answer, if what you say is all true?

— Then come out of this position of yours and come with us.

— Were it the will of God, I am most ready to come.

— Obey our shepherds and so you will attain the will of the Lord.

— How am I to know it?

— By coming to us.

— That is not enough!

Oh! then they broke out into as many insulting words and they very nearly used their hands, when the little beasts grew fierce and bit them, running after them while they fled, with shrieks and howls, and they dared not turn round again.

— How can I thank you, my dear companions and defenders? I would like to give you something to refresh you, but I am a poor slave of my Lord, and I have nothing but tears to shed for my sins.

But what! They came ever closer to me, and I began to stroke them. One gently took me by the hem and brings me near a tree. Oh! what did I see! a basket with provisions in it.

Who can have left it? I am afraid to touch it, because it must belong to someone, and how can I take these things? But she, standing still, absolutely wanted me to take it.

— No, dear little beast! You see, other people’s things may not be taken; it is forbidden by God. No, it shall never be!

And she insisted. That unfortunate Eve came to my mind and I felt myself go quite numb at the mere thought, and in a severe tone I said to the beast:

— No, it shall never be!

And I turned to go back; but she grew fierce.

— Even if you were to tear me to pieces, it shall never be that I give any of it to you or eat of it myself.

A strong voice, but one that was something beautiful, ordered the serpent to withdraw:

— If I have made use of you so that you might defend her and tempt her, now return to your dwellings. 59.

Oh! I was alone! I began to reflect: she wanted to make me sin against the seventh commandment! I did not even dare to turn my gaze toward that little basket. After a few moments there came — as he said — the owner of the basket; he comes up to me and offers me some fruit: something beautiful.

— Thank you, I do not eat fruit.

And then he offers me other exquisite morsels.

— No! I repeat to you. Leave me: I need nothing.

— Why refuse what the Lord sends you?

— I do not believe it; I have no need of refreshment. I seek only one, but I do not find it!

— If you come with me, we shall certainly find it.

— I have no need to be accompanied. In short, go away, for I do not want to listen to you at all.

Victory over the temptation to satisfy the demands of the flesh.

At last, by a most beautiful light, I see my way grow clear and a broad path has formed. Without saying anything, I rushed into it, running without turning round; but in his rage that man threw the basket after me, which, as it broke open on the ground, gave off a terrible stench. The blasphemies he shrieked were horrible; but meanwhile I felt that he was not coming toward me. All triumphant at the victory I had won, I felt very light as I walked.

Out of a bush comes a monster a meter tall and approaches me, mocking me. Without saying anything to him, a great laugh escapes me, and:

— How loathsome you are!

He tries to run with me, but because his legs are short he cannot catch me. Every now and then he turned somersaults and caught up with me, always mocking me. I could not restrain (my laughter). A good peasant passed by and stopped on seeing me laugh. Not seeing the buffoon, he asked me why I was laughing and where I came from.

— Good man, I will ask you: — where do you come from and why have you come onto my path?

— It is not yours alone, for if you knew the matter…

— O good man, I cannot stand still.

— It is not fitting for you to turn back: go on, for the path is beautiful. If God has placed you here, do not give up doing His will.

And on I went, with the buffoon always beside me; he gave certain butts of his head against the ground, so that his head seemed made of wood. He began to annoy me; I laughed no longer; but he did such filthy things that I stopped, ordering him to leave me.

— I cannot; I must make you suffer as much as you have mocked me.

— Oh! loathsome one, away!

— No!

I came back to myself: how? oh! I understand well: it would have been better had I driven him away at once. By allowing the jest, I now play the part of one who does not at once drive away the diabolical game, even in things that have the appearance of frivolity: one falls back into it. I threw myself on the ground and, weeping bitterly, I asked my God’s forgiveness: and the ugly one vanished.

Along the road there were very beautiful trees, with exquisite fruits. I felt strongly tempted, because the need for refreshment was already making itself felt, and the whisperer said to me:

— In necessity one does no wrong in departing from promises of abstinence one has made, and besides there is nothing wrong in taking, because the apostles too ate the grain from the ears they gathered in other people’s fields, and Jesus confirmed that they could do so (cf. Mt 12:1-8).

And this inner (voice), or rather, mental whispering, bewildered me, although it tried to make itself very sweet and almost melancholy and devout; but it did not satisfy me. I thought: no! I kept repeating to myself. At last, having come near a tree with fruits — something beautiful! — a voice calls me. It was a comely young woman offering me the fruits. At once I refused them. And as she begged me to accept them, I did not know how to refuse them. She only insisted that I should eat one.

— I cannot, because I have made a gift of this kind of fruit to my God.

But she insisted more and more. She begged me so much; but a strong fear arose in me. I threw to the ground those I held in my hand and ran away. But she came after me telling me not to fear, that she was sent by the Lord and that, if I did not take some of those fruits, my strength would fail me and I would no longer be able to continue my journey.

— No! — I said to her forcefully.

But she blushed and, in a compassionate manner (said):

— Never mind!

This manner of hers overcame me; I took ten of them and put them in my lap, telling her that I would give them away in charity. Oh! how cunning the devil is! The effort I had to make not to taste them was beyond compare; but on seeing myself so overcome by exhaustion, (so much so that) I seemed about to faint, then more than ever I said: here is diabolical art and it shall never be. I was about to throw them into a river, when a poor man comes up to me; opening my lap where the fruits were, they had become many little serpents and three fine pieces of bread to give to the beggar. Shrieking, I threw them on the ground and plunged into the river those parts of my garment in which such horrible monsters had been. My voice:

— You will learn not to let yourself be overcome by the thought that the truths of the Lord and what is promised to Him can be canceled. Nothing is disproportionate; what is of God is perfect in excellence.

I remained in ecstasy and at the same time downcast and confused; I wept bitterly, and my imperfections became ever clearer before me. Oh! how I ought to fight against this hungry humanity! Meanwhile I felt a fierce need of a little refreshment: in those arid fields, without a blade of grass, no planting of any kind, and not even water could be seen flowing. Oh! it serves you right! — the soul reasoned with the body — it is good that you should feel fiercely how much decay you have brought upon my spirit!

But the lament of need grew ever greater and my strength was failing. An old shepherd came up to me and asked me why I was so like a corpse, saying that I aroused his compassion. And he wanted to persuade me that, if I did not nourish my body, I could not do good for my soul. I said to myself: and is this that shepherd so renowned, who knows the way to heaven so well?

— I tell you to provide what is necessary and what your wretched humanity demands; otherwise you will do nothing but harm both the one and the other.

— Why do you speak to me so? perhaps because I make you feel pity? Are you that great shepherd who guides so many souls?

— And yet I shall guide yours.

— If it pleases God.

— The pleasure of the Lord lies in guidance.

— I beg you to let me go, because I still have a long way to go.

— I assure you that your body will prevent you. Do as I say, refresh yourself and try to feed it as it demands. 60.

— Oh! — I exclaimed — This enemy of mine will never suffer enough for what it has done to my imprisoned soul! You do not speak like a shepherd, but like a humanitarian; this is the misfortune of the present day: to look after the flesh very well so that it may have great strength to rebel and never find itself sated in its demands.

The combat became very strong. But no! I concluded that I had no need of the refreshment of bread, but desired something far different, for which I was languishing.

And without more ado I began to run.

These encounters are a scourge — I reasoned within myself —: in such sad moments humanity laments and finds someone to protect it; the soul fears being importunate and erring in wanting to lord it too much over all the faculties; it becomes confused and begins to fear. What torpor arises from this! Reason is confused, it would not want to let humanity win. The demands that humanity does in fact display, with the evidence that its existence is lacking what it needs, the murmur of the most learned shepherd’s words still ringing in the ear…: ah! in what straits the soul finds itself! The strength of the spirit, which is always ready to sacrifice everything for the good and the salvation of the soul, insists on not heeding, but on running without stopping, seeing in humanity something base and trivial. 61.

In the end, the lack of nourishment overcame me and I fainted. Lying abandoned on the ground, I commended my soul to God, seized by a strong fear of being deceived and that all this was the effect of illusion. I wept copiously. An angel appeared to me — it was not mine — and said to me:

— Why do you weep? That God who has sustained you until now, will He perhaps not sustain you always?

Having said this, he left me a little basket, in which there was a large piece of bread. I calmly began to eat: it was exquisite; I devoured it. And I thought how great the goodness of my God was! I would have been happier if He had sated me, not with bread, but with that food with which I feel so ardent a longing to be nourished. As I reasoned thus, I see a crystal-clear little spring gushing up from beneath my feet, as if inviting me to drink. Oh! how great a wonder I felt at it! I asked His forgiveness for my fear that what was necessary would fail me. I was left so downcast that I no longer knew how to find words and strength, because everything reproached me. I would have curled up in the depths of the earth to weep. My sorrow kept growing more and more.

Drowsy in so cruel a state, I lost consciousness and remained stretched out on the ground. At that moment my angel, Saint Michael the Archangel, came up to me and, taking me by the hand, raised me up; but (I was) so confused and exhausted that I did not recognize him. But the touch of his hand gave me life and, having recognized him, I burst into a flood of tears:

— My wicked deeds have made me lose my God! I was ungrateful to Him; I lacked confidence; I complained and desired food… Oh! never again will I ask for bread! I will die of hunger, but I will not complain. I had bread, but not that with which you satisfied me another (time), but the bread of men, not of heaven (cf. Jn 6:50 f.).

And he looked at me with compassion. I was sobbing hard; the sorrow was so great that I felt my breast was breaking open. Then my angel, stretching out his hand, (said to me):

— Enough, weep no more! dry your tears: they have been very pleasing to the Lord. Your imperfections are perfectly canceled. Your God was always near; had He not sustained you, you would have died of sorrow; His grace sustained you. If it pleased Him to nourish you so, is He not obliged always to sustain you with the bread of heavenly nourishment? [?] Come with me!

Strong as a giant I ran, and the consolation I felt wiped from my mind every remembrance of what had happened. I asked him a thousand questions: he explained to me how the soul is united to God in sufferings, above all in desolation of spirit; how, just as it feels sorrow at seeing itself abandoned, so it gains as much in grace and union with its God, while it believes itself abandoned.
