Overcoming great dangers, protected by a lion, she arrives at a field all laid waste.

I saw in the distance certain waves, so frightening, of a great river that seemed to have broken its banks and was rushing with all its force toward us.

— Oh! have pity! do not leave me!

Having said this, (my angel) vanished. The river was coming in fury with towering billows and, certainly, there was no other hope than to turn back. Turning to flee, behold, the torrent, which we had crossed dry, was full of water surging up in its midst. At that horrible sight I knelt down and, with my arms open, remembering the promises I had made, (I exclaimed):

— My God! Receive my soul into your arms and press it to your Heart; do with me what you will: if it pleases you that I be submerged by the waters, may your most holy will be done in me (cf. Mt 26:42).

Having said this, the torrent and the river join together; they roll me over, flinging me in every direction. I could utter nothing but: My God, mercy! A wave so huge envelops me and dashes me among the bushes. Oh! how I was left almost stunned!

The waters had withdrawn, the sun was scorching; I could not even think; I felt myself all burning: I thought it was the rays of the sun. Meanwhile my clothes were drying, and my pains were growing within me. When I was dry, I looked around me to find my path, and I saw nothing but rocks. And yet within myself I hoped to find it.

The sky was darkening, thunder could be heard in the distance and I continued to burn with fire. I looked near me to see whether there were things that were burning: nothing! The storm was approaching, and where was I to go? I saw one of these rocks where there was something like a cavern, and I thought of going into it.

— No! — my voice; — there are evildoers there.

What fright at once overtakes me, thinking what if they should come out of that enclosure! But, burning as I was, and yet battered by the waves, I sat down beside another rock. Having leaned back well, I rested my head on the palm of my hand. I hear a voice that says to me:

— It is I who brought you here and you are at my mercy.

Oh! what fright! I leaped up to flee, but where? I ran across those rugged rocks and each of them had a voice within it, which always seemed the first one I had heard. My God! Have pity, my angel: come and help me! I am lost! My Savior, open a way for me to flee; but if it is your will that these giants, or whoever they may be, should tear me to pieces, so be it!

While I was saying this, giants come out, all armed with certain irons such as I had never seen; fiercely they draw near to me. I do not know what my fear was: it is better to leave the mind to guess it than to describe it. They were urging one another to begin; the biggest one seizes his iron to strike me; but a flash of lightning, or to put it better a thunderbolt, wraps round him and he can no longer move. How the others were enraged! The second slips and falls headlong. And there were still others. One, frightened, took to flight, promising me that he would catch me another time and that he would make me pay for it fiercely. The two who seemed to be motionless suddenly raise their long cloaks and, with two horrible irons, run to seize me.

A great lion comes out of their own den and seizes them, throwing them to the ground badly mauled. Moved by the charity and pity they stirred in me, I would have wished to help them, and I took off my mantle to dress their wounds. But what! enraged, as I drew near, they drew out that iron to wound me; but the lion, roaring once again, came near them. Terrified, they tried to tame it so that they might catch it too; but the beast came close to me, as if it wished to say: Do not fear!

One of them, who seemed the most badly mauled, what did he do? He gathered all his strength and hurled the iron at the lion; but, horror! the lion leaped upon him and left him utterly destroyed. Taking me by the hem of my garment, it led me onto a rock where there stood a small image of the most holy Virgin; I knelt down and, weeping bitterly, I begged her to ask God’s pardon for my sins and to obtain for me the grace of forgiveness.

That fierce beast was looking at me and did not move. My voice:

— Do not fear, rise! The path is traced; run to save one who is shipwrecked.

When I had set out, my companion followed me; every so often I addressed a word to it:

— Poor beast! The will of God has reached you so well, taking away your fierceness, and you have become a lamb. O power of my God!

Whenever I spoke a word to it, it would bring its head close to me and try to caress me.

After so many hours of walking I felt my heart breaking with compassion at having nothing to give it. Its mouth was open, its tongue hanging out from the heat, but there was (nothing). I suspect that it kept a little distance from me [?]. When we came near a little stream of water, I stopped to invite it to drink. The poor beast tried, but as though it were afraid of falling. I thought I would do it a kindness: I set my foot out on a stone and, as best I could, joining my hands, I brought it water to drink, and it drank with such pleasure. And it looked at me, and then looked at the water, as if it wished to invite me to drink as well.

— No! This water is not for me!

And we took up our way again. When we arrived in a valley where noises and a great tumult could be heard, oh! what can it be? As though the poor beast knew something, it too pricks up its ears, sharpens its muzzle and puts itself on guard. All of a sudden armed people are seen coming toward us.

My God! I cried. But how wonderful was this beast when it wanted to persuade me that it still had all its fierceness and that I should not be afraid. Indeed, they drew near to lay hands on me and threaten me, so as to make me turn back; but my defender, whom my God had given me, made a slaughter of them and put them all to flight.

And victorious I entered (the field). How great the devastation was (I cannot say); they were terrible things. The keeper was not to be found, because she had gone off with that band of people. The workers turned against me and, almost threatening me, would have put me out had I not had my guard with me. At last, standing firm, I commanded them to work according to the will of God, not according to the will of men.

While I was giving these orders, the poor beast caressed me and went away. How can I thank you? I said to it; but it broke into a run and I saw it no more.

The workers grew quiet; but the keeper, from a distance, was making every effort to see whether she could cause trouble. I let her struggle and then I commanded her to withdraw.

And that field? Nothing had been sown in it; all the trees were without fruit, many were about to wither. The ground was full only of weeds. I wept much over it and prayed earnestly that God would water the roots of those trees with his grace and make them fruitful; that he would not look at the ingratitude of those workers, but only at his infinite mercy and at the good of his field; for if He did not make those plants flourish, I was not capable of making them bear fruit. I prayed and, at last, I fell asleep weeping.

When I awoke, I saw a beautiful picture of the most holy Virgin: in her hand she held a most beautiful basket of exquisite fruits. Oh! how my soul was filled with joy! O my Mother! are these the fruits of this field? Will they be like these in the future, oh! and pleasing to your Son? Will they be like these that you have?

— Yes! — and I remained in ecstasy with consolation.

In that position I asked her to give me one of them. She did not answer me. I insisted still more; she took one and said to me:

— In this you will find all the sweetness of those things which you have sacrificed for me. How I savored it! Oh! my lovable Mother! for so little, you give me so much! What is it I feel, this wish to sacrifice for love of you?

What ardor had been born in me! I would have wished to find something I could offer and sacrifice: I have nothing left!

Everything, everything I have consecrated to you, my God! Nothing else remains for me but to consume myself for you, my God!

Sweet and comforting rest upon the Wood of the Cross.

This said, a great road opens up. Carried away by the ardent desire to be able to consume myself wholly in the service of my God, I hastened my step as much as I could. At the end of it there was a very high mountain, all stony; here and there a bush. My track was marked out over rough and sharp stones. At the sight of so steep a road I was frightened; but I was very glad to be able to climb it. I clambered up with all the strength I had; I tried not to slip.

When I was halfway (up the climb), I found a great cross lying outstretched and, prostrating myself, I prayed before it. But I felt that I could not move. What can it be? Oh! my treasure! I kissed and kissed again that wood, and I saw so clearly all that my God had suffered upon it. From weariness and the pain in all my limbs I fell asleep with my head resting at the feet of the holy Wood. My voice:

— Wake up and take this cross and follow your way.

It was very large; I did not dare to put it on my shoulder because I was not worthy. What did I do? I embraced it tightly (saying):

— You will stay upon my breast and I shall climb Calvary!

So I set out, and the sufferings and pains I felt were sweet to me. And, as though I had been close to my Savior, I talked with him. I heard many things that were more than could come from me. I never reached the summit: the further I went, the more the mountain seemed to me to rise. Ah! my breast ached, my knees buckled and my strength no longer held. Oh! as with my Savior!

The night was dark; the track on this mountain was barely marked; I could not even find where to rest this treasure of mine, to which I felt myself so closely bound in affection and which I adored with the greatest veneration. What was I to do? When I looked down into the depth of this mountain I was terrified: a single instant, one movement, and I could fall headlong into that abyss! I began to tremble, when the thought is suggested to me that I had with me the treasure of my Crucified One. Every fear vanished in me.

Meanwhile I kept trying more and more to climb, in the hope of finding a little corner where I could stop, and I was thinking of this:

— Oh! fortunate apostles, who before Calvary saw and enjoyed the delights of Tabor, and saw my God beautiful in all his infinite majesty!

At last I found a little stretch of ground and thought of stopping there to regain my strength and pass the night. One worry I had: I did not know how to lay down the cross. What did I do? I spread out my habit and then laid it upon it with all delicacy.

Oh! how beautiful you are! You served as the last bed for my God, who breathed his last upon you! But how shall I ever be able to carry you upon my breast as you deserve? My voice:

— Take your rest upon it: you will gain strength from it to walk.

I did not hesitate a moment and I lay down upon the cross. Oh! sweet and gentle rest! what contentment I felt from it! I fell asleep, if sleep it can be called, for I learned from it the most beautiful lessons of mystical theology; I held a conversation and received the most beautiful answers, even on cases of conscience. How well he explained to me his law and that of the Church, and the parables of the holy Gospel!

At length, having awoken when the morning was well advanced:

— What? Am I alone? Where is the one with whom I was conversing until now?

I looked around me: I am truly alone! Strengthened, and as if I had risen from a sumptuous meal, I got up and knelt down to make a little adoration to the holy Wood. But all that I had heard was ever before my mind. My voice:

— Take up your cross and walk!

I laid it on my breast and continued to climb. How stony and very ruinous the road was! But I felt nothing. Every so often I kissed my companion, pressed it to my breast and repeated to it all that I had learned in the night and that had comforted me so much that it seemed to me I had no further need of anything else: only to seek to fulfill perfectly the will of my God. And knowing that this will make me attain him, it seemed to me that I would have defied everything and that nothing would succeed in grieving or upsetting me, nothing would have disturbed my mind, but that I would always have known how to defend myself.

Oh! how long the road was! I never arrived! At last certain very tall trees with very few leaves begin to appear; they had grown in the mud, and on them were certain insects, small but biting fiercely: they had a long sting which, driven into the skin, produced a very sharp pain. How could one ever find mud on so rugged a mountain, trees so tall, ill-grown and untended, with such tormenting creatures? But what? The torment was such that I could not bear them; they caused in all my nerves a kind of irritation which I could not describe. Only the cross did they respect. And the more torment I felt, the fiercer they grew. My hands had swollen. They were something!… What was I to do? An ugly voice says to me:

— Curse them! It is in your power to drive them away.

— No! How can I curse what my God has created?

It answers:

— You will have to succumb.

— So be it! but with resignation; helped by my God, I will bear them.

But they truly tormented me fiercely. Clinging to the cross, I compared them with the little imperfections in a soul favored by God, which one never thinks of removing. These are vexations done to the heart of my God; and how many times mine have been so very sharp! For a very great quantity of imperfections, vexing to the most sweet heart of my Savior, will many times have surrounded and closed that inexhaustible fountain of graces, since they have been so numerous! 62.

— So you seem to me, you poor creatures, who without meaning to have so painful a sting.

And I looked at the cross:

— Oh! precious Wood, if you could speak, how well you would describe to me the pains of my Savior!

But these kept striving to sting me. I felt such fierce pain from it that I did not know how to free myself, and I ran. But that field never ended. Weary, sorrowing and so martyred, I sat down and said:

— Eat, then, O creatures, small but very fierce!

And, resigned, I suffered much. In that bitter suffering my soul felt great joy; and I remained absorbed in my God for an instant. 63.

VII

“You will learn not to flee from suffering and not to let yourself be overcome by fear.”

Oh! what? who can it have been? The cross has been taken from my breast and I was freed also from the torment of the creatures. When I came to myself, I looked around; I searched for my cross, and nothing! the creatures neither! Freed from such fierce torments, I set about looking for my cross. My voice:

— Do not distress yourself: run along the path!

Doing so, and thinking of that sweet moment I had spent with my God, I did not notice where the road was or what it was like; but I reasoned within myself: how sweet it is to suffer! when two evildoers dressed as shepherds stop me.

“Stop!” they said to me.

“No!”

And, more frightened than ever, I began to run with all the strength I had; they ran too, but outside my path; they shouted because they could never catch up with me. At last, having reached the top of a precipice, (I thought): surely they will catch me, for I will never throw myself down to save myself. When they were about to come near, my angel took me by the hand and made me descend into that depth without my noticing. Oh! how I thanked him! I prostrated myself on the ground and begged him to stay with me, for in that valley there would certainly be nothing but savages; and I was even more afraid of evildoers than of tigers. He listened to me, and then lowered his gaze (and said to me): “Do not be afraid!”.

And he vanished. Alone on that stony road, for the river flowed close by, turbulent!… Every so often the cries of little birds could be heard, as though they wished to announce to me the approach of some storm. What terror! I ran, and never found either a hut or a living creature. Where shall I end up? I said within myself. The two mountains on either side grew ever more forbidding, one all caves, the other so wildly covered with bushes and great thorns, full of great trees which one could hear were inhabited by little birds; in short, it was a terror.

I held my crucifix tightly to my breast and walked on. At last I see in the distance a little old woman who was carrying a load of wood on her poor shoulders. Moved with compassion, I hastened my step. When I had reached her, I begged her to give me that wood, saying that I would carry it for her wherever she wished. The good woman gave it to me gladly. But the evil one, or to put it better my own wickedness, put it into my head that by doing this charity to this poor woman she would be obliged to give me lodging, and so I would get myself out of this terrible road.

Without heeding anything else, I go and, having arrived at the poor woman’s hut, I set down the wood there; and she tries to thank me and invites me to rest that night in her cottage. And I gladly accept. My God! what did I do? While I was going with her I left the path, and the farmhouse was full of people who were blaspheming!

I hurry out of it and no longer see my path. Where am I? I began to weep, very far from that horrible cottage, asking pardon of my God if I had failed in this; if I did it, it was to relieve that poor woman and so to do her a charity.

“Ah! no!” my voice, angered — “the double intention has taken from you all the merit, and the avoiding of suffering: lack of faith and of trust in God! Thus you gave occasion for your right path to be taken away.” 64.

Oh! with all the strength I had, I cried out, weeping bitterly: mercy! pardon, my God! Oh! abandoned by you! I am a monster of iniquity. I took a large stone and beat my breast: mea culpa! My eyes were swollen, my head had become so confused… I had no more strength, but every so often I went on beating myself with a large stone, and I tried to make the blows ever harder. At last I fell with the stone clutched in my hand and fainted from the sorrow of having lost my God!

My angel took the stone from my hand and placed in it the palm of victory; and then gently shook me, saying to me: “You will learn not to flee from suffering and not to let yourself be overcome by fear.”.

Oh! mercy! And looking at the palm: who… and what am I, that I should have the palm of victory?

“Then my God has forgiven me? He is no longer angry with me? Tell him that never will I flee from it in the very least; with his help I will hold all sufferings close to me.”

“Rise!”.

I obeyed at once. But my breast did not allow me to stand on my feet and I fell again face down on the ground. But I did not dare to complain, lest it be taken from me [?]. My angel raised me up and, when he had signed me with the sign of the cross, the pain vanished. And he said to me: “I knew it well.”

And he vanished.

“Neither men nor demons will be able to stop my way!”.

My path was very beautiful, in a lovely countryside with fruit and grapes of exquisite beauty. There were many workers and all, on seeing me, greeted me. There had remained in me a weakness with an inward pain, so that I could not help heaving deep sighs, and I went on with slow steps.

One of these workers came up to me and asked whether I wanted their superior, what was the matter with me and where I came from, since he saw me so afflicted. For a long while I did not answer him; but then, seeing that he kept following me, (I said to him): “I pray you, good worker, to withdraw and leave me alone; I need nothing. May God reward you for your charity.

And he left me. When I had gone some way, here comes another, hurrying, with a large bunch of grapes in his hand; he invites me to take it.

“No, thank you!”

“I feel sorry for you. Do not be afraid, I am the superior of these workers, the vineyard is ours. I beg you to accept it.”

“I cannot!”

“But if you go on like this, you will die of starvation.”

“Thank you, I cannot!”

“At least take refuge a little in this house of ours, to refresh yourself.”

“Ah! I heaved a long and deep sigh “that, never!”

“Who are you?”

“A poor handmaid of the Lord, who deserves to have nothing, and I seek another rest: never the one you wish to give me. Thank you, may God reward you for your charity.

“But night is drawing near; I do not think it right that you should be alone in this vineyard.”

“I am not alone!”

And he looked at me and turned his gaze around the vineyard (to see) whether someone was coming with me: no! But he insisted strongly.

“I pray you to leave me!”

“No! I will follow you everywhere, you know?”

“That shall never be!”

And I tried to walk on. He: “Perhaps (you are) an anchoress returning to her cave?”

I never answered. At last he told me that he would call his workers, who would stop me by force, and that he would not allow me to go wandering about that night. I looked at my path and saw it still beautiful.

“No!” I said in a firm tone “neither men nor demons will be able to stop my way!”

I sighed; but I felt growing in me such strength that no human person would ever have succeeded in touching me and stopping me. What came of it? They all arrived and tried to persuade me: nothing! They were setting to work to seize me.

“Stop!” I cried “in the name of my Lord, do not move!”

They remained like so many statues. And I ran off nimbly. I saw in the distance a crowd of people hurrying toward those whom I had left. Oh! can they too be of the same sect? What fear! They passed on the other side and did not see me. And I kept quickening my step.

At last I entered a field where there were good people; and I stopped, sitting down on a stone. And I thought over my past: and how? and where shall I go? how will this painful journey of mine end? Having rested a little, once again I went on walking. I saw a bell tower in the distance: oh! how revived I felt, thinking that my Good dwelt there and that there I would find rest.

But I found it quite otherwise: it was all destroyed! A poor little old man said to me: “Do not stop here, for pity’s sake, because there is nothing but wicked people.”

For fear of being seen a great panic seized me, and I reasoned about it within myself with much distress. I saw nothing, and the hope of getting out without being seen was very great. Having come out of that enclosure by grace, I found on the ground a large animal: it had its wings joined together on its back and all spread out; a muzzle like a falcon’s, but with great whiskers; over its brows large thorns. It dragged itself along to come toward me on its short paws shaped like a lion’s; it held its mouth open, and it was coming toward me. I began to scream and to command it to stop, to go back where it had come from. It stops, but it roars. My path lay exactly where that ugly creature was; I did not know what to do. Without more ado I passed, but it seized me by my garment; it held me tight in those great jaws.

“Away! Let me go! In the name of my God, withdraw!”

It let me go, but it had torn my garment to pieces. How frightened I was! It sent out from its mouth a smoke with a terrible stench; can it ever be that a beast holds so much vapor? The smoke followed me; the beast, standing still, made the smoke from its fierce mouth run toward me. The distress was very great, and that stinking smoke which followed me so much gave me much to think about. Oh! I was not slow to learn the cause: those meadows still belonged to those evildoers, and this was a diabolical monster that held complete mastery over them. Their filth infected the air; a foul pestilence reigned there.

I found a shepherd and, thinking I was doing him a kindness, told him not to go further into that field because it was infected.

He answered me: “I am going in search of sinners, not of those who are converted.”

“What?” I said to him “do you hope that by going in there those people can be saved?”

He told me with assurance that he did. And he marveled that I had not stopped there; he said it would be good for me to join him in going to save those poor people. But what! for an instant I stopped, but at once I looked at my path and saw that it ended just where I had passed.

“No!” I answered him.

But he insisted and was already raising his voice to make himself heard; but I broke into a run, and he kept pursuing me from behind, telling me that he would soon convince me. I answered him ever more sharply, commanding him to go away. There was no escape; then he took hold of a stick to strike me. I do not know what he saw: he throws away the stick and takes to flight. I thanked my God for it and continued on my way.

When good is not according to the will of God, it is not perfect.

Weary, I sat down and meanwhile I was praying, when a group of little girls who were skipping about came near and, seeing me, drew close to me. I asked them whether they knew who had created them; they looked at me as though I had said something utterly new.

“Do you not know that it was God?” (I said to one of them).

“Who is this person you are telling me about?”

Poor creatures! Moved with compassion, I tried to make them know my God, and how they ought to thank him for having brought them into the world. Oh! how I labored, and I would have wished them to understand everything in a flash! After I had been instructing them for a long while, some young women arrive with disheveled hair, and they rebuke me roughly, taking their little girls by the hand. I begged them to leave them with me. Oh! how many things they said to me! They heaped insults upon me and went away; but I thought within myself of a means of getting them back. Oh! how they moved me to compassion! I succeeded in having some of them, but not the ones I wanted.

Oh! how immense, my God, is your charity! Creatures so fierce, and yet you bear with them! Every minute you give me new lessons in patience, charity and humility. While I was reasoning thus, one of these fierce women comes, determined to beat me; but I was little frightened. As she raised her fist to reach me, behold, a shepherd coming out of a cottage seizes her and holds her back. He begged me to change my road; but what? I wanted to keep to my path and run. But she, having stopped to talk with the shepherd, made a thousand accusations against me and, screaming, threatened me. How terrible is the creature who has received benefits and, when she forgets, becomes a viper! So too, what she does with man she unhappily does with God, forgetful of the immense graces and favors received.

Meanwhile, moving further away, I heard nothing more; and I kept running with the assurance of doing the will of my God. I prayed and ran silently along my path, when I came upon a shepherd who greeted me by my name. My God, who can it be? He was not on my path, but very near it. He asked me to be so kind as to stop, for he had something to tell me.

“I cannot,” I tell him. And he: “It is my master who sends me to warn you that at the end of this road there are people who will trouble you not a little.”

I cast a glance at my path and see it beautiful and well traced.

“No! I will not stop, nor do I wish to listen to you.”

“Consider that I am the keeper of this road, and it is my duty to warn whoever is on it, so that he may not fall victim to those evildoers.”

I answered nothing; and he kept trying to come nearer. At last, in a severe tone, I told him to go away.

“But it is not possible! I pity you; I will not abandon you until you are safe.”

“My way is founded on solid ground and no one can enter it!”

The fierce man tries to set foot on it and slips, and went tumbling head over heels until he stopped at the bottom of a ditch. Oh! how many things he shouted at me! But I intoned the prayer of the Virgin and, without troubling myself, continued on my way.

A shepherd presents himself to me and begs me to go with him, for he has many sheep to tend and cannot do it alone, since they are very unruly.

“Who are you?”

“I come from very far away in search of you; the one who sends me is someone you know well. And he begins to tell me the name.

“I know no one!”

“You are mistaken!”

And insistently he begged me to go with him. Oh! how well he knew how to paint those plans of his and tried to color them vividly! But I kept looking at my path and saw that no change appeared in it. At last he insisted so much that, turning round, I told him severely that it was time to stop pestering me.

“So,” he said to me at last, “you allow those poor little sheep to go astray?”

And I, holding fast to my proof, (answered):

— When good is not according to the will of God, it is not perfect. What man has created out of his own head, to satisfy an ambition and make himself an object of admiration, does not last; his building will soon be thrown down.

He listened to me with a kind of sneer; my words pleased him little. He said:

“If you do not believe it is the work of the Lord, why do you not try to bring them onto your path?”

“You say it with your lips, but!…

Hearing this, he grows venomous, shouts and begins to call me names; he threatens to accuse me of having blasphemed because I have not spoken according to the doctrine of the Church.

“Do so, then! My judge is my Master!”

“Then who are you?”

“You see, O good shepherd, that you are mistaken, for I am a poor handmaid who can do nothing other than what my Master has commanded me.

He looks around, and then resumes: “Tell me, where is this Master of yours? After a long sigh: “Oh! do you not know him?”

At this answer he calls me a fool; and I see that my time is wasted. He turns away and leaves me.

Oh! my Love! this man wants to work and does not know for whom he works, nor where?

Folly of the ambitious man! He wants to be, he wants to do, and he accomplishes nothing, because he is off the path. 65.

A hard penalty to pay for the time lost in wishing to search into the secrets of God.

At last I found another shepherd, and this one was not on my path either, but a very beautiful one ran alongside it. When we were near, he asked me whether I would tell him something of what I knew about my God.

“I have nothing to tell; but I beg your charity to tell me where you come from and whether you have seen a shepherd to whom I was speaking and who did not understand me. He took me for something good, and evidently, being enlightened, he realized his mistake and drove me away, telling me that he did not understand my language.

But all this I said while walking. Stopping for an instant and marking down two words, (he said to me): “These will be for that shepherd.”

What can it be? Meanwhile he urged me to run along together with him.

“Thank you, I have no need of company, because I am used to going alone and because I have many things to set in order with my Lord.”

He said: “Do you see what these affairs of yours are?”

“I have no affairs of my own, because I am a poor handmaid to whom everything is commanded, step by step.”

He tried to persuade me that we too must cooperate a great deal, and that we must not claim to be directed by the Lord in everything.

“Very well, but I cannot give you so many reasons and explanations.”

He stops and tells me that he would like me to accept him as a worker in some field.

“If it were the will of God, I would call myself happy.”

At last he begs me that we stop for a moment. I look at my path and see that there is a large stone on it; I took this as if it wished to show me that I should stop. Seated on the stone, and he on another on his own road, he began to speak of God, of the beautiful graces that he possessed…, and that he had other sheep of his far advanced on the way of holiness. After much talking, almost in an instant he fell into ecstasy. I thought within myself: can it be true? I began to be afraid. When he had come back from the ecstasy, I asked him many questions: whether he had seen my God, whether He had said anything to him about me…

“Oh!” I exclaimed with a deep sigh “Blessed are you!”

And I almost felt like weeping from the great desire to be able to see my Lord too. But as soon as I asked him whether he had seen the Mother of God, he turned red and, stammering, answered me things that I could not understand. But meanwhile he changed the subject and wanted to go on telling me many things. I saw clearly that they had already happened to him; he told me others that were to come. Oh! how it pleased me! and on the other hand I felt something within, like fear. I began to ask him why he spoke to me so little of the most holy Virgin, and he made certain movements as though he wished to go into ecstasy again. Oh! I became ever more convinced that he was truly a servant of God. Speaking smoothly, it comes out that I ought to go with him and that he would obtain for me from God all the graces that he enjoyed. And he went on making me a great heap of promises. At last he said to me: “Many ways are mistaken because they do not have a guide truly as there should be.”.

Alas! this talk of his was sound doctrine, but beneath it I saw something. Seeing me thoughtful, he asks me why I take so much trouble, when I could at once free myself from every difficulty. My voice: “It is time to put an end to it!”

In a flash I got up and, without heeding anything else, I began to run. And behold, he did the same, but he could not enter my path.

A frightful animal comes toward me; beating its wings, it wanted to devour me. I screamed, and that shepherd, who was at some distance, said to me: “It serves you right!”.

And he encouraged the fierce beast to devour me. Oh! what? I called my angel: nothing! the most holy Virgin: nothing! Oh! I am lost!

But I did not want to ask the shepherd to come and free me, no!

While so fierce an animal made as if to devour me, it never came near enough to touch me.

I ran, and the other shepherd behind. Night was approaching, the din of this animal (was loud); at last I see it take a very high flight, and after a good while I could hardly see it. Oh! thank you, O my Lord!

But within me I felt great remorse and did not understand for what. As I went along, I made examination after examination, but I found nothing. It never came to my mind that I had stopped to sit on that stone. All of a sudden the great animal arrives with the large stone on its back and throws it down before me, and I, stepping over it, fled; and it took it up again and once more threw it on the path, giving me hard blows on the feet. But I paid no heed and went on all the while. At the end of the three times, I came to myself: “But this is the stone where I sat down!”

And the animal said to me in a terrible voice: “And so much time you have lost!”

What distress! weeping with all the strength I had and screaming: “Mercy, my God! And that shepherd, quite content, always at a certain distance, mocked me. Can he be a devil? a false shepherd? And all those things he told me…, the ecstasy that took place? In a flash these things passed through my mind. And that ugly animal went on rolling the stone in front of me, as if it had been a toy. At last, having sent it a long way ahead, it sits upon it (saying to me): “This way you will have to pass. This is the stone where you sat: you must make up for the time lost. As you stepped over it three times, so you could have done when you stayed still. And so you have lost many things. And now you are in my power until you have paid the penalty (you deserved) by listening to illusions.

And (the monster) always there, motionless! Oh! I am lost! How can it ever be? These things are told me by a monster! What palpitations! Can they be true? And the other kept coming nearer: “Make up your mind; and be sure that I will loosen these painful oppressions. I will give you the reason for them.”

And without my saying anything to him, he tried to guess. For a long while I did not answer him; at last, worn out by weeping and by the harm that beast was doing me with that stone, I turned to him: “Go, for you have nothing good: your illusions have brought me to this. I want nothing: only to fulfill the will of God, and nothing else! Away, away! go.”

But he: “This animal will devour you!”

“If it is the will of God, I am ready even for this.”

“Oh!” he cried “stop! I feel sorry for you.”

And he wanted to busy himself driving away that great animal, and showed great compassion for me.

“I repeat that I have no need of compassion. Go, for I seek something quite other than to be pitied by anyone at all.”

Oh! my God! this penance is well due to me: I will walk all night and weep until I have made up for the time lost and for the curiosity of wishing to search into your secrets. Oh! how difficult it is to master this wicked nature, which always seeks satisfactions! and when it cannot have any, it tries to join itself to the spirit in order to know and taste that consolation which in the things of God gives so much pleasure, but…!

That shepherd, tired of running after me, stopped to rest, and I saw him no more. My voice: “God wants you mortified in everything. He alone wants to be your satisfaction. That one was a pretender and a liar; what he did was all sorcery.

And I wept ever more. Meanwhile I walked on in the dark and, when I reached a certain point where I could no longer see, I heard only the noise made by the beast, which I always had with me together with the stone. All of a sudden, a great crash, and the stone was broken to pieces; each of these pieces gave off a burning stench with smoke. The beast vanished. Only, none of these pieces of stone lay on my path. The terror was dreadful! And all the while, as I walked, I looked to see whether any of these pieces were still rolling along: nothing! 66.

A purifying journey, between uncertain glimmers and stretches of total darkness: she is comforted by the holy Virgin.

The darkness grew ever deeper, because the night was far advanced. My strength was failing; but I had promised never to stop, and with lively resolutions. Never would I have stood still, except when it pleased my God. And I went on reciting the prayer of the most holy Virgin. I only commended myself to my angel not to allow me to stray from the path in so dark a night. Every so often I felt certain great thorns that gave me such sharp pain, but I did not dare to draw back my foot, so as not to avoid that suffering which perhaps my Lord had placed on that path on purpose, that I might do penance for the wrong I had committed.

At last I found myself knocking against a large rock; I lost my bearings and no longer knew what to do. I tried to clamber up by groping and, after going a little way, I was on the ground once more. What terror! I heard certain animals bellowing, which seemed to me to be great oxen. Oh! poor me, what distress! Where am I? After I had remained thus for a long while, a flash of lightning came and lit up my way.

I found myself in a most beautiful farmland, and my path well traced. The large rock was nothing other than a small mountain over which water flowed; and in the field there were great oxen sleeping with their keepers.

I had barely time to see, as best I could, all these things I have related, and once more (it grows) darker than before. I lost my strength; and moreover the sight I had had left me with a certain uncertainty whether I was not in the midst of those beasts. What did I do? I got down on my knees and made my way on all fours. Oh! my God! how long this night is! When will it please you to send a little light? not even the moon!

This said, behold another light, but of short duration; I could only see that I was walking rightly. The way was so ruinous that my legs and feet were all covered with sores. I could not see; I heard certain howls… Oh! poor me! My voice: “Keep walking like this, for you are going rightly!”

Oh! but this darkness frightens me! Day never broke; but can it be possible that a night must be so long? I could bear it no longer and began to weep aloud and to call my angel to come to my aid: nothing! And I went on clambering without understanding how or where I was.

A most vivid light let me see that that darkness was not of the night, but because I was in an immense cavern, and my path was in the midst of it; it was beautiful, but all varied: some stretches all paved with flints, others with thorn bushes and others with trees. How can there be, down here, in so dark a cavern, plants with fruits? Oh! what distress if I should stray on so rugged a road! Oh! what fear! a violent trembling seized me. My strength begins to fail me and I feel myself fainting. A voice comes near me and says to me: “I would gladly help you, but I do not know how. I too am in the dark and cannot understand you.”

“What distress!” I cried “Why do you not understand me? Who are you?”

“A shepherd who saw you at other times, and you moved me to compassion; but this time I feel no compassion. This road of yours is your own way: I find nothing to lean on in order to understand a road so lofty and mysterious.

“I tell you to have pity, if you are a shepherd, and of God!”

Nothing! And I could not understand where he was.

“Are you alone in this cavern? He answered me: “What cavern? I can see and it is not dark at all!

At last he told me to address my prayer to a shepherd who would be able to give a judgment on my darkness. My voice: “Obey! but nothing is for you.”

Running, I found him; at least I heard his voice.

He told me that he had seen a shepherd and that he had told him that a creature was in this cavern and was moaning.

“Is it you?” he said to me.

“And how do you see me, if I know no one?

“I know you well, and I must look at your path and then report to the one who sent me what there is in it of great and mysterious, and whether it is of the Lord or you are off the road, and whether into this cavern, furnished with delights but for you dark without the smallest light, it is the Lord who has brought you or the monster of darkness.

While he was speaking, I listened, but without stopping. I said to him: “Ah! of my path I am mistress, and a faithful handmaid of my Love. If he has brought me here into so painful a darkness, it can be for nothing else than to purge my negligences in working his fields; and if I feel myself fainting and am covered with sores, I know that I deserve it all. Clinging to the prayer of the Virgin, I run groping and weeping!

Having heard this, the good shepherd said to me in a faint voice: “Do you want help?”

“No!

And I heard another voice: it was the first one’s, who was also near the last. Here is what I heard: “I assure you that here man has nothing to do: it is all the work of God.

Meanwhile I trembled with fright, feeling myself fainting. The last one wanted to lift me up, urging me to stop, for the Lord wished it so; but I answered: “That shall never be!”

Moved with compassion, they would not have wished to go away, when the first, who understood little, withdrew, because he felt himself called to go to other souls who, according to him, were more intelligible; the other felt all the compassion for me, but I begged him to withdraw, because I was not worthy to have any creature who could relieve me. I thanked him and, with slow steps, partly on all fours, I went on.

I arrived at a spot where nothing else could be heard but a lovely murmur of water and of birds: in short, it was something…! Oh! if only I could refresh my sores a little with this water! I see in the distance a thread of light; I would have wished to run, but I had no more breath. Little was needed to reach it, when it moves away: ah! I am dying! I can hold out no longer! This said, collapsed on the ground, I prayed God that, if that was my last hour, he would take my soul and press it to his heart: into his hands I delivered it! And I lost consciousness.

A hand from paradise rouses me. As soon as it touches me, here I am revived. It is a great Lady, with a golden mantle, who says to me: “Rise!” and holds out to me something I know not what; and she said to me: “Eat!”

It was clear and shining. Oh! as soon as I recognized her I cried out: “Mother of my God, most holy Mary! Has Jesus abandoned me?”

“No! he is always close to you and is well pleased with your pains.

“But this darkness?” and this I said to her with joined hands, prostrate on the ground: “Rise!” she said to me». Sit down, for I must tell you very important things.

I sat down. Oh! what bliss! As soon as she had said two words, which contained a long discourse, she vanished. I remained on the illuminated path, full of strength, with a vigor that made me seem a giant. 67.

Never shall all the riches here below make me leave my Lord.

I got up to run, but the sores on my legs and body troubled me greatly. I entered a beautiful field, but very badly cultivated; a pleasant peasant woman came toward me and asked me what was the matter with me. Oh! I almost did not want to say, but she added once again: “Are you feeling unwell?”

“No!”

Only at her insistence did I tell her that I had certain sores on my legs and feet which would not let me walk. She looked at me with compassion.

“Come into my cottage; I have a certain ointment that will heal you.”

I looked at her, and then cast another glance at my path, which in no way led toward the cottage.

“Thank you! May God reward you for your charity, but I cannot stop.”

And I continued on my way. At last, having come near a brook, I sat down and meanwhile bathed my sores in that water. All of a sudden it came into my mind: Oh! my Crucified One did not have this relief for his innumerable wounds, and must I have it for this small portion? I immediately gave up this relief and walked on. Those sores which I had bathed and which burned me less, I at once tried to make sharper with stinging herbs. And all the while I asked pardon of my God.

I passed near a garden, magnificent for its flowers, graceful in its design; on every side handsome coats of arms could be seen, and here and there a guard. My path led straight into one of these. As soon as I had entered I found myself bewildered amid such a wealth of trees and fruits.

A guard comes up to me and roughly asks me where I am going, and tells me not to delay in leaving, because wandering people could not enter there. What was I to do? I tried to persuade him, but there was no reasoning that could convince him. That was my path and I could not leave it.

“In the name of my Lord, let me pass!”

“No! go back!”

Then I said to him: “Never shall I do that, because I have orders to come here.

“Who are you?” he asked me.

I am a handmaid of the Lord, who has sent me here.

While the dispute went on, I commended myself to my God, that he would change my path. No! A great Lady arrives, all dressed in brocade; she had with her a large dog; and yet she comes near me and tells me to go back, making as if to use force and drive me out. My Crucified One! thus were you driven out by Annas!

“Let me go on! I promise you that I will not harm you in anything, but will pass through in haste.”

“No!”

They set the dog on to drive me away. Nothing! the beast does not move. The woman wanted to give me alms and told me that she felt great pity for me.

“Thank you! I have no need of alms, because my Lord is very rich and lets me lack nothing. Ah! let me pass!”

Moved with compassion, she looked me over from head to foot and then begged me to sit down, for she wished to speak with me.

“Your charity and kindness in all that you ask of me would deserve my compliance, but I cannot: night is coming on and I must withdraw.

With a compassionate gesture she gave me leave to pass, telling the guard to accompany me. All of a sudden I find her close to me once again: “Stop!”

“No!”

“If you stay with me I assure you I will make you happy. Do you see?”

“Never shall all the riches and beauties here below make me leave my Lord.”

“Oh! who ever is this Lord of yours?”

“You will know him, but you will not possess him.”

“What heresies!” said the woman — “This is an ignorant bigot: let her go!

Thus I remained free and, running, I thought: poor unhappy woman: she does not know my God! What distress! And, praying much and weeping, I asked the Lord to give light to that poor soul, who grieved me so much. After much praying, my voice: “Your prayers will be granted and you will see the woman again, no longer proud but humble, and she will be in search of me. 68.

What a mystery! This said, a thick fog spreads over my path; I could no longer tell where I was. Oh! indescribable distress! How shall I ever avoid stumbling? and shall I be on my way? I was afraid to stop. O my Crucified One! where are you? It was strange: this fog was for me alone; all who passed spoke to me, and I asked them whether they were shepherds and where they came from; whether they had seen my road; and I spoke incoherently. Where can I be? Some mocked me, some called me ignorant. And that fog grew ever thicker. At last I stumbled on a large stone and fell with my face upon it.

“Thank you, my dear Crucified One! Oh! how you must have suffered when your most divine face remained imprinted on that large stone!”

Oh! how much pleasure I felt in thinking that I too had had to suffer in part a pain of my God! And so I went on groping my way; and when every so often I heard people running who kept telling me they were in the light, without the least suffering of darkness, oh! what distress I felt!

The fog cleared and I found myself right at the top of a precipice, without understanding where I was; not even a human creature could be seen. My road came to an end on that summit and no further track could be seen. Why? How could one go down that precipice? For this reason I did not even think of looking whether my path was there. I stood thus motionless. The loud tossing of the waters could be heard and the flapping of some great bird. I stood still a long while; at last one of these animals comes near me, takes me by the hem of my garment and drags me down that precipice. After a few meters, seeing myself dragged thus and entangled in those bushes, I screamed with all my might, calling my God, my angel, to help me: and no one!

At last, standing on my path, I thanked that animal and thought: how ignorant I am and incapable of anything! for I could have looked to see whether it was my duty, too, to descend so rugged a mountain. But hardly had I finished this reasoning of mine when a great fear seized me: why descend and not climb, when I shall have arrived down there? Oh! my Savior, ah! do not allow me to have to go down to the very bottom of this rugged mountain! I found a stone near a tree and sat down. So I must go down and no longer climb? It is true that I know myself well as an unworthy creature. And, weeping bitterly, I fell asleep on the stone.

All that is not of God is consumed upon the earth.

Awakened by a sweet call, like Samuel (cf. 1Sam 3:4-10), I answered: “Here I am, my Lord, ready to fulfill your most holy will!

But what a wonder! I no longer found myself (where I had been before). I turned my gaze this way and that: I saw nothing but charming groups of peasant women who were working the land and joyfully singing the praises of Mary. And their work was beautiful: there were fruits and flowers of every kind, and other things besides. Oh! how well it is worked! I went up to them and, with all courtesy, they asked me who I was and how I came to be in that field of theirs, where no living creature has ever entered.

“And are you alone? Why do you not answer our questions?” they said.

“You are right, good young women: forgive me. I am a poor handmaid of my Lord and He himself has brought me here.

They answered: “Who is this master of yours?”

“What, do you not know him?”

“No!”

“Do you not know God?”

“We have never heard him named.”

“But you are joking! I do not believe it.”

They rose from their work.

“We tell you that we know nothing!

“But tell me, I pray you: who do you believe has made these beautiful fruits flourish, if not my Lord? It is He who, with his grace, has made all these delightful plants grow.

They began to make fun of me and to tell me that they have a master who is very skillful and knows agriculture very well, and that it is for him they work.

“So you work for man and not for God? All that is not of God is consumed upon the earth.

One of them was looking at me attentively, and said to me: “Teach me these beautiful things! I feel within my heart a force that drives me to come with you.

Would that she had never said it! All the others (began) to scream and wanted to make themselves heard by the master, so that he would not allow it. But the young woman, nimble, leaps over a bush and gets out.

“Oh! if you others too would follow me, it would be very good: what great things you would understand!

But there was no way. Only one! and with her I continued on my way. And gently I instructed her. How blessed I was! Only, I kept thinking of those poor creatures I had left behind. She looked at me and said to me: “Why are you so thoughtful?”

“When I think of those who have remained, I feel a terrible pang.”

“Let us go back,” she said to me, and you will tell them what you have told me. Surely they will come.

My voice: “Onward! otherwise you will lose this one too.”

“No!” I said to her “the Lord will take care of those.”

This said, I noticed that she thought she had done wrong and was hesitating whether to go back; when a voice was heard calling us loudly. She, turning round, said to me: “It is those companions of mine who beg us to wait for them.

My voice: “Stop!”

These poor creatures came, telling me that the master had driven them out rudely. I welcomed them all, and began to make them understand how the world pays, and that God alone gives the just reward and never abandons.

“Yes, what I tell you is the truth; you will see: He assures you of bliss for an eternity.

At last, after long walking, a bell tower was seen in the distance.

“You see, that shows me the dwelling of my God!

They ran with me in haste and, as soon as we had entered, we found a good religious, whom I at once asked to help me bring those poor creatures to safety. This poor man busied himself with all his might and tried to set them on the right road and to make them understand who had created them. Then a great uproar is heard. My God, who can it be? Oh! terrible sight! it was the master who was coming in search of them! But, with God’s help, in a flash they slipped out of the sight of so horrible a man. But he came before me demanding an account of them. I answered him that I had seen them carried off by a great Lord, and that I could tell him nothing else. He asked me in which direction I had seen them, and I answered him: “On the right path!”

He understood nothing. Enraged: “I will find them!” and he goes out.

Oh! my sweet Love! Thrown on the ground before that altar, I fervently commended them to my God, when they come back, so happy to have given their whole selves to the Lord, and they confess to me that they already feel that they love him greatly. What a consolation was mine!

The good priest assured me that they would become good and holy servants of the Lord. And, having set them on my path, I taught them to walk without straying.

Souls that remain children, without freedom of spirit, because too bound to human guidance.

Along the way we found a very elderly shepherd. He wanted to stop us and to know many things; but, paying no heed, we went on our way; and he followed us, grumbling that we were without charity. Then, having heard this, I stopped, for fear that he might need something, so as to help him. But what was our surprise! Having taken off his cloak and seized one of these dear creatures by the arm, he wanted to carry her off with him, saying that he had accounts to settle with her; but the poor young woman screamed loudly, for in reality she had nothing to settle with him, because, to everyone’s amazement, no one knew what accounts he could ever have. Enraged, he accused her of having to fulfill obligations on behalf of certain souls she had never known. What terror! I held the dear creature firmly and in a severe tone commanded that shepherd to go away. But the struggle lasted a long time.

When my God gave us a moment’s time, just as he was about to compose himself, and we fled, what terrible things he said to us! But we went ever further away and at last he was seen no more.

As we talked it over, we came to understand that it was a debt of his own; that he would have liked to find persons onto whom he could transfer it. What a terrible stratagem! The poor girl was all upset, because she saw that he maintained the matter with such assurance.

Oh! how difficult it is to be able to make sure of having in everything a guide who sets out the facts with certainty and guides according to the right path, which (is the one that leads) to fulfilling the will of God! This shepherd had many flocks to govern and, among these, at one time there was also this poor girl. She told me that he had bound her strongly with certain ways of his own, by which he knew very well how to convince. But the Lord, who takes great care of his brides, defended her and set her free. How happy this poor creature was!

Unfortunately there are some of these poor souls, so bound that they cannot take a step unless they hear their guide, even in the most trifling things, and, thus bound, they do not dare to take a step without first having advice. I believe that it is a great good, but too much of it binds the soul in such a way that, without realizing it, it comes to share in something human, and that is why they make no progress, because the material part hinders it.

Everything must be ordered; above all in the way of the Lord everything is so well marked out, and the action must be pure and spotless. But when we put too much eagerness into having guidance continually in every step and, I repeat, not so much in order to be well directed as to have the consolation of being pitied, etc., I do not find it a good thing.

And so these souls remain children, who in order to walk need leading-strings to hold them up so that they can move. And so they remain stunted, they remain hardened for the whole of their life, and no one, however learned he may be, can succeed in straightening them. Oh! what a pity! a servant of the Lord, a son of Saint Francis, once said to me, that in these there is nothing good.

How much grief this poor soul caused me, who ran with me and, so timid, was always afraid of erring. She wanted to make a thousand plans, but then she would stop and go back, always with a great palpitation of being outside the way of the Lord. A thousand guides are not enough for such souls to assure them that they are doing well, but at every little pebble they stop and are afraid, and more often than not they go back, because for them the way of suffering is not a good sign for walking in the way of perfection: one must stay among the roses and never with the thorns; the smallest things give them great annoyance and they make terrible complaints about them.

After much reasoning, with the help of God, she was convinced and began to grow strong in suffering. 69.

A worker of the eleventh hour — The art of trading well with the talents received.

Oh! how great a consolation I felt, because I hoped to be able to lead her with me! But, as soon as I wanted to point out my path to her, my voice: “You must never do it, because it is not for her: all that you have obtained would immediately be lost.

What was I to do? I thought of seeking good people and putting her in safety, leading her along the way she had entered upon. While I was thinking thus, a little old woman came up to me and invited me to see her fields, which were beautiful and full of fruit. She begged me to accept one; but I refused it at once, pointing to the young woman I had with me. And so she graciously gave her some to eat, but the girl told me softly that they were very insipid, that they tasted of nothing. What? I was saying within myself: so beautiful, and they have no flavor? My voice: “These are like those works which have nothing good but the outward appearance: everything they do they color up thoroughly so that it may be seen, but they are without goodness; everything remains swallowed up by vainglory.

But the little old woman, having gone a stretch of the road with us, was about to take her leave, when she took me tightly by the hand: weeping, she implored me to take her with me.

“This cannot be: you are in a delightful garden, where all delights are found, and I have nowhere to lay my head (cf. Mt 8:20).

And pressing me ever more urgently, she begged me to take her as the last of the workers. I looked at her, and she moved me to such compassion that I let myself be persuaded to take her. Along the way I asked her why she had resolved to leave her delights and come with me. Weeping, she told me of the terrible pains she suffered, because in that house there was a shepherd who (kept her) bound to certain wishes of his which she clearly felt were in no way satisfying to her heart; his doctrine was a continual exhortation to self-preservation. Poor man! — I kept saying to myself — he must do it out of ignorance.

This poor creature went on speaking, when we heard a loud tramping of feet, and turning round: what could it be? It is he, coming to make her turn back; but she cuts across his path and takes to flight. I do not know what I felt within me, for fear that he would believe I was the cause of that flight. I begged the one who had remained with me to say nothing, for pity’s sake. As soon as he was near me, he looked at me with a severe gaze: «Where is the one who was here with you?

«Good shepherd, many people (are seen) passing by, men and women.»

But he: «I mean the one who was in that castle, who went away from me together with you.»

«Well,» I said to him, «I saw her running along her way, but she told me nothing of where she was going.

More furious than ever, he threatened to beat me. I was afraid for that worker I had with me, lest she should see this and take to flight as well. But no! She took up my defense and answered the shepherd with energy, as he deserved, yet always with reserve and charity. Meanwhile I was thinking to myself how that little old woman had run: truly she seemed a young girl. Where can she have gone to take refuge? At last he saw that he could learn nothing; he gave us a good scolding and left us.

I was thinking where I might place this one whom I kept with me. Arriving at a small hut, where the flock lacked a guide, I was able to leave her there and to go in haste where I felt the need of other creatures to be saved was urging me, but always thinking of the poor little old woman. Then a poor man comes toward us and tells us that that lady was waiting for us and that we should quicken our pace to reach her. And so it happened. As soon as she saw us, I cannot describe the joy and the questions, one tangled with another, that she put to us to know how it had gone and what would happen.

«Nothing!» I answered her. «In whatever we try to do for God we always have extraordinary help.

Poor thing! She understood little of this language. One could see that the grace of the Lord was at work, but she knew nothing of it. I tried to instruct her well, and she showed herself very content. Oh! how, though she was old, when she was left in a field at the head of so many workers, how well she made those cultivators work! Here one could very well apply the parable of our Lord: that the last would have a greater reward than the first (cf. Mt 20:16). She, old as she was, did more than a young one cold with a sluggish spirit, one of those who do not work for love and with eagerness to give this to the Beloved, and so seek to lay up treasures for eternal life (cf. Mt 6:20). A soul that knows how to trade well with the talents that Jesus gave her, even if she had only one, knows how to do so much that she multiplies them by hundreds. And so many who have the good fortune of having them in abundance are not capable of gaining others, but with their indolence end by losing everything (cf. Mt 25:14-30). Oh! how many of these we have to see continually!

A hard struggle in defense of the workers.

Alone, I was running where I said I was called. Oh! how horrible was the sight! On every side of that field there were evildoers singing with all their strength: they wanted to destroy and drive out the workers, and make a slaughter of them. But, as soon as I arrived, I cried: «Stop!»

And these poor creatures, all around, were shrieking and calling for help. When these men saw me, they mocked my words and went on devastating worse than before. My God, see what these men are doing! What must I do to prevent it, since they will hear nothing? This said, others come out and join them. I no longer knew how to save these creatures, because they seemed so many ferocious lions; the calumnies and the rumors were many, so much so that for an instant I saw myself lost. But no! With firmness and without using the least violence, I sat down; they came before me to seize me, but turning to the leaders, I said to them: «Why do you wish to outrage me so and drive me out of a field that is my property?

«Who gave it to you?»

«My Lord!»

«What is his name?»

«Oh! why do you put such questions to me?»

«Because we do not know him.»

«Then are you Jews?»

«What?» they answered, in a tone as if I had insulted them.

«Well, if you are not, surely you must know my Lord.»

They look at one another and then, in a sardonic manner, tell me that they will no longer put up with my chatter, but that I should withdraw. What must I do?

«Fine indeed! You tell me to go away; if your lord had given you a jewel to guard, how would you act if a thief came, or people who wanted to take possession of it, what would you do?

«Certainly, our duty would be never to yield.»

«Well then, here is our case!»

With charity, but with energy, I said to the workers: «Do not draw back, but stand firm! The ground is yours.»

But how they raged, not against the workers, but against me! At last they went away. But terrible threats they made me, when they took their revenge and wove certain intrigues by which I found myself so cast down that I felt myself fainting. So subtly had they known how to weave the calumnies that no human creature could ever have uncovered such cunning.

«Oh! my Love, I have no more life! — Have you not mine?»

Battered and scourged on every side, I begged my Father for mercy and pity. I had nothing to lean on in an arid field with only sharp thorns: to this they had reduced me. And they were full of joy for the victory they had won. My mind could no longer find a point on which to rest.

Exhausted, I threw myself on the ground in the midst of these terrible thorns, but the pain was beyond compare. Is your work, then, to be destroyed by such fierce evildoers? And weeping, face down on the ground, I went on making loud laments. Will everything be lost? My voice: «Arise! My work shall never suffer from it; it shall triumph ever more!»

I sat on the ground and was still weeping, when I see my hands all bloodied and great pains in my knees, which also had certain sharp thorns in them. What was I to do? Wherever I turned my gaze I saw nothing but the same field, whose end I could not manage to see; and so arid! only dry great thorns that kept me from moving, because I felt horrible pricks from them. There was no longer any trace of a path, not even in the midst of these terrible points. Where am I? Will there be no more hope for me of getting out of here? My God! have pity on your slave! why have you condemned me so terribly? I know that my negligences in your service, alas, deserve worse; but I am dying of sorrow for having displeased you; my breast is breaking with sorrow, my hands and body are all pricks! Oh! my God! I know only too well that this loathsome body is the cause of my having lost you.

At this thought I rose and gathered a good number of these thorns, and with all my strength I set about beating myself fiercely.

My voice: «Stop!» it cried to me.

And fainting, I let myself fall to the ground. How long I remained there I do not know. I heard a voice, so sweet, that said to me: «My beloved, arise!»

And it was as if he had taken me by the hand. I opened my eyes: «Oh! my Love! I have no more life!»

He answered me: «Have you not mine?»

Oh! with what boldness I rose! Having knelt, I did not dare to stand up; with joined hands I begged him not to leave me any longer in this devastated field, where I had been led by people who have done so much harm to your (slave).

«Take me with you, I can no longer remain here below!

«There is still too much time,» he indicated to me; and he disappeared.

And I, seated on the ground, looked at my wounds, in which I no longer felt the least pain. Night was drawing near.

«My Good, you have left me here alone! Is there no path to go out by?

So saying, I rose. Here is my path! After a few steps, no more thorns, but how beautiful! it was a delight of paradise. I met a gracious young woman, and she wanted to stop me to tell me…: what? I was afraid to stop, but (I had) a desire to hear. The first word she said to me was: «Rejoice, for those persecutors have been put to scorn and to flight. They have left the field; and you will see it again far more beautiful than before.

I said to her: «Do me the charity of coming with me and telling me.

The gracious young woman obliged me, and along the way told me all that had happened to them: while they believed themselves victorious, there came a person who was well informed and brought everything to light, and full of shame they went away. One of them, however, the fiercest, said that he will never abandon his opinion and declares that he will always molest us.

Always on the path traced by God, without yielding to difficulties, nor to flatteries or threats.

With my usual calm I was running along the way, when the sky grew dark and on every side rumblings of thunder were heard. At last I was able to find a hut to shelter in, and I felt a keen desire for it; I did not take heed whether my way led to that cottage. No! At last, moved by fear of the lightning, I was about to turn aside and make for the hut, when I notice that I can no longer move a step. What could it be? why this? I looked around and saw that my path was marked straight ahead and that, to reach the cottage, I would have had to turn aside. What did I do? I set out on the straight path and ran well along it.

Oh! poor me! What then was I doing? perhaps in that dwelling there would have been wicked people?

«No!» answered my voice. «Why were you trying to flee this thunder?»

Without uttering anything else, I began to weep bitterly, and within me (I felt) a sorrow so deep that I could not utter a word, on seeing the goodness and mercy of my God and my ever-present ignorance and ill-founded fear, in seeking human means to shelter myself from the storm. Oh! how is it that I learn and yet always fall back again! Oh! what pain! my God, forgive me!

As soon as I could utter a word, I kept repeating: Forgive your slave, my God!

Having risen, in the midst of so terrible a tempest I ran on; I thought of nothing but my God.

The water poured down in torrents, but attentive to my path I went forward in that darkness of the night and of the dark sky! I heard a voice calling me and telling me to stop. No! — I kept saying to myself — It shall never be! But this person, drawing near and with compassionate words, begged me to come to him, for he would show me a flock that he wished to entrust to me. I looked at my path, and it marked the way straight ahead.

«No! good shepherd; I am in haste and I am not permitted to come.»

So (I said to him), running. And he kept following me. I did all I could to persuade him not to come, because I felt sorry for him; and in any case he would have obtained nothing. But the darkness did not allow me to see him; I only heard his voice. At last, seeing him insist so much, I asked him kindly who he was and who had sent him.

«A good lady, who is at the head of this scattered flock, and who is no longer able to put it in order again.

«What can I do about it?» I answered him.

«And yet she says that the Lord wills that you come to help her.»

«She is mistaken. I tell you that neither she nor you can understand who I am, and that is why you have made a mistake.»

«How can that be?» he said to me. «Are you not called by this name?»

«Yes, the name is mine, but as to the capacity, and what you believe me capable of, you are mistaken, because I am capable of nothing; because, a poor slave, I have nothing else and know how to do nothing else but the will of my Master; and for this reason I cannot come, for, being directed elsewhere, I must go where I am directed.

Then he flew into a rage: «What! have I not told you that I am a shepherd of souls and that I come in search of you because the Lord so wills? And you make fun of me! This shall never be!

I still saw my path straight ahead; I had to run until I saw it turn or the way stop. «What am I to do? I must obey my Master.»

«This is an insolent answer, because the Master speaks through my mouth!»

I set about calming him: «In the darkness of this night, in the midst of such a tempest, I beg you with joined hands to turn to some other creature, skillful and truly capable, and to leave me in peace. I implore you.»

In an altered voice: «This shall never be, no! I intend to stop you.»

«It shall never be!»

It was a very curious thing. He would have liked to enter my path to seize me, and he could not find it; he kept toiling, but in vain; and I ran on ever faster. Because of the darkness of the night he could not see me; at last he could be heard continually stumbling and falling and getting up again.

«The day will come when you will find yourself sorry for not having stopped.»

No! I kept repeating within myself, and I kept quite silent, and walked on as fast as I could. Morning was approaching, and already, on turning round, I saw him, not clearly; I could make out the person, but he had remained very far behind. When it had grown lighter, I recognized him. Alas! a shepherd of such worth, poor me! what will happen to me for not having stopped? My God, if it is you who have so traced the road for me!… What can it be? The sky darkens and, without my noticing it, I find myself — where? in a delightful garden where there was nothing but delightful plants and fruits and flowers. Oh my Love! how beautiful is what you have created for ungrateful man! and I, more than any other, am so wretched and so little capable of serving you! Oh! useless slave!

As I said this, a cultivator appeared to me and asked me who had brought me to that place. And I, frankly: «I do not know!»

Then he set about attacking me, telling me that no human person had ever penetrated into that place.

«Oh!» I exclaimed. «How can that be, when I see such beautiful cultivation, with so many well-tended plants? Are you not the cultivator?»

«No! to you — he answered me — I need give no account!»

I asked his pardon and went away, always on my path.

But he, grumbling, ran after me. At last he cried out loudly to me: «Stop!»

He did not want me to go on crossing that garden any longer; but I paid no heed to anything; always forward! A terrible fright: he unleashed a herd of lions and, provoking them, sent them toward me. Oh! how I shrieked! I called on my angel and on the most holy Virgin, on my God…: but nothing! Already I saw myself lost, when he stopped them and, halting me, told me that I had stolen a great quantity of goods and money from him.

«What?» I answered him. «Since I do not know your dwelling, why do you say this to me? Let me go, and I ask your pardon again for having passed through your beautiful countryside, or rather garden; but I did not take even a leaf from a tree. I did nothing but bless the Most High for so beautiful and magnificent a creation. Ah! stop those lions and leave me in peace.»

«Never!» he answered me. «This accusation is true and you will have to suffer the penalty for it. A horrendous theft! be ashamed of yourself for once!»

And he went on with other insulting words. But I no longer knew what course to take. Those lions went on roaring, and I feared and trembled more and more. At last I see that they withdraw. And he falls silent, as if he had seen people coming.

Grave accusations of theft, of embezzlement, and of discontent among the workers, of not having her papers in order.

I was walking and thinking of what had happened, which was so engraved in my mind. After a few steps a lady stops me and gives me such a severe look. Having come near, she tells me that I have stolen: that I had better see about withdrawing as soon as possible, because there were people who wanted to come and do me harm, making me pay for the robbery I had committed.

«But how? where have I ever stolen? Either these people are mistaken, or they have wished to cast upon me what belongs to others.

Oh! the more I thought, the less I could unravel this painful tangle. At last another shepherd stops me and threatens me, telling me that an abyss of accusations had been made against me and that I was to answer what he was about to tell me: when I hear him too tell me that I had stolen and that I was still continually stealing, and that I permitted many scandals in the fields entrusted to me, and that the workers were tired of being so badly (treated), and that I spent their earnings wherever I pleased.

«Oh!» I exclaimed thus. «How? and where?»

But he went on, and for a good two hours after that, recounting all that they had put together. Robbed here and there, he pointed at me from every side. At last he told me that I did not want to bind myself to anything, and that I liked to lead a life without ties, and that I never sought to have a sound tie with my superiors; and lastly, that this was necessary in order to work the fields well. My God! He said moreover that I was on very close terms with one of the highest of these shepherds.

Hearing this, I wished to step in to defend, not myself, but one who was not (present), and I began to say: «How can this agree with what you say, that is, that I want no one, and then that I am on good terms with the greatest of the shepherds?»

Oh! would that I had never said it! He raged more than ever and ordered me to be silent and listen; I did not delay to obey and to set before my mind the event of my Savior before Annas; all that was lacking was for me to receive the slap from the servant! (cf. Mt 26:63; Jn 18:22). What I receive is always as nothing to me. My Love, my Beloved and Master! why do you spare this your servant the slap? why do they not treat me worse? Oh mercy! Thinking thus, I lost attention; and he was preaching, but I understood little of it. He noticed my distraction and rebuked me: «Pay attention, answer what I say!»

What could I do, I who had understood nothing, or at least very little? I became confused and limited myself to saying that the documents I hold are very different from what he was saying. Again he went on saying many calumnies. Still I understood little of it, because my Lord was occupying me with heavenly discourses.
